This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain</term> <note>The public domain consists of all the creative work to which no exclusive intellectual property rights apply. These rights may have expired, been forfeited, or be inapplicable.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia</term> <note>From the Latin *marginalis*, these are marks, comments, or doodles made by previous readers in the margins of a page, providing a historical record of how the book was used.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file - a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## **Usage guidelines**

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, <term>optical character recognition</term> <note>Often abbreviated as OCR, this is the technology used to convert images of text into a format that a computer can read and search.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. # TO THE KIND READER

## THE BRESCIAN EDITORS.

Theological writings, which commonly circulate under the name of **DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE** <note>Dionysius was a judge of the Areopagus in Athens converted by St. Paul. While these influential mystical texts were long attributed to him, modern scholars identify the author as a 5th-century writer known as Pseudo-Dionysius.</note>, and indeed belong to Christian antiquity, were published quite late—specifically in the 15th, 16th, and 17th centuries—by the presses of Florence, Antwerp, and Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note>. Furthermore, Antonio Zatta published these same works in Venice <note>original: "Venetiis"</note> in the year 1757 in Greek, and with Corderius <note>Balthasar Corderius (1592–1650) was a Jesuit scholar famous for his translations of Greek Church Fathers into Latin.</note> as the Latin translator. This Venetian edition surpassed all previous ones—even those of Antwerp and Paris—not only for the sake of its accuracy, but also because it was enriched with variant readings taken from a manuscript <term>Codex</term> <note>A "codex" is a hand-written book from the ancient or medieval period, rather than a printed one.</note> in the Library of St. Mark <note>The famous Bibliotheca Marciana in Venice.</note>.

However, at the present time, if one considers the needs of scholars, the copies of these Works that are available here and there are very rare and indeed of a great price. Therefore, we have resolved [to publish] these same Works exactly as the most faithful Corderius rendered them into Latin, and with skill— 

<summary>This preface by the Brescian editors introduces a new edition of the works of Dionysius the Areopagite, citing the scarcity and high cost of previous reputable editions like the 1757 Venetian version.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysius the Areopagite, Balthasar Corderius, Antonio Zatta, Venetian edition, Brescian editors, theological manuscripts, Bibliotheca Marciana</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>Continuing from the bottom of Page III, completing the sentence regarding the Venetian printer Antonio Zatta and his edition of the works of Dionysius the Areopagite.</meta>

...[the most] skilled <note>The Latin text here is a fragment, "-tissimus," the end of a superlative adjective likely meaning "most skilled" (peritissimus) or "most famous" (celebratissimus), referring to the printer Antonio Zatta mentioned on the previous page.</note> Venetian printer produced, we now bring forth once more into the light in a more convenient format and at a very modest price. Whether we have acted inopportunely in this matter, let fair judges of such things decide. But if, by their judgment, we understand that our undertaking was not ill-timed, then we shall take heart to faithfully reproduce, under the modest format of this volume, other theological writings of Christian antiquity <note>The "Church Fathers" or early Christian theologians from the first few centuries of the Church.</note>, which until now have been sought in vain by most people, either because of the scarcity of copies <term>exemplarium</term> <note>In the context of early printing, an "exemplar" refers to an individual physical copy of a book.</note> or because of their great price.

---

<summary>The Brescian editors conclude their preface by explaining their goal: to provide affordable and portable editions of rare ancient theological texts, starting with Dionysius. They hope the success of this volume will allow them to reproduce further works of Christian antiquity that are currently too expensive or rare for most scholars.</summary>

# ON THE CELESTIAL HIERARCHY

---

## CHAPTER I.

### Dionysius the Priest to Timothy, his fellow-priest.

Every divine illumination, which according to the Father's goodness flows out in various ways to those things governed by providence, remains simple; and not only this, but it also unites those who are illuminated. <note>original: *simplicem... unificare*. This reflects the author's Neoplatonic view that while God’s light reaches many different people and things, the light itself remains one (simple) and its purpose is to pull us back from our many distractions into a single union with God.</note>

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER

1. It teaches that all spiritual light and grace is derived from God the Father to us, and joins us with God.
2. Having called upon Christ, he proposes to interpret the celestial Hierarchies from the Scriptures: which, although they admit a manifold figurative sense, always have a simple literal sense. <note>In medieval theology, "literal sense" refers to the direct meaning intended by the author, while the "figurative" or "spiritual" sense finds deeper symbolic meanings behind the words.</note>
3. It shows that celestial and spiritual things, for the sake of our understanding, are described in Scripture by material figures; it suggests a method and reason for how our mind can rise from those physical descriptions to celestial contemplations.

<margin>
Section 1.
James 1:17.
Every illumination of Scripture is from God, and leads to God.
</margin>

**E**very good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights: <note>original: *Patre luminum*. This is a direct quote from the New Testament, James 1:17.</note> moreover, every outpouring of illumination moved by the Father, overflowing bountifully into us, once again, like a unifying power, [leads us back upwards...]

<summary>This page introduces the treatise on the Celestial Hierarchy, establishing that all spiritual knowledge and "illumination" comes from God the Father. It explains that the author will use the Bible's physical descriptions of angels to help the human mind grasp higher, spiritual truths.</summary>

<keywords>Dionysius the Areopagite, Timothy, Celestial Hierarchy, Divine Illumination, Father of Lights, Scriptural Interpretation, Spiritual Ascent</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the "Celestial Hierarchy." The previous page ended by quoting James 1:17, explaining that all light comes from God. This page concludes that thought and begins Section 2, which focuses on Christ as the source of enlightenment and the necessity of using symbols to understand divine truths.</meta>

-># SAINT DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE<-

<margin>Romans 11:36.</margin>
...by calling us back to higher things, [this light] simplifies us and turns us toward the unity of the gathering Father and to a deifying simplicity. <note>original: *deificam simplicitatem*. In this mystical context, "simplicity" refers to being undivided or focused solely on God, rather than being scattered by worldly distractions.</note> For "from Him and to Him are all things," as the sacred word says.

<margin>Section 2. John 1:9. Access to the Father through Christ. <note>The original margin notes John 1:8, but the text quotes verse 9.</note></margin>

## CHAPTER II.

### How divine and heavenly things are aptly explained even through dissimilar signs.

->SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.<-

*1. He provides the structure of this work. 2. He warns that the figures used to describe heavenly and spiritual things are dissimilar to the realities themselves; at the same time, he addresses an objection and explains why it was more beneficial for these heavenly things to be depicted through the forms of lowly things rather than noble ones. 3. He shows that there are two modes of <unclear>sacred</unclear> description: one through similar figures, the other through dissimilar ones. Just as certain things are predicated of God through affirmations and others through negations, he states that negations are <unclear>superior</unclear> to affirmations, and that "clashing" similarities are more suited for raising our minds toward the truth. 4. He teaches that something good can be gathered from all things, and explains how passions like anger, desire, and similar traits are to be understood when they are attributed to Angels. 5. He shows how even God himself is sometimes named in the Scriptures after the highest things, sometimes after middle things, and sometimes even after the lowest things.*

---

Then, the celestial Hierarchies must be celebrated according to their mystical explanation in the Oracles <note>original: "Oraculis," a term Dionysius uses to refer to the Holy Scriptures as the spoken word of God</note>. Finally, we must state in what sacred forms the sacred writings sketch out these celestial orders, and to what kind of simplicity <note>A state of spiritual focus or unity, moving away from complex physical images</note> one ought to be led through those forms, so that we do not—like the common folk—<note>The text cuts off here, but Dionysius is beginning to warn against taking biblical descriptions of angels (like having wings or many eyes) too literally.</note>

<margin>What irrationality is.</margin>

...ointment, and even as a **cornerstone**. I will even add what seems the most lowly and absurd of all: for those skilled in divine things have handed down that He even fashioned for Himself the appearance of a **worm** <note>original: "vermis." Rather, divine things are celebrated both through the most true **negations** <note>original: "negationibus." <margin>§ 1. The goal of Hierarchy.</margin>
The goal of Hierarchy, then, is to be as like as possible to God and to be joined to Him. Having God as the guide of all sacred science and activity, and by looking constantly upon His most divine beauty, a Hierarchy expresses Him as much as possible. Therefore, he who speaks of "Hierarchy" designates a certain holy arrangement altogether—an image of the original divine beauty—which celebrates the mysteries of its own enlightenment in holy and primary orders and sciences, and is conformed, as far as is right, to its own principle.

</margin>
All inanimate things, by the very fact that they exist, participate in Him; for the "being" of all things is the Divinity which transcends all being. Living things, however, share in that same life-giving power which is above all life; while those beings that are endowed with reason and spirit share in the self-perfect and pre-perfect wisdom that exists beyond all human reason and intelligence. It is clear, therefore, that those natures are closest to the Divinity which participate in it in many different ways.

**A**s to how many and of what sort the arrangements of the super-celestial beings <note>original: "essentiarum" — literally "essences" or "beings"</note> are, and in what manner their sacred orders are initiated, I consider that only the divine Principle <note>original: "principatum" — referring here to God as the source and ruler</note> by whom they are consecrated knows this exactly. Therefore, we shall say nothing of our own accord, but having been taught those angelic visions seen by the holy Theologians <note>original: "Theologis" — referring to the biblical authors who recorded their visions of heaven</note>, we will set them forth as best we can.

<margin>The meaning of Seraphim and Cherubim.</margin>
...are interpreted as either **Fire-makers** <note>original: "Incensores"</note> or **Warmers** <note>original: "Calefacientes"</note>; and the **Cherubim** as a **Fullness of Knowledge** or an **Outpouring of Wisdom**. It is with good reason, therefore, that this first of the celestial Hierarchies <term>Hierarchies — the sacred order or government of angels</term> is administered by the most sublime natures, since it holds a rank more exalted than all others. This is because it stands immediately before God, and the first-born manifestations and initiations of God are channeled primarily into it, as the rank closest to Him. Thus, they are named "The Warmers" and "Thrones"; and the "Outpouring of Wisdom" is an explanatory name for their God-like <note>original: "Deiformium"</note> dispositions. Indeed, the name **Seraphim** clearly designates their perpetual and unceasing movement around divine things; their fervor, sharpness, and the bubbling over of an intense, never-interrupted, and never-waning motion. It also represents their power to uplift those beneath them to higher things, effectively rousing and kindling them to a similar fervor, as well as their ability to purify them completely through a lightning-like and all-consuming fire. Finally, it signifies their light-like and illuminating property, which is incapable of being hidden or extinguished—a property that remains always the same, driving out and destroying all dark obscurity. The name **Cherubim**, on the other hand, refers to their power of knowing and beholding God, their capacity for receiving the highest light, and their ability to contemplate the divine beauty in its original power. It also signifies the skill of their wise transmission, through which they generously share and pour out the wisdom granted to them upon the lower orders.

<margin>The meaning of Thrones.</margin>
Furthermore, the name of the most sublime and exalted **Thrones** denotes that which is set apart and pure from every earthly lowliness. This rank is carried toward the heights with a divine zeal, and never in the lower reaches...

Because of their supreme purity, they are placed above even the most **Godlike** powers, far surpassing every sacred thing beneath them. They constantly maintain the movement proper to their own order through a steady love for God, never varying or acknowledging any decline toward lesser things, but always holding an unshaken and immovable...

<margin>
How perfect the first Hierarchy is.
</margin>
...they have the seat of their **godlike character** <note>original: "Deiformis suæ proprietatis"</note>. These beings are also contemplators, but not as spectators of symbols perceived by the senses or the mind, nor are they raised to God by the various contemplations found in the holy Scriptures. Instead, they are filled with a simple knowledge of a higher light that surpasses all other understanding. They are replenished by the contemplation of that **Beauty** which is the creator and origin of all beauty—a beauty that exists beyond all substance and shines forth in three persons <note>A reference to the Trinity</note>, as far as it is lawful to see it. 

Furthermore, they are made partakers in the communion of Jesus in a similar way: not through holy images that express a godlike likeness in form, but by truly approaching Him in the very first participation in the knowledge of His deifying lights. They are also granted the method of imitating God in the most sublime way possible for them, sharing in His divine and human **virtues** <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the powers or miracles of Christ, both in His divinity and His humanity</note> in their original power. 

In the same way, they are perfect—not because they have been enlightened with the skill to resolve sacred complexities, but because they are satisfied by the first and most excellent union with God. This follows that supreme discipline of divine works of which only Angels are capable. Indeed, they are not initiated into sacred mysteries by any other holy spirits, but by the **Divinity** <term>Divinity — the Godhead or the essence of God</term> itself. They are raised directly to God by a power and order that is superior to all things, and they are established in Him with the highest purity and constancy. Because of their immaterial and spiritual beauty, they are promoted—as far as is permitted—to contemplation, and they are taught the spiritual reasons of divine works. As the first beings and those closest to God, they are educated by the very Principle of **initiation** <note>original: "initiandi principio." This refers to God as the source of all sacred teaching</note>, having been consecrated in an eminent and extraordinary manner.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## Concerning the Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, and the Middle Hierarchy between them.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*1. It explains what the **Dominions, Virtues, and Powers** signify; and by what reasoning this middle Hierarchy is initiated or enlightened. 2. It declares by example how illumination is passed down from the superior spirits to the inferior ones.*

<margin>§. 1.</margin>
**N**ow we must pass on to the middle rank of celestial spirits, contemplating those Dominions with eyes that look beyond this world, as far as we are able, together with the truly powerful spectacles of the divine Powers and Virtues; for every name given to these heavenly natures denotes their <term>deiform <gloss>literally "God-shaped" or having the form of God</gloss></term> properties, which imitate the Divine. <margin>*What the "Dominions" signify*</margin> Thus, I believe the name which designates the holy Dominions indicates a certain absolute movement toward the heights, free from all earthly self-interest <note>original: "terrena utilitate." Dionysius means the Dominions are not motivated by the mercenary or petty concerns of the material world.</note>. It is a dominion not bent in any way toward a tyrannical lack of likeness <note>original: "tyrannica dissimilitudine." In this philosophy, "dissimilitude" or "unlikeness" refers to falling away from the perfect image of God. Tyranny is seen as a corrupted, "unlike" version of true divine authority.</note>, but a "freely stern" lordship, which is higher than all low-born servitude, superior to all downfall, and removed from all lack of resemblance to the Divine. Constantly eager for true lordship and the very Source of lordship itself, this rank beneficially transforms both itself and its subordinates into its own genuine likeness as far as it is able. Turning itself entirely away from things that merely appear as empty illusions and toward that which truly *is*, it remains a constant participant in the Lordly deiformity. The title "Holy," however...

<margin>What the Virtues signify.</margin>
The name of the **Virtues** <note>In the celestial hierarchy, "Virtues" does not just mean moral goodness, but spiritual "virility" or raw power and strength derived from God.</note> signifies a certain strong and unshakable courage which flows into all their godlike activities. It ensures they do not admit anything that might diminish the divine illuminations bestowed upon them. This rank strives with great strength toward the imitation of God; it does not fall into sluggishness or turn away from the divine movement. Instead, it gazes constantly toward that super-essential <term>super-essential <gloss>that which transcends all categories of being or "essence"</gloss></term> and power-bestowing Virtue which is the source of all power. As far as is permitted, the Virtues become a reflection of that original power, turning toward it as their source while simultaneously flowing out toward those below them to provide them with strength in a godlike manner.

<margin>What the Powers signify.</margin>
Furthermore, the name of the holy **Powers** signifies an equal distribution of rank alongside the divine Dominions and Virtues. It represents a perfectly ordered arrangement for receiving divine matters, and the disposition of an intellectual and <term>super-mundane <gloss>existing beyond or above the physical world</gloss></term> authority. This power does not tyrannically abuse its strength for evil, but is itself directed toward divine things in an orderly and invincible way. It kindly leads the ranks that follow it and, as far as possible, approaches the Source of all power. It reflects that Sovereign Power, as far as Angels are able, through the illustrious functions of its own powerful strength.

<margin>How the middle Hierarchy is initiated.</margin>
Relying on these godlike properties, that middle rank of celestial intelligences is purified, illuminated, and perfected <note>original: "purgatur, et illuminatur, atque perficitur." These are the three traditional stages of mystical ascent in Christian Neoplatonism.</note> in the manner already described: through the divine illuminations granted to them by the first hierarchical order, and then passed down through this middle rank in a second manifestation.

For this reason, in our <term>Priestly Tradition <gloss>The collective teachings and liturgical practices of the Church</gloss></term>, the first intelligences are named as the perfecting, light-giving, and purifying powers <note>original: "perfectivæ ac lucificæ, expiatoriæque virtutes"</note>. ...the arrangements of beings <note>original: "essentiarum dispositiones"</note> participate in the holy and beautiful illumination of the lowest ranks, in a different manner than the lowest participate in the first. For this reason, all the celestial powers are indeed called "divine spirits," but the **Seraphim**, **Thrones**, and **Dominations** are by no means called by the names of the lower ranks. This is because the lowest ranks do not participate universally in the specific properties of the superior ones. Thus, the **Angels**, and before the Angels the **Archangels**, **Principalities**, and **Powers**—since they are placed by Theology <note>In this context, "Theology" refers to the Holy Scriptures or the divine revelations handed down through tradition.</note> after the rank of **Virtues**—are frequently called "celestial powers" by us, along with the other holy natures.

<margin>*Celestial Spirits are divided into essence, power, and operation.*</margin>

However, we deny that when we use the common name "Celestial Powers" for all of them, we are introducing any confusion of the properties of each order. Rather, because all divine minds are divided according to their celestial nature into three aspects—namely, <term>essence <gloss>the core being or substance</gloss></term>, <term>power <gloss>original Latin: "virtutem"; the capacity or faculty to act</gloss></term>, and <term>operation <gloss>the actual exercise or work of that power</gloss></term>—when we call all of them, or some of them, "celestial essences" or "celestial powers" indiscriminately, we should be understood to be describing those of whom we speak by a general term, derived from the essence or power that exists within each of them. 

For it would not be right for us to attribute that eminent property of the holy rank of **Virtues** (which we have already properly categorized) to the inferior natures universally, as that would throw the unconfused order of the Angelic distinctions into turmoil. For according to the reasoning we have often given, the superior distinctions possess an abundance of the sacred properties of the lower ranks, but the lowest ranks do not possess the eminent qualities of the highest. These primary illuminations are passed down into the lower ranks only partially, according to the capacity of each to receive them.

He reports another opinion, which considers that this Angel was indeed from a lower order, but attributed the duty of purification to that highest order because he purified by its power—just as, for example, the Sovereign Pontiff is said to ordain through Bishops and baptize through Priests, because they do so by the power received from him; he finds this opinion more probable. 4. He describes the vision of Isaiah. 5. Where he saw the Lord sitting on a throne, and the Seraphim surrounding him, and he relates how Isaiah was purified, and explains each detail mystically.*

diffusion, because the materials to be illuminated are ill-suited for spreading the light; from there, the light is gradually drawn back until it can hardly be distributed any further. In the same way, the heat of fire spreads more effectively into objects that are more capable of receiving it—those that easily yield and are drawn toward a likeness of the fire. However, in substances that resist fire or are its opposite, either no trace of its fiery power appears, or only a faint one. Furthermore—and this is even more significant—fire reaches into things that are not of its own kind by using materials that are already adapted to it. It first makes those things that ignite easily "fiery" (if the situation allows), and by using these as conduits, it then heats water or other things that are difficult to set on fire.

Following this logic of the natural order, the supernatural <term>Source of all order</term> <gloss>original: "fons omnis ordinis"; a reference to God as the origin of the hierarchical structure of the universe</gloss>—the origin of both visible and invisible distribution—primarily reveals the splendor of its own enlightenment through most blessed outpourings to those supreme <term>essences</term> <gloss>the highest rank of angels: Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones</gloss>. It is through them that the remaining ranks subsequently participate in that divine ray. Because these highest beings were the first to know God and were held by a supreme desire for His divine power, they were also the first to attain an imitation of divine power and action, according to their capacity. 

These same beings then kindly promote the lower ranks to that same imitation as much as possible, as they pass on a portion of the light bestowed upon them to those below without any <note>original: "absque invidia"; "without envy"—a key concept in Neoplatonic and early Christian thought, suggesting that higher beings naturally share their abundance with the lower</note> envy. These lower ones, in turn, pass it to those below them. Thus, step by step, the first rank makes the one next to it a participant in what it has received, and so, through <term>Providence</term> <gloss>God's governing care and guidance over the universe</gloss>, the divine light is distributed to all according to the capacity of each. Therefore, the supreme arrangement of the celestial <term>intelligences</term> <gloss>a term for angels as pure minds without physical bodies</gloss> is rightly and deservedly considered—after God—the source of all sacred knowledge and of the imitation of God for all other angelic essences. The arrangements of the lower essences also participate in these fiery, wise, knowledgeable, and God-receptive virtues, but they do so at a lower degree. They look toward the higher orders as their "pre-shaping models" of divine imitation, through whom they are raised toward a <term>likeness of God</term> <gloss>original: "Deiformitatem"</gloss> according to their own capacity. Consequently, they acknowledge that these sacred properties—which the second-tier natures receive through the first—are gifts received from those higher orders as their leaders, second only to God.

# CHAPTER XIV.
## What the traditional number of Angels signifies.
### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*Drawing from Daniel chapter 7, verse 10, the author teaches that the number of Angels is immense. Although it is not strictly infinite—since it is limited and known to God—it is nevertheless so great that it cannot be grasped by human beings, and it exceeds the total number of all physical things in existence.*

<margin>Angels are beyond counting. Daniel 7.</margin>
**I** indeed also deem this worthy of spiritual meditation: that the tradition of the <term>Scriptures</term> <note>original: "eloquiorum"; Dionysius frequently uses this term to refer to the "divine oracles" or the Bible.</note> regarding the Angels says there are "thousands of thousands" and "ten thousand times ten thousand," taking the highest numbers we use and piling them upon themselves and multiplying them. Through these, it clearly declares that the orders of the celestial <term>essences</term> <note>original: "essentiarum"; the spiritual "substances" or "beings" that make up the angelic ranks.</note> cannot be numbered by us. For many are the blessed armies of the <term>super-worldly</term> <note>original: "supermundanarum"; beings existing beyond the physical, material universe.</note> minds, which entirely exceed the weak and narrow reach of our material numbers. They are skillfully defined only by their own super-worldly and heavenly intelligence and knowledge, which is most abundantly granted to them by the primal and creative Wisdom of God, which knows all infinite things. This Wisdom exists <term>above all being</term> <note>original: "superessentialiter"; a key Dionysian term meaning God exists beyond the very category of "existence" as understood by creatures.</note> as the simultaneous beginning and substance-making cause of all things, their sustaining power, and their all-encompassing boundary.

<margin>Hebrews 10.</margin> ...particularly commends. Therefore, I judge that the fiery form signifies the greatest conformity <term>conformitatem: a state of being in the same shape or likeness</term> of the celestial intelligences with God. For indeed, the holy Theologians <note>original: "Theologi"; Dionysius uses this term to refer specifically to the authors of the Bible.</note> frequently describe the super-essential <term>superessentialem: that which exists beyond the limits of physical essence or "being" as we understand it</term> essence, which cannot be given a shape, through the image of fire, as something that displays many visible images (if one may say so) of the divine property. 

<margin>What the properties of fire are.</margin> For sensible fire <note>original: "Ignis sensibilis"; fire as it is perceived by the physical senses.</note> is present in all things, so to speak, and passes purely through everything and is received by all. While it shines as a whole, it is also hidden and remains unknown in itself, provided that no material is added upon which it might exert its power. It is unbearable and invisible, it surpasses all things, and it draws those things in which it resides into its own operation. It possesses the power of transformation; it gives its fellowship to all things that approach it in any way. It renews all things with vital heat and illuminates with open brightness. It cannot be held or mixed; it has the power of separation; it is immutable; it is carried upward; it is penetrable. It is sublime and suffers no dejection; it is always mobile, moved by itself and moving others. It is powerful in its ability to grasp, yet it cannot be grasped. It needs no other; it increases itself secretly and shows its majesty in any capable material. It is effective, powerful, and invisibly present to all. If it is neglected, it does not seem to exist; but by friction, as if by a certain natural and proper search, it suddenly shines forth and immediately flies upward uncontrollably, and it is not diminished at all in its many brilliant communications of itself. One can find many other properties of fire that exist as sensible images of divine efficacy. When the Theologians realized this, they fashioned the celestial essences from fire,

<margin>Section 3. What the human form denotes in celestial beings.</margin>
The scriptures also describe these celestial beings in **human form**, because of their high powers of understanding and their ability to look upward; because of the straightness and uprightness of their form; and because of their natural prerogative of leadership and rule. Although a human may be physically weaker than the wild beasts in terms of raw senses, he nevertheless rules over all of them by the superior power of his mind, the dominion of his rational knowledge, and the naturally free and unconquered nature of his soul.

<margin>What the faculties of the senses signify.</margin>
Indeed, I believe it is entirely appropriate to draw fitting images from the various parts of our own bodies to represent the celestial powers. For example, we might say that the **power of sight** declares their most clear-sighted looking-up toward the divine lights, as well as a simple, transparent, and unresisting—yet active, pure, and open—reception of divine illuminations without any earthly passion.

The **power of smell** represents the ability to discern, which perceives (as far as is holy) the spreading fragrance of the mind that surpasses all things, skillfully distinguishing between what is holy and what is foul, and utterly fleeing from the latter.

The **virtue of the ears** signifies that quality in them which shares in knowledge and skillfully receives divine inspiration.

The **powers of taste** represent their fullness of spiritual food and their reception of divine and delightful streams.

<margin>What the eyelids, eyebrows, teeth, and other parts of the body signify.</margin>
Furthermore, **tactile sensations** <term>tactiles sensationes: the sense of touch</term> represent the ability to discern with knowledge that which is beneficial or harmful to them.

The **eyelids and eyebrows** represent the protection and preservation of the spiritual understandings and notions gained from the divine vision.

# ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL HIERARCHY

## CHAPTER I.

->**Dionysius the Priest to his fellow-priest Timothy.**<-

->**What the tradition of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy is, and what its aim is.**<-

->**SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.**<-

**1.** Intending to describe the Ecclesiastical <term>Hierarchy</term> <note>From the Greek 'hieros' (sacred) and 'arkhe' (rule/order); a sacred order, state of understanding, and activity approximating as closely as possible to the divine.</note>, he warns that the sacred mysteries of the Christian Religion are not to be rashly revealed to the uninitiated, but are to be clearly explained, as far as possible, to the baptized, according to each person's capacity and measure, by those to whom the duty of both teaching and administering the Sacraments has been granted in the Church, who imitate the **Angels** in this world. **2.** Since he described the *Angelic Hierarchy* in the previous book, he says that our hierarchy agrees with that one in this: that the lower ranks are instructed toward perfection by the higher, and are led to God. It differs, however, in this: that the angels are enlightened in a simpler and more spiritual manner; while we, because we consist of both soul and body and cannot focus directly on spiritual things, are raised up toward spiritual contemplations through sensible <note>Meaning things perceptible by the five senses, like water, oil, and bread.</note> images and figures, which is also why we participate in God in a varied way. **3.** He defines what *Hierarchy* is in general, and what this our *Hierarchy* is—namely, that it is the administration of all sacred things, whose principle is the **Most Holy Trinity** and whose end is union with God. **4.** He says that God [has established] for each a hierarchy suited both to us and to the **Angels**...

## SAINT DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE

...they may advance those who are lower to the things ahead; that those who have already advanced may also provide leadership for others according to their strength; and that through this divine and sacred harmony of order, each person, according to their own measure, might truly exist as a participant in the Beauty, Wisdom, and Goodness of His essence.

Furthermore, those higher natures and orders, of which I made venerable mention above, are both incorporeal, and their sacred administration is spiritual and beyond the world; but we see our own order, in a different manner from them, multiplied by a variety of sensible signs <note>original: "sensibilium varietate signorum"; Dionysius refers to the physical elements of the sacraments—like water, oil, and bread—which humans need to understand spiritual reality.</note>, through which we are sacredly moved toward a uniform god-likeness <term>deiformitas: the process of the soul being shaped into the likeness of God</term> according to our capacity, and toward God and divine virtue. For those angelic beings, as pure minds, understand as is lawful for them; but we, through images perceived by the senses, are raised up as much as we can be to divine contemplations. And to speak truly, there is indeed one thing that all who are god-like desire, yet they do not participate in that which is entirely one and the same in a single way, but according to how the divine balance <note>original: "divina trutina"; a metaphor for God's perfect judgment in distributing grace according to a person's soul</note> distributes a portion to each according to their merit.

But these things have been more fully explained by us in the work *On Those Things which Fall under Intellect and Sense* <note>This refers to a work that is either lost to history or was one of Dionysius's theoretical references.</note>; but for now, I shall endeavor to explain our sacred order, and its origin and essence, as far as my ability allows, invoking Jesus, the beginning and the perfection of all sacred orders.

## ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL HIERARCHY — CHAPTER I

...is a function, embracing all sacred things within itself, through which the divine Pontiff <note>original: "Pontifex"; here referring to the High Priest or Bishop as the summit of the earthly hierarchy</note> is initiated, becoming a participant in all the most sacred things by his own virtue, insofar as he is called the High Priest. For just as he who named the "sacred order" spoke of the distribution of all sacred things at once in a summary; so he who calls someone "High Priest" signifies a man intimately united to God and clearly divine, polished by all sacred knowledge, in whom all the sacred power that resides within him is fulfilled and recognized.

<margin>The origin of Hierarchy is the Most Holy Trinity.</margin>
The origin of this sacred leadership is the source of life, the essence of goodness, the single cause of all things: the Trinity, from which—through the abundance of goodness—comes both existence and well-being for all things. To this most divine blessedness, which transcends all things, this triune unity, truly existing—in a way indeed incomprehensible to us, yet most known to Himself—the salvation of rational creatures is a desire, both our own and that of the supernal minds <note>the angels</note>. Nevertheless, this salvation can only be obtained for those who are saved once they have already been deified <term>deificatio: the process of being made like God; theosis</term>. Moreover, this deification is a certain assimilation and union with God, as far as this is possible.

<margin>What the goal of the Hierarchy is.</margin>
Furthermore, the common goal of every sacred order is a continuous love toward God and divine things, which is divinely implanted and fulfilled through union with Him; and, prior to this, a complete and irreversible flight from things contrary to Him; a knowledge of things as they truly are; the vision and science of sacred truth; a divine participation in the simple perfection of Him who is supremely simple; a feast of intuition, which restores and deifies <note>original: "deificatque"; transforms the soul into a god-like state</note> every one of its contemplators in a spiritual manner.

<margin>
How He gave each of the Angels a hierarchy suited to them.
</margin>
...those who are to be deified are deified <note>original: "deificari"; the process of "theosis" or becoming god-like through grace</note>, and that Divine Goodness has granted a sacred order for the salvation and deification of all, both rational <note>human</note> and spiritual <note>angelic</note> essences. To the higher beings [the angels] who enjoy a blessed rest, He granted this in a more immaterial and spiritual way; for God does not move them toward divine things from the outside, but rather through an intelligible reason, radiating His most divine will into them from within through a pure and clear illumination. To us, however, that which was granted to the angels simply and as a whole has been given through divinely handed-down words, according to our capacity, through a variety of divided signs and a multitude of symbols. 

<margin>
The substance of our Hierarchy is the word of God, both written and handed down.
</margin>
For the substance of our Hierarchy is the divinely handed-down Oracles <term>Oracles: here referring to the Holy Scriptures and divine revelations</term>. We say those Oracles are most especially venerable which were handed down to us in the Holy Scriptures and theological books by our sacred Initiators <note>the Apostles and their immediate successors</note> who were inspired by the Divine Spirit. Likewise, we honor those things which our teachers were taught by these same holy men through a more subtle transmission—not entirely learned from the celestial order—passing from mind to mind through the medium of the word. Though this word is corporeal <note>spoken/physical</note>, it is simultaneously immaterial because it is passed without writing through a certain sacred tradition. Furthermore, these monuments of the sacred leaders, inspired by the Divine Spirit, were not passed down for the common use of the sacred order in plain meanings, but through certain sacred symbols; for not every Priest—nor indeed everyone, as the Scriptures tell us—possesses this knowledge.

He emphasizes that sacred knowledge is passed down both through written text and an unwritten, "mind-to-mind" tradition intended for the initiated.</summary>

<margin>That they may be handed down through sensible symbols.</margin>
...they [the Apostles] looked upon these things and handed down to us the heavenly realities through sensible figures <note>original: "sensibilibus figuris"; physical shapes or metaphors that can be perceived by the human senses</note>. What is gathered into a single unity, they expressed through a variety of distinctions and multitudes; they showed divine things in human form, the immaterial in material ways, and the beyond-substantial <term>supersubstantialia: things that exist beyond the realm of physical substance or essence</term> in our own earthly things. This they did through both written and unwritten traditions in the most sacred Oracles <term>Oracles: the Holy Scriptures and divine revelations</term>. This was done not only for the sake of the uninitiated—for whom it would be forbidden even to touch these signs—but because our own sacred way of ordering ritual, compared to that of the angels, is symbolic in nature. It requires sensible signs <note>physical objects, gestures, or words</note> to lead us by a more divine path from these material things toward a spiritual elevation <note>original: "sublimationem"; the lifting of the soul toward intellectual or divine truths</note>.

<margin>That the symbols are open to the Priests of our Hierarchy.</margin>
Nevertheless, the reasons behind these signs are clear to the Priests <note>original: "Sacerdotalibus"; those in the priestly order</note>, though it is forbidden to explain them to those who are still candidates for the sacred mysteries. This is because the Lawgivers of the divinely handed-down rites <note>referring to the Apostles and early founders of the Church</note> established the sacred order with stable and unmixed distinctions between ranks, adapted to each person's merit through diverse and holy divisions.

<margin>The Hierarchy communicates sacred things to each according to their merit.</margin>
Therefore, being convinced by your own most holy vows (for it is a holy thing to remember them), you shall by no means communicate the order of the Episcopacy <term>Episcopacy: the office or rank of a Bishop</term>—which is superior to the others—to anyone except your fellow God-formed <note>original: "deiformibus"; shaped by or mirroring the divine likeness</note> Priests. You shall urge them to profess, according to the hierarchical rite, that they will handle holy things in a holy manner; that they will share the god-making things <note>original: "deifica"; things that make one more like God, such as the Sacraments</note> only with those who are divine, the most holy things only with those capable of the perfection of fulfillment, and the most sacred things only with the holy. For among the other duties of the sacred orders, we entrust this divine task to you as well.

<summary>Dionysius explains that because humans lack the purely spiritual perception of angels, divine truths must be cloaked in material symbols (sacraments and scriptures). He also emphasizes the strict "discipline of the secret," where higher mysteries and the office of the Bishop are only shared with those properly prepared and ordained.</summary>

# CHAPTER II.
## I. Concerning those things which are performed in illumination <note>original: "illuminatione"; in the early Church, Baptism was frequently called "Illumination" because it was believed to enlighten the mind of the believer with divine knowledge</note> or baptism.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*In the first part of the chapter, he shows the order by which one reaches the holiness of life, and how Baptism is a kind of spiritual birth and the beginning of supernatural works; at the same time, he warns that only the holy <note>the "initiated" or those already baptized</note> are to be admitted to the sight of the Sacraments.*

*In the second part, he describes the solemn rite of baptizing, which proceeds as follows: 1. The Bishop <term>Pontifex: literally "High Priest," referring here to the Bishop as the head of the local church hierarchy</term> proclaims the sacred Gospels. 2. The lover of religion seeks out a sponsor <term>susceptor: a "taker-up" or godparent who supports the candidate</term>, by whom he is instructed and led to the Bishop. 3. The Bishop receives him kindly. 4. He assembles the clergy to give thanks to God and questions the candidate, who has been brought forward by the sponsor, using a solemn formula. 5. He places his hand upon the one who detests unfaithfulness <note>who renounces his former life</note> and commands that his name be enrolled. 6. After prayer is made, the one to be baptized is stripped of his clothes, and breathings <note>original: "insufflationes"; the ritual of blowing or breathing upon the candidate to signify the driving away of spirits or the gift of the Holy Spirit</note> are performed. 7. A solemn profession of Faith is made, and he is baptized. 8. Clothed in a white garment, he is handed back to the sponsor and is made a participant in the sacred communion.*

*In the third part, he adds a contemplation <note>a spiritual or mystical interpretation of the physical actions</note>, in which: 1. He shows that this rite is holy. 2. That these ceremonies signify spiritual grace. 3. That God communicates His grace to all. 4. He explains the order by which one arrives at perfection. 5. What is meant by the leading forward and the enrollment of the one to be baptized, and likewise what the renunciation means. 6. What the turning toward the East means. 7. What the anointing signifies. 8. What the immersion into and emergence from the water signifies. 9. What the white garment means. 10. What the final anointing signifies. 11. What the communion means.*

## II. THE SACRAMENT
### Of Illumination, or Baptism.

<margin>
§. 1.
The rite of conferring Baptism.
</margin>
The Leader of the sacred rites <note>original: "Præsul"; a term often used for a Bishop or presiding officer</note>, since he desires all individual men to be saved by becoming like God and to come to the knowledge of the truth, proclaims to everyone from the true Gospels that God Himself—being merciful to those born of the earth through His own natural goodness—has descended to us out of His supreme love for humanity. He did this so that, by union with Himself, He might transform those united to Him into His own likeness—after the manner of fire—to whatever extent would lead toward their deification <note>original: "deificationem"; in this context, it refers to "theosis," the process of being made like God through grace</note>.

<margin>John 1. 12.</margin>
> For as many as received Him, to them He gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in His name: who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God.

<margin>
§. 2.
The candidate for the Religion seeks a godfather.

The duty of the godfather or sponsor.
</margin>
Whoever desires to be a holy participant in these truly super-worldly gifts <note>original: "supermundialium"; referring to things that transcend the physical or material world</note>, approaches someone already initiated into the sacred mysteries and begs to be led by the hand to the Leader of the rites. He promises to obey all the holy decrees completely and asks that the sponsor not refuse to take charge of both his admission and his entire life from then on. Then, though the sponsor is holy and desires that person's salvation, he weighs the loftiness of the task against human frailty; immediately, a sense of awe and anxiety surrounds him. Nevertheless, he finally agrees kindly to fulfill the request and, taking the candidate under his care <note>original: "susceptoris"; literally "the one who takes up," which is the root for the word "sponsor" or "godparent"</note>, leads him to the high Priest.

<margin>
§ 3.
What is customarily done by the Priest who is about to baptize.
</margin>
The Priest <note>original: "Sacerdote"; here referring to the presiding minister</note> receives those two men <note>the candidate and his sponsor</note> with joy—much like a shepherd taking a sheep upon his shoulders. First, with a spiritual act of thanksgiving and a bodily gesture of adoration, he venerates the one and only Source of all blessings, from whom those who are called receive their calling, and those who are saved receive their salvation.

<margin>§ 4.</margin>
Next, he gathers the entire sacred order into the holy place, both so that they may work together for and rejoice in the man’s salvation, and so that they may give thanks to the divine goodness. He begins by chanting a hymn from the Scriptures along with the entire Clergy of the Church. When this is finished, and after he has kissed the holy altar, he approaches the man who is present and inquires what he has come to seek.

<margin>
§ 5.
The one to be baptized must renounce his lack of faith.
</margin>
Then, following the instruction of the sponsor <note>original: "fidejussoris"; a legal term for a guarantor, used here for the person vouching for the candidate</note>, the candidate expresses his hatred for his former lack of faith, his ignorance of the true Good, and his lack of spiritual life; he then asks to obtain God and divine things through the Priest's holy intercession. The Priest warns him that he must approach God with complete integrity, as one who is to become entirely perfect and blameless. After setting forth the divine way of living and asking if he intends to live by it, and receiving his assent, the Priest places his hand upon the man's head. Marking him with the sign <note>the Sign of the Cross</note>, he commands the Priests to record the names of both the man and his sponsor <note>original: "susceptorem"; the one who "receives" or "takes up" the newly baptized</note>.

</margin>

...having pronounced the prescribed words <note>This refers to the formal renunciation of evil mentioned at the end of the previous page</note>, the Priest turns him toward the East, and as the candidate gazes into heaven and lifts up his hands, the Priest commands him to give his assent to Christ and to all the sacred Words <note>original: "Eloquiis"; a term Dionysius uses for the Holy Scriptures as the direct utterances of God</note> handed down by God.

<margin>§ 7. The rite of profession.</margin>
§ 7. When this is done, the Priest commands him to make a threefold profession of faith; after he has made the third profession, the Priest receives him with a blessing and lays his hand upon him. While the ministers <note>original: "ministri"; likely referring to deacons or assistants assisting in the ritual</note> strip him completely, the Priests bring the holy oil of Anointing. The Bishop <note>original: "Pontifex"; Dionysius uses this term for the "High Priest" or head of the local church hierarchy</note>, beginning the Anointing with a threefold seal <note>making the sign of the cross three times on the candidate's forehead</note>, hands the man over to the Priests to be anointed over his whole body.

<margin>The ancient rite of solemn baptism.</margin>
The Bishop himself goes to the "mother of adoption" (that is, the Font); after he has sanctified its waters with sacred prayers, and has consecrated them by pouring out the most holy ointment <term>ointment: "unguenti", referring to the sacred chrism or myrrh used to sanctify the water</term> three times in the form of a Cross, while simultaneously chanting the most holy Hymn of the divine inspiration of the God-breathed Prophets <note>This likely refers to a specific psalm or the "Alleluia" chanted during the blessing of the waters</note>, he commands the man to be brought forward. 

While a Priest proclaims from a written register both the man's name and that of his sponsor <note>original: "susceptorem"; the person who "takes up" or vouches for the newly baptized</note>, the one to be initiated is led by the hands of the Priests into the water toward the hand of the Bishop. The Bishop, standing above, after the Priests near the water have proclaimed the name of the initiate to the Bishop, immerses him three times, invoking the three Persons of the divine Blessedness <note>the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note> during this threefold immersion and emersion. Then the other Priests, receiving him, hand him over to the sponsor or author of his admission; and when, together with the sponsor, they have clothed the initiate in appropriate garments, they lead him back to the Bishop. The Bishop, sealing the man with divinely consecrated oil, declares him a partaker of the most holy Eucharist.

### III. CONTEMPLATION.

<margin>§ 1. That this rite is holy.</margin>
This initiation into the sacred symbols of divine birth <note>original: "divinæ generationis"; Dionysius uses this term to describe Baptism as a spiritual rebirth into the family of God</note> contains nothing unseemly or profane, nor even merely sensory figures. Rather, it contains mysteries <note>original: "ænigmata"; literally "riddles" or "enigmas," referring to how physical rituals hide and reveal spiritual truths</note> of a contemplation worthy of God, fashioned in natural mirrors <note>A favorite concept of the author: the physical world acts as a mirror reflecting the higher spiritual reality</note> adapted to human understanding. For what might seem to be lacking in it—even if the underlying reason is suppressed by a more divine silence concerning the mysteries—when by its divine institution it sufficiently proves the integrity of life of the person approaching? Through a virtuous and divine life, does it not announce more physically to the candidate the total purging of all malice by the natural cleansing of water? <margin>The ceremonies of Baptism signify expiation.</margin> Thus, even if the symbolic tradition of these initiations held nothing more divine than this, it would by no means, I believe, be void of holiness; for it introduces a discipline of right living and naturally suggests a total cleansing from the vices of a past life by having the whole body thoroughly purified with water.

<margin>§ 2.</margin>
Let this, then, be a spiritual introduction for the more simple <note>original: "rudioribus"; referring to those new to the faith or those who only see the surface level of the ritual</note>, which distinguishes the holy and unifying Sacraments, as is right, from common things, and provides an uplifting experience suited to each rank of the faithful. We, however, who contemplate the principles of the Sacraments through sacred ascents <note>The "ascents" refer to the mental and spiritual process of looking past the physical ritual to the heavenly reality it represents</note>, having perceived them by a sacred inspiration, shall recognize the patterns of which these are the visible marks, and the hidden things of which they are the images. For just as we have shown in our work *On the Intelligible and the Sensible* <note>original: "Opere de Intelligibilibus ac sensilibus"; a reference to another (now lost or perhaps fictional) treatise by Dionysius intended to explain the relationship between the physical and spiritual worlds</note> per- 

<summary>Dionysius begins the "Contemplation" phase of the chapter, explaining that the physical ritual of baptism (washing with water) is not merely a sign of cleanliness, but a "natural mirror" reflecting the spiritual purification of the soul.</summary>

<margin>**Sacraments are sensory signs of spiritual grace.**</margin>
...it has been clearly <note>original: "conspicue"; the first syllable "con-" was at the end of the previous page</note> declared that the sensory Sacraments <term>sensory Sacraments; physical rituals like water baptism or anointing that can be perceived by the five senses</term> are images of intelligible realities <term>intelligible; spiritual truths understood by the mind or soul rather than the physical senses</term>, toward which they guide us by the hand and pave the way. Indeed, these intelligible realities are the very source and the true knowledge of the sensory Sacraments.

<margin>**§. 3. God extends His grace to all, as the sun extends its light.**</margin>
We say, therefore, that the goodness of the divine Beatitude <note>original: "divinæ beatitudinis"; a term for God's perfect, blissful nature</note>, which remains always the same and in the same state, has abundantly extended the beneficial rays of its own light to all mental eyes. Thus, if the free will of those endowed with a self-moving mind should desert the spiritual light—shutting out, through a love of evil, the powers naturally implanted within them for receiving that light—it withdraws itself from the light that is present. Yet the light does not abandon that person; rather, it shines even upon the one who closes their eyes, and meets even the one who turns away with total kindness. 

But if a person, equipped with only a modest faculty of sight, should overleap their boundaries and rashly dare to gaze upon rays that surpass their vision, the light itself will do nothing contrary to its nature; instead, because the light presents itself to those who are imperfect in an "imperfect" way <note>The author means that if we aren't ready for a truth, we see it only dimly or incorrectly, not because the truth is dim, but because our "eyes" are weak</note>, the person will by no means grasp things that are beyond them. Furthermore, if one is insolently proud of their own mediocrity, they will be frustrated by their own fault. Nevertheless, as I have said, the divine light is always open to the eyes of the mind, and one may have an abundance of it, for it is present and most ready for its own God-worthy communication.

<margin>**The Hierarch likewise is ready to impart the light of Baptism to all.**</margin>
In imitation of this divine light, the divine Prelate <term>Antistes; a high-ranking priest or bishop</term> is formed. He clearly spreads the bright rays of divine instruction over all, and, in imitation of God, he is most ready to illuminate whoever approaches him. He uses no reproach, nor any dire curse for a person's previous falling away or lack of restraint; instead, following the example of God, he always shines his priestly illuminations upon those who approach him, doing so with dignity and order, and according to the proportion of each person's capacity for sacred things.

<margin>
§. 4.
*By what steps one arrives at perfection.*
</margin>
But since the divine Godhead <note>original: "divinum Numen"; referring to the divine power or presence of God</note> is the starting point of that sacred discipline through which holy minds come to the knowledge of themselves, anyone who turns back to the light implanted in their own nature will first see who they truly are. By this arrival of light, they will receive a sacred gift. Furthermore, the person who considers their own state rightly with unswerving eyes will indeed banish the hidden darkness of self-ignorance. However, being still without the most perfect union and participation in God, they will not be spontaneously moved by a desire for it. Instead, they will be raised up in a sacred manner toward the sovereign height of God—moving gradually, first from their own concerns to better things, and from those to the most powerful things, until they are perfected in their rank. The evidence of this beautiful and sacred order is the reverence of the person approaching the faith, and their realization of the things concerning themselves, having found a sponsor <term>sponsor; original "susceptor," a person who acts as a godparent or guide for a new convert</term> to serve as a guide on the path to the High Priest. Once led forward in this way, the divine Blessedness admits the person to its own communication. Like a kind of seal, it shares its own light with them, making them intimate with God and a sharer in divine gifts and the sacred order. The sacred token <note>original: "tessera"; a sign or password used to prove membership</note> of these gifts is the seal <term>seal; original "signaculum," a spiritual marking often associated with the ritual of baptism or anointing</term> given by the High Priest to the one approaching, as well as the saving enrollment of the Priests. This enrolls the person among those to be saved and inserts them into the sacred records <note>original: "sacris monumentis"; the official lists or registers of the church community</note> along with their sponsor, as if onto a life-giving path to the truth. It places the initiate as a sincere lover and companion of the divine leader, and the sponsor as a guide who does not wander, following the institutions handed down by God.

<margin>*[The soul] must aspire toward perfection.*</margin> [The sacred order] allows for participation; but it is proper that the candidate be free and devoid of all divisions that oppose <term>uniformity</term> <note>original: "uniformitatis"; here meaning a state of being "one-like" or having a single, undivided focus on God</note>. This is what the sacred tradition of signs implies, when it strips the one approaching of their former life, and, stripping them down to their outermost affections, it places them naked and barefoot, looking toward the <term>West</term> <note>In the ancient Church, the West—where the sun sets—symbolized the kingdom of darkness and the devil</note>. There, by the pushing away of their hands, they refuse any communion with dark malice, and they "blow away" <note>original: "efflantem"; referring to the ritual of exsufflation, where the candidate literally breathed or blew out to symbolize the expulsion of the devil</note> the state of dissimilarity born within them, professing total renunciations of those things opposed to <term>conformity to God</term>.

<margin>*What the turning to the East signifies.*</margin> Once the person is entirely free and stripped of these worldly affects, the ritual transfers them toward the <term>East</term> <note>The East—where the sun rises—symbolized Christ, the "Sun of Righteousness"</note>, announcing that by fleeing malice in every way, they will possess a pure state and vision of divine light. The ritual then receives them—now made uniform by their holy professions and in total harmony with the One—with a truly loving embrace. Truly, as I believe, it is clear to those skilled in sacred principles that spiritual things attain the immutability of a god-like state through constant aspirations toward the One, and through the total killing and abolition of their opposites. For one must not merely withdraw from all malice, but must manfully harden oneself and always resist the slackening into harmful things without fear; nor must one ever cease from sacred love, but must continually and perpetually insist upon it with all one’s strength, always directing one's actions holily toward the more perfect height of the divine sovereignty.

<margin>*§. 6. What the anointing signifies.*</margin> You can see the exact images of these things in the rituals administered by the High Priest. For the <term>High Priest</term> <note>original: "Antistites"; the leader or bishop presiding over the ceremony</note> himself begins the <term>Anointing</term> <note>original: "Unctionem"; the ritual smearing of oil on the candidate, symbolizing the strengthening of an athlete for a contest</note> that conforms the person to God, which the other Priests then complete, urging the one who has been initiated into these sacred contests through this symbolic action...

What the white garment signifies.

# II. THE MYSTERIUM
## Of the Synaxis or Communion.

<margin>*The rite of consecrating the <term>Synaxis</term> <note>original: "Synaxin"; an assembly or gathering for worship, specifically the Eucharistic liturgy</note>.*</margin>
The <term>Pontiff</term> <note>original: "Pontifex"; referring here to the Bishop or high priest presiding over the ceremony</note>, about to celebrate the sacred prayer at the altar of God, begins by censing the altar and then circles the entire area of the Choir; until, returning again to the divine altar, he begins the sacred melody of the Psalms, with the whole Ecclesiastical order singing the sacred psalmody along with him. Then, in proper sequence, the reading of the Holy Scriptures is recited by the ministers. When this is finished, the <term>Catechumens</term> <note>those being instructed in the faith but not yet baptized</note> are kept away from the sacred precinct, and with them the <term>energumens</term> <note>those troubled by spirits or "possessed"</note> and the <term>penitents</term> <note>those undergoing public discipline for sins</note>, while those who are worthy of the sight and the Communion of the divine things remain. Furthermore, some of the ministers stand at the closed doors of the Temple, while others perform some other task belonging to their specific order. Those who hold the first rank among the order of ministers, together with the <term>Priests</term> <note>original: "Sacerdotibus"</note>, place the sacred bread and the chalice of blessing upon the divine altar, after a common <term>hymnology</term> <note>a choral song or hymn of praise</note> has been offered by the entire fullness of the Church. In addition to these things, the divine Bishop performs the sacred prayer and prays for holy peace upon all; and while all embrace one another, the mystical recitation of the sacred names <note>original: "voluminum"; literally "volumes" or "scrolls," referring here to the Diptychs or the list of names commemorated during the liturgy</note> is finished. Then, once the hands of the Bishop and the Priests have been washed with water, the Bishop stands in the center of the divine altar, with only the leaders of the ministers and the Priests standing around him. Furthermore, once the Bishop has praised the most holy gifts of God, he consecrates the most divine mysteries, which, having been celebrated...

### III. CONTEMPLATION.

<margin>§ 1.</margin>
<margin>Useless <note>Referring to the futility of ritual without understanding its inner meaning.</note></margin>

§ 2. Who and in what manner are barred from the Venerable Sacrament, and what is the order among them.

Those who are completely ignorant of these **Sacraments** <term>Sacramentorum</term> do not even see the symbolic images, because they impudently reject the saving discipline of divine birth <note>original: "divinæ generationis"; referring to Baptism</note> and disastrously clamor against the **Sacred Words** <note>original: "Eloquiis sacris"; the Scriptures</note>, saying: *I do not want to know your ways* <note>original: "Vias tuas scire nolo"; a quote from Job 21:14</note>. However, it by no means invites them to the subsequent Sacrifices and visions, but only the "perfected eyes of the perfected" <note>This refers to those who have been fully initiated through Baptism and are allowed to witness the Eucharist</note>. For that God-like and sacred order is full of holy justice; it grants to each person a participation in divine things according to their merit, and in a manner that is beneficial, granting it holily in due time according to the capacity and measure of each. And indeed, the lowest rank is assigned to the Catechumens, because they are without part in and ignorant of all Hierarchical perfection; not yet having attained a divine state through divine birth, they are still nurtured by the "paternal words" <note>the basic teachings of the faith</note> and are shaped by life-giving forms toward that blessed progress to the Prince of life and light which proceeds from divine generation.

Furthermore, I believe—or rather, I have found it to be certain—that the most sincere judgment of the sacred Orders <note>the ecclesiastical authorities or the clergy</note> holds that those truly held by a most detestable "obsession" are those who, deserting the **God-like life** <term>deiformem vitam</term>, align themselves with demons through their ruined thoughts and behaviors. This happens while they, through an extreme and ruinous madness, turn away from those things that truly exist, are possessed immortally, and provide eternal delight. Instead, they seek out and pursue material change—which is subject to many disturbances—along with ruined and corrupting pleasures, and that unstable, alien, and false delight which only appears to be real but does not truly exist.

These people, therefore, should be the first—and indeed more properly than the [physically] possessed—to be barred by the minister’s segregating voice <note>Referring to the liturgical command "Depart, all you who are..." which dismissed the uninitiated before the Eucharist began</note>. ### §. 11.

Instead, He **truly became a sharer in all our conditions, yet without sin, and was united to our humility, while the status of His own properties remained safe, being entirely unconfused and inviolate.** <note>The author is describing the "Hypostatic Union"—the belief that in Jesus, divine and human natures were joined without mixing or changing.</note> He also granted us—as being of the same race—fellowship with Him, and declared us partakers of His own goods. He also liberated the dwelling place of our soul, along with the perfect health of our essence and nature—which had nearly collapsed and fallen—from all those most foul passions and harmful defilements.

Why the altar is consecrated with the Ointment; and why the Ointment is called a <term>Rite of Completion<note>original: "τελετὴ" (telete); a Greek term denoting a finishing rite, initiation, or the state of perfection.</note></term>.*

<margin>The mystery of the Ointment is akin to the Eucharist.</margin>
I. **S**o great and so excellent are the spiritual visions of the most holy Gathering <note>original: "Synaxeos"; the Synaxis or the assembly for the Eucharist.</note> which, as we have often said, bring our people into communion and union with the One through that preeminent sacred rite. Nevertheless, there is also another consecration coordinated with this one, which our teachers call the "mystery of the Ointment." Therefore, having looked at its parts in order according to the sacred images <note>the symbolic ceremonies</note>, we are raised by these same images toward its singular essence through hierarchical contemplations.

## II. THE MYSTERY.
### Of the Consecration of the Ointment.

<margin>The rite of consecrating the Ointment.</margin>
It is performed in the same way as in the Gathering: the orders of those who are less perfect are excluded, following the sacred procession throughout the entire temple with the fragrance of incense, the sacred chanting of Psalms, and the proclamation of the most divine Oracles <note>original: "Eloquiorum"; referring to the reading of the Holy Scriptures.</note>. Then the High Priest <note>original: "Pontifex"</note>, having received the Ointment, places it upon the divine altar, veiled by twelve sacred wings, while everyone sings with a most holy voice that song of inspiration from the divinely inspired Prophets. After the consecrating prayer over it is completed, he uses it in almost every holy consecration of things to be sanctified, and for nearly every Hierarchical rite.

### III. CONTEMPLATION.

<margin>
§. 1.
What the veiling of the Ointment suggests.
</margin>
<margin>
The example of a painter imitating something.
</margin>
The introductory <term>spiritual elevation<note>original: "anagoge"; a Greek term for the process of leading the mind upward from visible symbols to invisible, divine truths.</note></term> of this perfecting consecration suggests, I believe, through those things which are consecrated by that divine Ointment, that holy men must veil the sanctity and fragrance of their minds. For godlike men are divinely commanded not to display the beautiful and fragrant likenesses of the hidden God for the sake of vain glory. Indeed, the hidden beauties of God—whose sweetness surpasses the reach of the intellect—are entirely undefiled; they appear spiritually only to spiritual men, because they require that we possess within our souls images that are conformable to them through virtue and incorruptibility. For that <term>infinite<note>original: "incircumscriptum"; literally "uncircumscribed" or "without boundaries," referring to the nature of divine virtue.</note></term> likeness of godlike virtue must be duly imitated, so that a spiritual and fragrant beauty may reflect it, forming and shaping itself according to its most beautiful model.

And just as in the case of visible images, if a painter looks constantly at the original model <note>the "archetype" or the subject being painted</note>, distracted by no other visible thing and not divided in his focus, he will—in a sense—replicate the very person who is to be depicted (if one may say so). He will express the truth itself in the likeness, and the model in the image, representing the one in the other without a difference in essence <note>Though the paint and the person are different substances, the "likeness" is the same.</note>. In the same way, for those "painters" who love beauty in their minds, an intent and constant contemplation of the fragrant and hidden beauty will instill an infallible and most godlike formation. Rightly, therefore, do the divine painters, when they direct their minds toward that <term>beyond-essence<note>original: "supraessentialem"; a characteristic Dionysian term used to describe God as being "above" or "beyond" the category of "being" or "essence."</note></term>, fragrant, and spiritual beauty...

From this it happens that they themselves become a terror to the opposing powers, and they are even placed in charge of healing others.
