For those who have returned from a life of wickedness to a holy mind, these mysteries implant a certain holy disposition so they are not captured by iniquity again. For those who lack anything for total purity, the mysteries perfectly cleanse them. They promote the holy toward divine images and to the contemplation and fellowship of those same images. Likewise, they feed those who are already fully holy, fulfilling and unifying their singleness of mind with that "One" <note>original: "uno illo"; referring to the Divine Unity or God</note> through blessed and spiritual visions.

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
What further? Does not the present consecration being celebrated here also dismiss those ranks that are not fully pure—those we mentioned earlier—without distinction? This is done in the same way as in the <term>Synaxis<note>original: "Sinaxi"; the gathering for the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note></term>. Indeed, this mystery is perceived only in sacred images <note>symbolic representations</note>, and is immediately beheld and celebrated only by the most holy men in the spiritual elevations of the <term>Hierarchy<note>original: "Hierarchicis anagogiis"; the process of being led upward from material symbols to spiritual truths</note></term>. However, since these things have been said by us many times, I think it is superfluous to repeat them in the same words. Instead, passing on to what follows, let us look upon the <term>Pontiff<note>original: "Pontificem"; the Bishop</note></term> as he is veiled by twelve wings <note>original: "alis duodecim obvelatum"; likely referring to the liturgical fans or veils decorated with Seraphim, who have six wings each (6x2=12)</note> while holding the sacred Ointment and consecrating the most pure Sacrament within it. <margin>What the composition of the Ointment signifies.</margin> We say, therefore, that the composition of the Ointment is a certain collection of fragrant materials, which contains within itself an abundance of sweet-smelling qualities; and he who...

Being sweetly moved by these and filled with sacred perceptions, these minds enjoy spiritual food as those fragrant distributions enter the spiritual part of the soul by divine generosity.

By no means, therefore, did the most divine order of celestial essences <note>the angels</note> ignore that the most divine Jesus descended for the sake of our sanctification; rather, it knew that He, on account of His divine and ineffable goodness, had holily lowered Himself to our level. Seeing Him sanctified in a human manner by the Father and the Spirit, the angelic order recognized its own Principle <note>Christ as the source of their existence</note> in those things which He did divinely, remaining unchanged in His essence.

<margin>Why the Ointment is called a <term>consecration</term> <note>original Greek: *teletē*</note>.</margin>
Through divine dispensation, these blessings flow down benevolently to us—who are, as it were, born of God. For this reason, I believe, according to the <term>Hierarchical</term> <note>the sacred order or "holy rule" of the Church</note> sense handed down from God, the divine leaders of our sacred order call this holy <term>mystery of the Ointment</term> a <term>consecration</term> <note>original Greek: *teletē*</note>. This is because it actually consecrates and brings things to their final perfection. One might call it a "consecration of God," speaking of His divine perfection in two ways: it is a consecration of God because He was sanctified in a human way for our sake, and also because, as God, He Himself consecrates and sanctifies everything that is to be made holy. Furthermore, those who know Hebrew say that the sacred melody of the divinely inspired Prophets <note>referring to the word "Hallelujah"</note> means "praise of God" or "*Praise the Lord*." Since every sacred appearance and action of God is described through various combinations of <term>hierarchical symbols</term>, it is entirely fitting to remember the praise of the Prophets which they learned from God; for it teaches clearly and holily that divine benefits are worthy of the highest praise.

<margin>[Conse]cration of the celestial spirits.</margin>
...that which is most removed from matter, through which they know themselves and God, and which is a state of divine imitation as complete in <term>deiformity</term> <note>original Latin: *deiformitatis*; the state of being God-like or shaped by the divine</note> as is possible. <margin>To whom the Legal Hierarchy was given.</margin>
Following that celestial and super-worldly Hierarchy, the Divinity, kindly bestowing its most sacred gifts upon us, granted the **Legal Hierarchy** <note>This refers to the religious system and laws given to the Israelites in the Old Testament</note> to those who were "infants," as Scripture testifies. This was granted under slender images and likenesses of the truth which differed greatly from the originals, and through obscure enigmas and figures which possessed a hidden and not-so-easily discerned understanding,

pouring out upon them a light proportioned to their capacity, as if for weaker eyes, without causing them harm. The mystery of this Legal Hierarchy was a kind of introduction to spiritual worship. Its leaders were those who had learned the ritual of that sacred tabernacle from **Moses**, the first Teacher and leader of the <term>Pontiffs</term> <note>original Latin: *Pontificum*; here used to describe the high priests or chief religious leaders of the Law</note> of the Law. Moses, in describing the Hierarchy of the Law for the purpose of instruction in that sacred tabernacle, referred everything that was sacredly done in the law back to the image and imitation of the original pattern <note>original Latin: *exemplaris*</note> that had been shown to him on Mount Sinai.

<margin>Our hierarchy is intermediate between the Legal and the Celestial.</margin>
...those individuals were perfected <note>original Latin: *perficiebantur*; the text begins mid-word from the previous page</note> who, according to their capacity, were promoted from the signs of the <term>Legal Hierarchy</term> <note>referring to the religious system of the Old Testament Law</note> toward a more perfect discipline. Indeed, Sacred Scripture calls our own Hierarchy a "more perfect discipline of the mysteries," naming it the fulfillment and sacred end of that [Legal] system. 

Our Hierarchy is, in fact, the same as both the Celestial and the Legal through a certain communion of its "middle condition." It shares in the "extremes" because it participates with the Celestial Hierarchy in spiritual contemplations, while it participates with the Legal Hierarchy through a variety of signs perceived by the senses, through which one is led toward the divine presence. Furthermore, it possesses a threefold distribution of sacred order, being divided into the most holy ceremonies of the mysteries, the <term>deiform</term> <note>original: *deiformem*; shaped in the likeness of God</note> ministers of the sacred rites, and those who are promoted by these ministers toward the sacred things appropriate to each person. 

Each of these three divisions of our Hierarchy is established as a first, middle, and last rank, similar to both the Legal Hierarchy and the Hierarchy that is more divine than our own <note>the Celestial Hierarchy</note>. This structure is supported by the virtue of a sacred proportion that is most beautiful, appropriate to its own order, and a fellowship that connects all things together.

<margin>§. 3. There are three functions of the Hierarchy.</margin>
Thus, the most holy consecration of the mysteries possesses a first deiform power, by which it purifies the uninitiated <note>original: *profanos*; those outside the sacred mysteries</note> through sacred rites; a middle power, by which it initiates those already purified by illuminating them; and finally, a last power—the highest of the preceding ones—by which it completes and perfects those initiated into the sacred rites through the knowledge of their own specific consecrations. 

Furthermore, the distinction among the sacred ministers likewise holds these powers: by the first power, they purify the uninitiated through the mysteries; by the middle power, they illuminate those who have been purified; and finally, by the last and supreme power of the sacred ministers, they [perfect] those who [receive] the divine light... <note>the text cuts off here at the end of the page</note>

<margin>§. 5. The Bishop is first in the Hierarchical order.</margin>

Therefore, the divine order of Bishops <note>original: *Pontificum*; literally "Pontiffs," referring to the highest rank of the clergy</note> is the first of those orders that behold God, and it is likewise both the highest and the last; for in it, every distinction of our Hierarchy is perfected and fulfilled. For just as we see the whole Hierarchy culminate in Jesus, so too does each particular hierarchy culminate in its own divine Bishop. Furthermore, the power of the Hierarchical order is grasped in all sacred distinctions, and through all the sacred orders of the Hierarchy, it perfects the mysteries which are proper to itself. Yet the divine law has assigned more divine duties to this rank, preeminently above the other orders, for its ministry. These duties are truly the principal images of God's perfecting power, by which all the most divine symbols and all sacred distinctions are brought to completion. For although certain venerable Sacraments may be performed by Priests, nevertheless a Priest will never complete that divine regeneration without the most divine <term>Ointment</term> <note>original: *Unguento*; the sacred Chrism used in baptism and confirmation</note>, nor will he consecrate the mysteries of the divine Communion unless the Sacraments of communion have been placed upon the most divine altar. Indeed, he will not even be a Priest unless he has been promoted to that lot by the initiatory rites of a Bishop. The order of the Bishopric <note>original: *Pontificatus seu Episcopatus*</note> is, therefore, the rank which, supported by a perfecting power, preeminently completes every fulfilling duty of the sacred order. It hands down the interpretations of the sacred disciplines and teaches which sacred dispositions and virtues are appropriate for them. The order of Priests <note>original: *Sacerdotum*</note>, however, is that which illuminates; it leads those who have been initiated toward the contemplation of the sacred mysteries. This order is subject to the rank of the divine Bishops, with whom it celebrates its own proper duties. In the things it performs, it demonstrates divine works through the most holy signs and Sacraments, making those who approach into spectators <note>Dionysius often describes the liturgy as a "spectacle" or sacred drama that allows the faithful to see spiritual truths through physical signs</note> and admitting them into the society and communion of the holy mysteries. However, the Priest refers those who seek the discipline <note>the deeper theological instruction or "theory"</note> of the mysteries they have seen back to the Bishop.

But the order of ministers, or Deacons <note>original: *Diaconorum*</note>, is that which purifies <note>original: *expiat*; to cleanse or make ready</note> and distinguishes the dissimilar <note>those not yet ready for the higher mysteries</note> before they come to the sacred rites of the Priests. It cleanses those approaching so as to render them immune from contrary influences and worthy of the sight and communion of the sacred mysteries. Thus, in the sacred "regeneration" <note>the sacrament of Baptism</note> of God, the Deacons strip the one who approaches of their old clothing and remove their shoes; they then face them toward the West <note>traditionally associated with the darkness of the world and the devil</note> for the purpose of renunciation, and turn them back toward the East <note>the direction of the rising sun, symbolizing Christ</note>. For the Deacons are of a purifying rank and power, urging those who approach to completely set aside the garments of their former life. By exposing the darkness of their former error, they teach them that by dismissing obscure things, they may transfer themselves toward those things that provide light. The order of Deacons is therefore one of purification, leading those who have been cleansed toward the noble sacred rites of the Priests, and...

ST. DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE

Just as the Supreme Deity first purifies the minds into which He enters, then illuminates them, and finally leads those who have been enlightened toward a certain god-like perfection, so too does the sacred Order <note>original: *Ordo*; here referring to the Hierarchy as a whole</note>—which presides over the divine images—rightly divide itself into different ranks and powers. This clearly demonstrates that those primary divine actions <note>The triad of purification, illumination, and perfection</note> consistently and distinctly reside within the most holy and pure orders. But since we have already explained the ranks and duties of the Priests, as well as their powers and actions to the best of our ability, let us now consider their most sacred consecrations <note>The rites of ordination or "mysteries" by which a person is set apart for office</note> as far as we are able.

## II. THE MYSTERY
->of the consecration of the sacred Orders.<-

<margin>The rite of consecrating a Bishop.</margin> The Bishop <note>original: *Pontifex*; Dionysius uses this term for the highest rank, the "perfecter"</note> who is being elevated to the Episcopal consecration, kneeling on both knees before the altar, has the God-given Scriptures <note>The Bible</note> placed upon his head, along with the hand of the presiding Bishop; in this manner, he is consecrated with the most holy prayers by the Bishop who ordains him.

<margin>The Priest.</margin> The Priest, however, kneeling on both knees before the altar, has the right hand of the Bishop placed upon his head, and in this manner, he is consecrated with holy invocations by the Bishop who ordains him.

<margin>The Deacon.</margin> Furthermore, the Deacon, kneeling on only one knee before the divine altar, has the right hand of the ordaining Bishop placed upon his head, and is consecrated by him with invocations suited to the consecration of ministers <note>The lowest of the three holy ranks</note>. Each of these candidates receives the sign of the cross from the ordaining Bishop, and for each, a holy proclamation <note>The public announcement of the candidate's name</note> and a perfecting greeting <note>A ritual kiss of peace signifying full entry into the order</note> is performed, while all the clergy present join with the Bishop in— <note>The sentence continues onto the next page</note>

### III. CONTEMPLATION

<margin>§ 1. What is common to each order and what is specific to them.</margin>
There are indeed certain actions common to Bishops <note>original: *Pontificibus*</note>, Priests, and Ministers <note>original: *ministris*; referring to Deacons</note> when they are being consecrated: the approach to the divine altar, the bending of the knees, the laying on of the Bishop's hand, the sign of the cross, the proclamation <note>The formal announcement of the candidate's name and rank</note>, and the concluding greeting of peace. However, there is a special rite reserved solely for Bishops: the placing of the Holy Scriptures upon the head, which the lower orders do not receive. For Priests, the specific ritual involves kneeling on both knees, a requirement not found in the consecration of Ministers; for Ministers, as has been stated, bend only one knee.

<margin>§ 2. What the approach to the altar and the kneeling signify.</margin>
Therefore, that approach to the divine altar and the bending of the knees suggests to all those being initiated into the sacred Orders that they must completely submit themselves to God—who is the author of all consecration—and must offer a spiritual integrity that is entirely pure, cleansed, and single-minded. This is so that, as much as possible, the candidate may be worthy of the divine temple and the altar of Him who, in a most holy way, consecrates <term>deiform minds</term> <note>minds that have been reshaped into the likeness of God</note>.

<margin>§ 3. The meaning of the laying on of hands.</margin>
The laying on of the Bishop's hand signifies "Hierarchical protection." By this gesture, the Bishop, with paternal affection, cherishes them as holy sons, imparts the status and power of their sacred Order, and drives away all opposing powers from them. At the same time, it teaches those who have been so consecrated to perform all the sacred functions of their office as if they were performing them under God’s own eye, having Him as the guide for every one of their actions.

What the proclamation of names means.

The Bishop <note>original: *Pontifex*</note> proclaims the sacred announcement of the ordinations and of those being initiated. This mystery declares that the provider of these sacred orders, who is beloved by God, acts as the interpreter of God's own choice. He does not promote those being initiated to a sacred Order by his own personal favor, but is guided by the inspiration of God in all these hierarchical ordinations.

We say, therefore, that the orders being cleansed are those crowds who are separated from the sacred functions and consecrations, whom we mentioned earlier. Within this group:
* One part is kept away from sacred things because they are still being nurtured and formed toward a life-giving birth by the ministers using "midwife-like words" <note>original: *verbis obstetricantibus*; a metaphor for catechumens being prepared for baptismal "rebirth" through teaching.</note>;
* Another part is kept away because they are still being called back to that holiness of life from which they fell, through the encouraging discipline of good words <note>This refers to penitents: baptized Christians who have sinned and are seeking readmission to communion.</note>;
* Another because they are still weakly terrified by contrary fears and must be strengthened by powerful words <note>Likely referring to the "energumenoi" or those believed to be troubled by spirits or spiritual anxiety.</note>;
* Another because they are still being led from perverse works toward sacred actions;
* And yet another because, although they have already been led toward the right path, they have not yet attained constancy in divine and unchanging knowledge.

These are the orders which are cleansed <note>original: *expiantur*; purified or purged of obstacles to the divine.</note> through the care and purging power of the ministers. The sacred ministers advance these people by their own virtues so that, once perfectly purified, they may be led to the illuminating contemplation and communion of the most illustrious sacrifices.

The middle order <note>This "middle order" refers to the general body of the faithful (the laity) who have been baptized but are not monks.</note> is that which enjoys the sight of certain sacred things and, according to its own capacity, participates in them in all purity. This group has been entrusted to the care of the priests in order to receive light. It is clear, I think, that this group is free from all...

The highest of all those who are being perfected <note>In this context, "perfected" refers to reaching the final stage of initiation or spiritual completion.</note> is the sacred order of **Monks**. They have been purified of every sin with all their strength and with total holiness in their actions. They have become spectators and participants in every mystery which it is lawful for them to behold. Having been handed over to the "perfecting order" of **Bishops**, they are educated by divine illuminations and the Bishop's instructions regarding the consecration of the sacred mysteries pertaining to them. From this sacred knowledge, they are raised to the most complete perfection possible according to their own capacity. For this reason, our holy teachers have addressed them with divine names: some call them <term>Therapeutes</term> (or "worshippers/servants of God") <note>original: *Therapeutas*</note>, others call them <term>Monks</term> <note>original: *Monachos*</note>. They are named both for their sincere devotion to and worship of God, and for their "individual" and "singular" (solitary) life. This life leads them away from the distractions of divided things toward a certain "deiform" <note>God-like in form or character.</note> unity and a perfection pleasing to God. For this reason, the holy Law has granted them a "perfecting grace," and employs for them a certain consecrating invocation—

## II. THE MYSTERY

->Of Monastic consecration.<-

<margin>The rite of consecrating Monks.</margin>The Priest stands before the altar, holily reciting the Monastic invocation; but he who is being consecrated stands behind the Priest. He bows neither both knees nor even one, nor does he have the divinely handed down <term>Scriptures</term> <note>In the ordination of a Bishop, the Gospels were placed on the candidate's head; here, Dionysius notes this is omitted for monks.</note> placed upon his head, but he simply stands near the Priest as he continues the mystical invocation over him. When this is finished, the Priest approaches him and asks him first whether he renounces all <term>divided things</term> <note>original: "rebus dividuis". This refers to the distractions and multiplicity of the material world, which the monk leaves behind to seek the "Unity" of God.</note>, not only vices, but even worldly imaginings. Then he explains to him the most perfect life, testifying that he must surpass a mediocre way of living. When the one being initiated has steadily professed all these things, the Priest, having marked him with the **sign of the cross**, tonsures him <note>The ritual cutting of hair.</note>, invoking the three persons of the divine Blessedness. Then, having removed all his clothing, he dresses him in another garment, and greeting him along with the other holy men standing by, he makes him a participant in the divine mysteries.

<margin>
§ 5. What the sacred Communion signifies.
</margin>

Finally, at the conclusion, the Priest invites the initiate to that most excellent communion with God. By this, he sacredly indicates that if the initiate has truly attained that singular **Monastic** state, he will not merely be a spectator of the sacred mysteries that pertain to him—nor will he approach the communion of the Most Holy Sacraments in the same manner as the <term>middle order</term> <note>The "middle order" refers to the baptized laity, who occupy the rank between the uninitiated/penitents and the clergy.</note>. Rather, being supported by a divine knowledge of those Sacraments he has received, he is to be advanced to the participation of the Divine Communion in a different way than the holy [lay] people. 

It is for this very reason that the communion of the most divine **Eucharist** is also given to the sacred **Orders** <note>The clergy.</note> at the conclusion of their most holy consecration by the Bishop <term>Pontiff</term> <note>original: "Pontifice". In Dionysius's writings, this specifically refers to the High Priest or Hierarch (the Bishop).</note> who consecrated them. This is done not only because the reception of the divine mysteries is the highest point of any Hierarchical participation, but also so that all the sacred Orders may participate in that most divine gift being shared—each according to their own capacity—for the advancement and perfection of their own **deification** <note>original: "deificationis". This is the process of "theosis," or becoming unified with God’s grace.</note>.

We therefore conclude that the holy initiations consist of **purification**, **illumination**, and **perfection**. The ministers belong to the order that purifies; the priests to the order that illuminates; and finally, the God-like Bishops belong to the order that perfects. However, the order that is currently being purified is kept away from the sight and communion of the sacred things, because it is still occupied with its purification.

The order to which the sight of the sacred mysteries is granted is the pious people <note>This refers to the baptized laity who are permitted to watch the liturgy but do not perform the priestly duties.</note>. The order of perfection, however, is that of the solitary **Monks**. For thus our Hierarchy, being holily arranged through the orders handed down by God, is made conformable to the heavenly Hierarchies, while it preserves—according to its strength—the **God-like** <term>Deiform</term> <note>original: "deiformes". This describes being shaped into the likeness of God.</note> marks and signs that express God.

<margin>§ 6.</margin>
<margin>
*In what way there are purifications for the heavenly orders.*
</margin>
But you will object that in the heavenly Hierarchies there are no orders to be purified (for it is wicked and false to say that any heavenly rank is subject to crime <note>original: "sceleri". In this context, it refers to sin or moral failing.</note>). I, however, unless I should wander entirely from the Most Holy mind, would altogether affirm that the heavenly essences are inwardly spotless and possess every purity in a **supramundane** <note>Beyond the physical world or earthly limitations.</note> manner. For if any had fallen into vice, it would have immediately failed from that heavenly and most pure harmony of divine minds, and would belong to the dark ruin of the **apostate** <note>The OCR reads "apostolicæ" (apostolic), but the context of "ruin" and "vice" clearly indicates "apostaticæ" (apostate), referring to the fallen angels.</note> crowd. Yet it may also be holily confessed that, in the heavenly Hierarchy, the illumination concerning things they previously did not know is a kind of **purification** <term>expiation</term> <note>original: "expiationem". Dionysius explains that for angels, "purification" does not mean washing away sin, but rather removing the "cloud" of not knowing something yet.</note> for the lower natures. By this, they are both led to a more perfect knowledge of divine things and are, in a way, purged from the ignorance of things they previously lacked knowledge of, while they are promoted by the primary and more divine essences to the more sublime and clearer illuminations of divine contemplations. And thus, in the heavenly Hierarchy, there are also orders that are illuminated and perfected, just as there are those who purge, those who illuminate, and those who perfect; so that those natures which are supreme and more divine than the rest may purge the sacred and heavenly ranks subordinated to them from all ignorance (in ways, of course, accommodated to those heavenly Hierarchies).

**§. 2.** Among the profane, however, some unreasonably believe that our bodies are completely destroyed; others think that this union of the body with its own soul is to be once and for all dissolved by a divorce, as if it were unsuitable for them in the God-like life <note>original: "deiformi vita"</note> and blessed rest. Others, meanwhile, assign the unions of other bodies to souls <note>This refers to the concept of reincarnation or the transmigration of souls.</note>; in this, in my opinion, they do an injustice to the bodies that have labored alongside the divine souls, and they defraud those bodies of their sacred rewards when they have completed their divine course. Furthermore, others—having slipped into earthly thoughts in I know not what way—have said that the most holy and most blessed lot promised to the blessed is similar to this present life, and they have wickedly attributed foods proper to this changeable life to those who are equal to the Angels. But far be it that any holy man should ever fall into errors of that kind. Instead, those holy men who have recognized that they will receive their whole Christ-like <note>original: "Christiformem"</note> lot, when they approach the end of this life, look upon their path to incorruption <term>incorruptio</term> <note>The state of being free from physical decay and death in the afterlife.</note> as something now made nearer. They praise the gifts of the highest God and are filled with divine pleasure, no longer fearing that they might be turned aside <note>meaning they no longer fear falling into sin or losing their salvation</note>, but knowing well that they will possess the good things they have acquired firmly and forever.

After this is done, the Bishop pours oil over the deceased, and having offered a prayer for everyone, he places the body in an honored location together with other holy bodies of the same rank.

<margin>§. 6. *Why prayers are made for the deceased.*</margin>
Perhaps, however, you will say that while we speak correctly, you still doubt for what reason the <term>Bishop</term> <note>original: "Antistes" — the presiding high priest or leader of the sacred rites</note> prays to divine mercy, asking that forgiveness of sins be given to the deceased and that they be granted a bright lot equal to that of godlike men. For if everyone receives from divine Justice a reward for those things which they did in this present life, whether well or poorly, and the deceased has already completed their actions in this life, what prayer of the Bishop could transfer them to a different reward of rest than that which they earned in this life? Indeed, I know well, in agreement with the Scriptures, that a portion must be rendered to each according to their merits. For the Lord, it says, has concluded within Himself, and each person will give an account of <margin>1 Cor. 5:10 <note>Note: This citation likely refers to 2 Corinthians 5:10, regarding the judgment seat of Christ.</note></margin> the things proper to the body, according to what they have done, whether good or evil. For just as if someone, while the Sun bestows its light upon healthy eyes, should seek to become a partaker of the solar light after tearing out their own eyes; so does someone hang from an impossible and empty hope who demands the prayers of the Saints while they themselves destroy the actions natural to such prayers, <margin>*To whom prayers are beneficial.*</margin> neglecting divine gifts and turning away from the most clear and beneficial commandments of God. I surely affirm that the prayers of the Saints are very useful in this life, provided that a person—burning with a desire for sacred gifts and piously disposed to receive them, while remaining conscious of their own frailty—approaches a holy man and asks that he help them and pray to God on their behalf. Indeed, it has been established by divine decrees that divine gifts are distributed to those worthy of participating in them, in an order befitting God, by those who are appointed to distribute them. 

Therefore, if anyone violates this sacred order and, seduced by an unfortunate pride, considers themselves worthy of divine familiarity and despises the Saints—and if they should ask for things unworthy of God and profane, lacking an intense desire for divine things because of their own ignorant petition—they will obtain none of those things they seek by their own effort.

<margin>§ 11. That infants who are not yet capable of reason are baptized.</margin>

But the fact that infants too, who by their age are unable to understand, become participants in the divine <term>regeneration</term> <note>original: "regenerationis" — a reference to being "born again" through the sacrament of baptism</note> and the most holy mysteries of divine <term>communion</term> <note>original: "communionis" — the Eucharist</note>, seems (as you say) to profane people to be rightly worthy of laughter. They find it no less ridiculous that others would pronounce the sacred renunciations and holy professions on their behalf. 

However, your holy prudence ought not to be angry with those who err, but should religiously and with charity provide a reason for their instruction and solve their objections. Furthermore, one should add this according to the sacred decree: that all divine matters are by no means to be measured by our own intelligence. Instead, many things that are hidden from us have causes worthy of God, which we ourselves may not know, but which are clearly understood by the orders of beings superior to us <note>This refers to the celestial hierarchy of angels</note>. Likewise, many things remain hidden even to those highest and most sublime substances, which are known only to the all-wise and wisdom-giving Divinity. 

Nevertheless, regarding this matter, we also say what our God-like teachers, having received it from ancient tradition, have passed down to us. For they say—and it is true—that infants, if they are instructed in the sacred law, will arrive at a holy state of mind free from all error and without any danger of an impure life. When this occurred to the minds of our divine instructors, it pleased them that children be admitted in this holy manner: that the natural parents of the offered little one would hand over their son to one of the faith...

Therefore, in my opinion, there is nothing absurd in bringing a child to this divine institution when he has a leader and a sponsor who both imbues him with knowledge of divine things and keeps him safe from spiritual adversaries. Furthermore, the <term>Pontiff</term> <note>original: "Pontifex" — the high priest or bishop</note> makes the child a sharer in the sacred <term>mysteries</term> <note>original: "mysteriorum" — here referring to the sacraments, specifically baptism and the Eucharist</note> so that he may be raised within them, and lead no other life than one which always looks toward divine things. Through this kind of holy communion, the child may progress, possess a sacred character within these rites, and be zealously advanced by his <term>godly sponsor</term> <note>original: "susceptore deiformi" — literally a 'god-formed receiver' or godparent</note>.

These things, my son, are the great and magnificent sights of our <term>Hierarchy</term> <note>original: "Hierarchiæ" — the structured order of the church's sacred rites and offices</note> that have been manifested to me; but to other, perhaps more perceptive minds, not only these things, but even other much more illustrious and god-like visions have been perceived. Indeed, to you also, I believe, clearer and more divine beauties will shine forth if you ascend to that more sublime ray by the steps I have described.

# ON THE DIVINE NAMES

## CHAPTER I.

### Dionysius the Priest to his fellow-priest Timothy.

->The purpose of this book, and the traditions handed down concerning the Divine names.<-

**SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.**

1. He teaches that every doctrine concerning God must be sought from the Scriptures, and that from sensible things <note>Meaning things we can perceive with our physical senses</note> it is impossible to know what spiritual things are, and much less to know God. 2. One must not presume to say anything about God except from the <note>Original has "Sripturis," a typo for "Scripturis"</note>Scriptures, in which God communicates a knowledge of Himself to us according to our capacity. 3. From this he concludes that the secret of God is not to be searched out rashly, but that God is to be praised from the Scriptures; and at the same time he reveals what we may learn about God from them. 4. He explains that the divine names are mostly taken from divine providences <note>The ways God looks after and interacts with the world</note> and emanations <note>The "outpourings" of God's grace or presence into creation</note>, and that in this life we know God as in a mirror or a riddle <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly"</note>, but in heaven God is seen clearly as He is in Himself—a state which we cannot now conceive, nor can we understand the state of the Blessed. 5. He says, however, that God is to be celebrated by everything and by nothing; that is, through <term>affirmation</term> <note>original: "positionem" — the "Way of Affirmation" (Kataphatic theology), stating what God is, like "God is Good"</note> and <term>negation</term> <note>original: "ablationem" — the "Way of Negation" (Apophatic theology), stating what God is not, like "God is infinite" (not-finite)</note>. 6. That God is at once <term>nameless</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνώνυμον (anonymon)</note> and <term>many-named</term> <note>original Greek: πολυώνυμον (polyonymon)</note>. 7. In what sense God lacks any name, and yet is called by every name. 8. That God is named in various ways not only from His providences, but also from His appearances.

**N**ow, blessed man, after the *Theological Outlines* <note>A reference to a previous work by the author, likely intended to be his "Theological Representations," which has not survived</note>, I apply myself to the explanation of the Divine names as far as I am able...

<summary>This page serves as the introduction to Dionysius’s famous treatise, establishing that all talk of God must be grounded in Scripture and introducing the paradox that God is both beyond all names and described by many.</summary>

# ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER I.

<margin>God exceeds all understanding.</margin>
...they are able to take on a figure and form: by this same logic of truth, that <term>suprasubstantial</term> <note>original: "suprasubstantialis" — a term meaning existing above or beyond the very category of "substance" or "being"</note> infinity is above all substances, and that unity which is above the mind is above all minds. That One which is above all reasoning is inscrutable to all our logical <term>reasonings</term> <note>original: "ratiocinationibus"</note>; and that Good which is above the word is <term>ineffable</term> <note>original: "ineffabile" — something that cannot be expressed in words</note> to every word. It is the <term>unity that creates</term> <note>original: "unitas effectrix"</note> all unity, a substance above all substance, a mind that does not fall under the grasp of intelligence, a reason that cannot be expressed by any logic; it is nameless and without intelligence, having no likeness to any other thing. Indeed, it is the cause of all things that exist, yet it is not itself one of those things, as it rests outside of everything that exists, just as it alone can properly and wisely speak these things concerning itself.

<margin>§ 2. Nothing is to be said of God except from the Scriptures.</margin>
Concerning this <term>supersubstantial</term> and hidden divinity, therefore, one must not presume to speak, nor even to think anything, except those things which have been divinely declared to us in the <term>Sacred Oracles</term> <note>original: "Sacris Eloquiis" — a term Dionysius uses to refer to the Bible as the direct utterances of God</note>. For, as the divinity has kindly handed down concerning itself in the <term>Sacred Scriptures</term>, the knowledge and contemplation of what it truly is remains inaccessible to all substances, as it is <term>super-essentially</term> <note>original: "superessentialiter" — in a manner that exists beyond the essence of created things</note> removed from all. You will find that many Theologians <note>The biblical writers</note> have praised it not only because it escapes our sight and our grasp, but also because it cannot be tracked or investigated, since no footprint exists that might lead to its most secret infinity.

<margin>God communicates Himself to us according to our capacity.</margin>
Yet, none of the things that exist are entirely without a share of its goodness; for it mercifully tempers that <term>supersubstantial</term> ray, which is persistently planted within itself, with illuminations appropriate to each thing. Furthermore, it raises holy minds to whatever level of contemplation, communion, and likeness is permitted, as they strive toward it...

->### ST. DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE<-

...they should strive as much as they are able, provided they do not presumptuously attempt anything more sublime than the divine illumination allows according to their capacity, nor fall headlong into error through a perverse inclination. <margin>§ 3. The mystery of God is not to be scrutinized, but the mind is to be stirred to the praise of God from the Scriptures.</margin>
Imitating, then, those divine scales which govern all the holy distinctions of the heavenly orders, we should leave the mystery of the supreme Divinity—which transcends all intelligence and substance—free from our scrutiny. With sacred venerations of the mind, and following those ineffable <note>ineffable: something that is too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note> things with a certain modest silence, let us attend to the splendors that shine upon us from the sacred <term>Scriptures</term> <note>original: "Eloquiis" — literally "utterances" or "oracles," referring to the Bible</note>. By these sacred songs of praise, we are shaped to contemplate the divine lights granted to us in the Scriptures according to our capacity. Thus, we should praise the beneficent source of every illumination, just as it has expressed itself concerning itself in those same Scriptures.

<margin>What things we may learn about God from the Scriptures.</margin>
For instance, we learn that it is the cause and origin of all things, the essence and the life, the calling back and resurrection of those who have fallen away from it, and the renewal and reformation of those who have obscured the divine image in themselves. It is likewise the stability of those who waver with impure movement, the security of those who stand fast, the guidance of those striving toward it, the illumination of those being enlightened, the perfecting principle of the perfected, the supreme divinity of those being <term>deified</term> <note>original: "deificatorum" — the process of "theosis," or becoming God-like through divine grace</note>, the simplicity of the simplified, the unity of the united. It is the <term>super-original principle</term> <note>original: "superoriginale principium"</note> of every principle in a way that is <term>super-essential</term> <note>original: "superessentialiter" — existing beyond the very category of "essence" or "being"</note>, and the beneficent communication of that hidden secret, as far as is lawful...

# ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER I.

...communication, and to speak plainly, the life of the living, the essence of beings, and the principle and cause of all life and essence. This is because of His goodness, by which He both brings all things into existence so that they may be, and sustains them so they do not perish.

<margin>§ 4. Divine names are mostly derived from emanations.</margin>
We have learned these things from the divine <term>Scriptures</term> <note>original: "Scripturis divinis"</note>; and, so to speak, you will find that almost all of the sacred Scripture, in declaring God to us and praising Him, forms divine names according to the <term>emanations</term> <note>emanations: the outward flow of divine power, life, and goodness from God into the created universe</note> of divine goodness. Hence, in almost every theological treatise, we see the divinity itself holily praised: as a **monad** <note>monad: a single, indivisible unit or "oneness"</note> and **unity** because of the simplicity of His supernatural, indivisible nature, from which—by His unifying power—we exist as a single whole. When our own divided differences are joined together in a way that transcends the world, we are led back to a certain God-like "monad" and a union that imitates God. 

He is praised as a **Trinity**, however, because of the manifestation of <term>super-essential</term> <note>super-essential: existing beyond the very category of "essence" or "being"; used to describe God's nature as higher than anything we can define</note> fruitfulness in three persons, from which all fatherhood in heaven and on earth exists and is named. 

He is praised as the **Cause of things**, because all things have been produced through His goodness, the maker of all. 

He is also called **Wise** and **Beautiful**, because all things, as long as they keep their nature uncorrupted, are full of all divine harmony and sacred beauty. 

Finally, He is described as embracing the human race with a singular love, because He truly and completely communicated Himself to us in one of His persons, calling back to Himself and joining to Himself our human lowliness. From this union, the "simple Jesus" <note>original: "simplex Jesus" — referring to the unity of Christ's person despite having two natures</note> exists in an inexpressible way; He who is eternal took on a temporal beginning, and even descended to the innermost parts of our nature—He who <term>transcends</term> the entire order of all nature in a way that is beyond essence.

<summary>This page explains that the names used for God in the Bible (such as Monad, Trinity, and Cause) are based on the different ways His goodness interacts with and creates the world. It emphasizes that while God is a single, simple unity, He reveals Himself through these various roles to bring humanity back into union with Him.</summary>

On the contrary, it is necessary to praise it as being supremely abstracted from every habit, motion, life, imagination, opinion, name, speech, thought, intelligence, substance, state, foundation, union, end, immensity, and finally from all things whatsoever that exist. 

However, since goodness itself, by the very fact of its being, is the cause of all things, the providence of God—the Prince of those who are called "gods" <note>"those who are called gods": A reference to Psalm 82 and John 10:34, referring to angels or deified humans who participate in God's grace.</note> and the source of all good things—must be praised through all of its effects. This is because all things exist around it and for its sake, and it is itself before all things, and in it all things consist. Its very being produces all things and makes them exist, and all things desire it; spiritual and rational things through know[ledge]...

**§. 7.** Thus, therefore, it is fitting for Him who is the cause of all things and above all to be without a name; and yet, conversely, all the names of all things are fitting for Him, so that there may be a perfect kingdom of the universe. All things exist around Him and depend upon Him as their cause, their beginning, and their end. He Himself is, as the Scripture says, *all in all* <note>1 Corinthians 15:28</note>. He is truly praised as the one who brings all things into being, who begins, perfects, and contains them—both a protection and a home—and the one who turns all things back toward Himself. He does this in a way that is unified, irresistible, and excellent. For He is not only the cause of the sustaining of all things, and of life and perfection, such that the Goodness which surpasses every name is named only for this providence (or for some other); rather, He has anticipated all things simply and without limit within Himself through the perfections of His unique and all-effective <term>providence</term> <note>The "providence" of God refers to His purposeful governance and care for the world</note>. Thus, He is fitly praised and named by all things.

<margin>
God is named in different ways not only from His providences, but also from His appearances.
</margin>

**§. 8.** Indeed, the <term>Theologians</term> <note>Dionysius uses this term to refer to the inspired authors of the Bible</note> do not only celebrate these divine names which are drawn from His universal or specific providences, or from those things which receive His care. They also name the Divine Goodness—which surpasses every name and every splendor—based on certain divine visions. These visions, at various times in holy temples or perhaps elsewhere, illuminated the masters of the mysteries or the Prophets. For many reasons and by His power, they attribute to Him human forms and shapes, or forms of fire, or of <term>electrum</term> <note>original: "electri"; a naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver, often used in ancient descriptions of divine radiance, such as in the visions of Ezekiel</note>. They describe His eyes, His ears, His hair...

These things must be kept by you, most excellent Timothy, according to the most sacred decree, so that you do not bring forth or divulge divine matters before the profane. But may God grant that I may celebrate the many and various names of the Divinity—which cannot be called or named—in a way worthy of God, and that He may not take the word of truth from my mouth.

Those divine attributes which are fitting for God are praised by the Holy Scriptures not in part, but in the total, perfect, whole, and full divinity. All these things are referred to the complete entirety of the whole, perfect divinity without participation <note>original: "imparticipate"; this technical term means God possesses these qualities inherently and absolutely, rather than "participating" in them as created beings do</note>, absolutely, without the observation of any difference, and universally. Therefore, it must be said that these names ought to be understood as applying to the whole Deity. For even the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Verbum"; a title for Jesus Christ as the eternal Reason or Speech of God</note> itself, which is good by nature, says: <margin>Matthew 20:15</margin> *I am good*, and a certain <margin>Psalm 142:10</margin> Prophet, inspired by the divine Spirit, praises the *good Spirit*. And unless they say the whole divinity is Life, how is the holy Word true which says: <margin>John 5:21</margin> *Just as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will*; and that: <margin>John 6:64</margin> *It is the Spirit who gives life*? Furthermore, since the whole divinity holds dominion over the entire world, one cannot even say, in my opinion, how many places in Holy Scripture the name "Lord" is celebrated for the Father who begat God, or for God the Son; yet the Spirit is also Lord. "Beautiful" and "Wise" are also predicated of the whole divinity, as are "Light," and that which makes God <note>original: "id quod Deum efficit"; referring to the "deifying" power of God that raises humans to a higher state</note>, and "Cause," and whatever...

<margin>Scripture predicates some things of God unitedly, and others distinctly.</margin>
...under the guidance of theological grace? If we attend to the truth of the <term>Sacred Oracles</term> <note>original: "Eloquiorum"; Dionysius uses this term to emphasize that the Scriptures are the direct, living speech of God</note>, we shall rely on this rule and light, and hasten without hesitation to give an account according to our ability. We say that Theology teaches some things unitedly, and others distinctly; it is not permitted to separate what is united, nor to confuse what is distinct. Rather, by following the Scriptures to the best of our power, we must aspire toward the divine splendors. It is from there that we receive divine explanations—as a beautiful rule of truth—while we strive to preserve within ourselves the things hidden there, adding nothing, subtracting nothing, and perverting nothing. In this way, we are preserved by our guardianship of the Oracles, and from them, we receive the strength to defend those who observe them.

<margin>§. 3. Which things are said unitedly and which discretely.</margin>
The names that are "united"—applied to the whole divinity as a unity—which we have demonstrated at length from the Holy Scriptures in our <term>Theological Outlines</term> <note>original: "Theologicis informationibus"; a reference to a now-lost or perhaps fictional work by Dionysius</note>, are: **Beyond-Good** <note>original: "supraquam bonus"</note>, **Beyond-God** <note>original: "supraquam Deus"</note>, **Beyond-Substance** <note>original: "supraquam substantia"; this refers to God being above all created categories of "being" or "essence"</note>, **Beyond-Life**, **Beyond-Wise**, and whatever pertains to <term>negation by way of excellence</term> <note>original: "ablationis secundum exuperantiam"; the practice of saying what God is NOT to show He is greater than any human concept</note>. Along with these are numbered all things pertaining to God as Cause: the Good, the Beautiful, the Existing, the Life-giving, the Wise, and whatever gifts of His are fitting for His goodness, from which the Cause of all good things is named.

But the things that are "discrete" and distinct are the beyond-substantial name and reality of the **Father**, and of the **Son**, and of the **Holy Spirit**. In these, there is no exchange or any commonality introduced. Furthermore, a discrete and distinct matter is the perfect and immutable essence of **Jesus** as it exists among us, and all the substantial mysteries of His humanity.

§. 4.

<margin>
Unions in God are called essential attributes, while distinctions are the names taken from his emanations.
</margin>
I think it is expedient to resume the argument from a slightly higher point, so that the most perfect mode of divine union and distinction may be explained. In this way, our entire discourse may be so clear to us that it rejects all variety and obscurity, and instead defines—distinctly, plainly, and in order—those things that are proper to God, as far as that is possible. The authors of our theological tradition <note>Dionysius usually refers to the Apostles or his mentor, Hierotheus, when he mentions "tradition."</note> call "Divine Unions" those hidden and foundational placements of the more-than-ineffable and beyond-measure unknown indwelling, which nowhere reveals itself. However, they call "distinctions" the beneficial <term>emanation</term> <note>original: "emanationes"; the process by which God’s goodness "flows out" to create and sustain the universe without losing its own essence</note> and manifestations of God. By following the Holy Scriptures, they assign certain properties to the aforementioned union, and likewise to the distinction, as well as their own respective joinings and separations. 

For example, regarding the divine union—or <term>supersubstantiality</term> <note>original: "supersubstantialitate"; refers to God existing beyond the category of "substance" or "being" as we understand it</note>—what is joined and common to the Trinity (which is the principle of all unity) is: a super-essential existence; a divinity that is beyond-divine; a goodness that is beyond-good; the supreme identity of the whole property of that which is above all things; a unity that is above the very principle of unity; ineffability; the state of having many names and yet no name; undemonstrability; and the quality of being the source of all understanding. To this union also belongs the <term>position</term> <note>original: "positio"; the "cataphatic" way of affirming all things of God as their cause</note> of all things and the <term>removal</term> <note>original: "ablatio"; the "apophatic" way of denying all limited qualities to God</note> of all things, which exists above every affirmation and negation. It includes the mutual indwelling and placement of the divine persons within themselves—if it is permitted to speak this way—entirely and more-than-joined into a unity, yet not confused in any part. 

It is like the lights of lamps <note>This is one of Dionysius's most famous analogies for the Trinity: separate sources of light that fill a room with a single, indistinguishable glow.</note> (to use familiar examples that fall under our senses) which are in a single house: they are entirely within one another in their entirety, yet they are not mixed. They exist perfectly distinct from one another in their individual identities, joined into one distinctly, and distinct joinly.

How the three persons are united as whole selves without confusion and are one. An example.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 160 regarding the "unions" and "distinctions" within the Godhead. Having established the theoretical definitions, Dionysius now employs the famous analogy of the lamps to illustrate how the persons of the Trinity can be simultaneously united and distinct.</meta>

<page-num>161</page-num>

-># ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER II.<-

For indeed, we see in a house where there are many lamps that the lights of all coalesce into one single light and produce a single, undivided radiance. No one, I think, is able to distinguish the light of one lamp from the others in the air that contains all the lights, nor can one see one light apart from the others, because they are all entirely mingled with one another without confusion.

Moreover, if someone were to carry one lamp out of the house, its own specific light would go out with it, without dragging any of the other lights along with it, and without leaving any of its own light behind for them. For as I said, there was a perfect joining of the whole of them to the whole of them; a joining that was entirely pure and in no part confused, even though that light existed in a physical body (that is, the air) and depended upon material fire. Therefore, we say that the <term>supersubstantial</term> <note>original: "supersubstantialem"; referring to that which exists beyond the realm of "substance" or created being</note> union is far superior, not only to those unions that exist in physical bodies, but even to those that occur in souls and minds themselves. These minds possess their unions in an unconfused and beyond-the-world manner, while those God-like and super-heavenly lights participate in each other—whole to whole—through a certain union that is more eminent than all others, by a participation proportionate to themselves.

<margin>§. 5. *The Divine persons are distinct by relation alone.*</margin>

Furthermore, there is a distinction in the <term>superessential</term> <note>original: "superessentialibus"; meaning above or beyond the very essence or nature of things as we understand them</note> names of God. By this distinction, not only is each of the principal persons placed as unmixed and unconfused according to the union itself (as I have said), but also those things which belong to the <term>supersubstantial</term> divine generation <note>The internal "begetting" of the Son by the Father and the "procession" of the Spirit</note> are by no means reciprocal among themselves. Thus, the Father alone is the source in the <term>supersubstantial Deity</term> <note>original: "supersubstantiali Deitate"; the Godhead that exists beyond the category of substance</note>, and so the Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father, but—

...so that the proper praises belonging to each of the divine Persons <note>The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note> are preserved inviolate. These indeed are the unions and the distinctions within that ineffable union and essence. But if the "divine distinction" is understood as the <term>procession</term> <note>original: "emanatio"; the way God "comes out" of Himself to create and sustain the world</note> belonging to the Good—flowing from the divine union which is multiplied beyond unity by the goodness of God—then those "distinctions" are actually united in their incomprehensible state. These include the communications, the <term>bestowals of being</term> <note>original: "substantificationes"; the act by which God gives "substance" or "being" to things</note>, the bestowals of life, the bestowals of wisdom, and the other such gifts of the goodness that causes all things. According to these gifts, those things which are participated in without being shared <note>original: "imparticipate participantur"; a paradox meaning God gives of Himself without losing any part of Himself</note> are praised through the participations and the participants.

<margin>
**God, in His whole self, is both participable and non-participable.**
</margin>

And this is common, joined, and one for the whole divinity: namely, that the divinity itself is participated in by each of those participating in it, yet by no one in any specific part. It is like the center point in the middle of a circle: it is shared by all the straight lines which are drawn around it in the circle. Or it is like many impressions of a seal that share in the <term>original seal</term> <note>original: "archetypum sigillum"</note>; in every single figure impressed by the seal, the whole and same seal is present, and in no figure is it present only in part. However, the "unparticipability" of the divinity—which is the cause of all things—surpasses these examples; for in God's case, there is no physical touch, nor any other mixing or shared contact with those things that participate in Him.

<margin>
§. 6. **The seal is not the cause of unequal participation, but rather the underlying matter.**
</margin>

But someone might say that the seal is not truly "whole and the same" in all the figures it produces. In truth, the seal is not the cause of this difference (for the seal communicates itself as a whole and as the same to each one), but rather the difference between those receiving the impression makes the images of the one, whole, and same original form appear dissimilar. For example: if the <term>underlying materials</term> <note>original: "materia subjecta"; here referring to the wax or surface being stamped</note> are soft, easy to shape, smooth, and without a form of their own—neither resistant, nor hard, nor so fluid that they run—then...

...constancy, they will have a clear, open, and permanent form; but if anything is lacking in the said fitness <note>Referring to the capacity of the recipient to receive God's light</note>, that will surely be the reason why the form is less expressed and clear, and other things happen which usually occur from an unfitness for participation.

Furthermore, in the beneficial <term>restoration</term> <note>original: "reparatione"; referring to the salvation of humanity</note> of us, this gift is distinct from the Deity: namely, that for our sake and from our own nature, the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Verbum"; the Second Person of the Trinity</note>—who is above all substance—assumed our whole and true substance, and performed and suffered those things which are specific and unique to His human action. For these actions are in no way common to the Father and the Spirit, unless perhaps one says they are "common" by the community of a kind and humane counsel <note>i.e., the Trinity agreed on the plan, but only the Son became human</note>, and according to all that eminent and ineffable divine operation which He, who was immutable, exercised while existing among us, insofar as He is God and the Word of God. We also similarly strive to join and distinguish divine things in speech, just as they are indeed either united or distinct in themselves.

<margin>
§. 7.
</margin>
But whatever reasons agreeable to God regarding these unions and distinctions we find in the <term>Scriptures</term> <note>original: "Eloquiis"; literally "the Utterances," the author's preferred term for the Bible</note>, we have explained them as best we could in the *Theological Outlines* <note>original: "Institutionibus Theologicis"; a lost or perhaps fictional work by Dionysius</note>, discussing each separately. We did this partly by unraveling and explaining them with true reasoning, and thus bringing a pure and tranquil mind to the contemplations of the light of the Scriptures; 

<margin>
We know divine things only from participations.

## ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER II.

<margin>Effects are like their causes, but not the reverse. Examples.</margin>
...between those things which are produced as effects and their causes: rather, the effects possess images of their causes as far as is possible; however, the causes themselves are set apart from their effects and are established and founded above them, according to the logic of their own primacy. To use examples from our own experience: pleasures and pains are said to produce joy or sorrow in men, yet these feelings themselves neither rejoice nor suffer. Even though fire heats and burns, it is not said to be burned or heated itself. And if anyone were to say that Life itself "lives," or that Light is "illuminated," in my opinion, he would not be speaking entirely correctly—unless perhaps he says this in another sense: namely, that the causes possess the qualities of their effects beforehand in a more abundant and essential way.

<margin>§. 9. The manner of the incarnation is unknown to everyone</margin>

We have received through the sacred mysteries that He indeed assumed the form and substance of a man, but it remains unknown how He was formed from the Virgin's blood by a law other than that of nature, or in what way He walked with dry feet—despite possessing the physical bulk of a body and the weight of matter—across the liquid and flowing substance of the water, and performed other deeds which indicate the supernatural nature of <term>JESUS</term>. # CHAPTER III.

## What the power of prayer is, and concerning the blessed Hierotheus, and concerning piety and theological writing.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.

*1. It teaches that one must approach God through prayer; not because God is absent from us, but so that we may be present to God in mind and spirit. <meta>This page continues Chapter III, which explores the nature of prayer. It follows the discussion of the Trinity and the divine names, moving into a famous philosophical explanation of how prayer functions not by changing God, but by changing the person who prays.</meta>

<page-num>170</page-num>
->ST. DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE<-

...and the gifts that are placed within her <note>original: "ipsam" - referring to the feminine Latin noun "Divinitas" (the Divinity)</note> disposal; for she is indeed present to all, but not all things are present to her. But when we entreat her with holy prayers, with a tranquil mind, and a heart prepared for divine union, then at last we ourselves are truly present to her.

<margin>Note: God is also beyond the universe.</margin>
For she is not in any one place in such a way as to be absent from another, or to migrate from one place to another. Indeed, to say that she is "in all things" is an understatement of her infinity, which both exceeds and contains the entire universe.

<margin>In prayer, it is not so much that God approaches us, but that we approach God.</margin>
Let us, therefore, lift ourselves up through prayers to the more sublime contemplation of the divine and benevolent rays. It is as if a most luminous chain were suspended from the heights of heaven and reached down to us here. If we were to grasp it with our hands, reaching upward one after the other, we would seem to be pulling the chain down to us; but in truth, we would not be drawing it down—since it is present both above and below—but we ourselves would rather be hoisted up to the more sublime splendors of those brilliant rays. 

Or, imagine we have boarded a ship and hold onto ropes stretched out to us from a rock to help us; we would not be pulling the rock toward us, but in reality, we would be drawing ourselves and the ship toward the rock. Just as, conversely, if someone standing in a ship pushes against a sea-rock, he will not move that fixed and immobile rock at all, but will instead push himself away from it; and the more violently he pushes, the further he will be removed from it. 

Therefore, before all things—and especially in <term>Theology: the study or discourse concerning God</term>—we must begin with prayer. This is not so that we might "pull down" a power that is already present both everywhere and nowhere, but so that through divine remembrances and invocations, we may give ourselves over to that power and be united with it.

<summary>Dionysius explains that prayer does not change God or bring Him down to us, but rather elevates the human soul toward the Divine, using the analogies of a hanging chain and a ship pulling toward a rock.</summary>

# ON DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER III.

<margin>
§. 2.
Why Dionysius wrote these books after Saint Hierotheus.
</margin>

And here, perhaps, we should not without cause provide a reason as to why—since our distinguished teacher Hierotheus <note>Hierotheus is described by the author as his mentor and a disciple of St. Paul, though his historical existence is debated by scholars.</note> has accurately collected the principles of Theology—we have written other works and this present theological treatise, as if his were not sufficient. Truly, if he had intended to publish all his theological treatises in a systematic order, explaining the sum of all Theology with even the briefest expositions, never would such foolishness or stupidity have taken hold of us that we would think we could penetrate these theological matters more clearly or more divinely than he. Nor would we wish to exhaust ourselves with superfluous and empty labor by repeating the same things twice, thereby inflicting such an injury upon our friend and teacher as to seize through <term>plagiarism</term> <note>original: "plagium" — in a classical sense, this refers to "kidnapping" or stealing the intellectual offspring of another.</note> the most excellent knowledge and exposition of the one by whom we were instructed, following the divine Paul.

<margin>
Saint Dionysius's praiseworthy testimony concerning Hierotheus.
</margin>

But since he, in explaining divine matters with true depth, handed down to us certain subtle definitions in a compendium <note>A "compendium" is a concise summary or abridgment of a larger body of knowledge.</note> which gather many concepts into one, I have been commanded, together with my colleagues who are dedicated to instructing souls that are still unrefined, to explain and arrange these subtle and singular conclusions—in which the spiritual power of such a great man shone forth most brightly—in a language more accommodated to our own capacity. Indeed, you yourself have also frequently exhorted us to do this, and you returned the book itself to us as being exceedingly sublime. Therefore, we assign him as a master for those of perfected and mature senses, and his writings as "secondary Scriptures" <note>original: "alterasque Scripturas" — this suggests the author viewed his teacher's work as being nearly equal in authority to the Bible.</note> which nearly reach the level of the divinely inspired authors, for those who can grasp more sublime things. But for those like ourselves, according to our capacity...

...it was your concern that you should never pursue divine matters in a perfunctory <note>To do something "perfunctorily" means to do it as a routine duty without real interest or care.</note> way.

<margin>Section 3.</margin>
<margin>*Dionysius’s humble opinion of himself.*</margin>
But let us set aside those mystical matters—since they are not to be broadcast to the general public and are already very well known to you. When the time had come to proclaim our faith to the masses and to draw as many as could be reached into our sacred discipline, [Hierotheus] surpassed many holy Teachers in this duty. He did so through his long experience, the purity of his mind, the sharpness of his arguments, and his other sacred practices, to such an extent that we never even attempted to gaze directly at such a Sun <note>Dionysius uses the Sun as a metaphor for Hierotheus’s blindingly brilliant intellect and spiritual insight.</note>.

Indeed, we are conscious—in fact, we know—that we are not at all adequate for understanding divine things; much less are we able to speak of them as if they were fully known, for they are <term>ineffable</term> <note>original: "ineffabiles" — describing something so great or sacred that it cannot be expressed in words.</note>. 

Because we fall far short of the ability of those divine men <note>Likely referring to the Apostles and their immediate successors.</note> when it comes to explaining Theological truth, we were led by an abundance of religious devotion to a point where we would not presume to hear or speak anything regarding divine Philosophy <note>In the early Church, "Philosophy" often referred to the lived pursuit of divine wisdom and the study of God, rather than just academic logic.</note>. However, we realized that we must not neglect whatever knowledge of divine things we are actually capable of attaining. 

We are persuaded of this not only by the natural desires of our minds—which are always lovingly stirred, as far as is permitted, toward the contemplation of divine things—but also by the most excellent instruction of the divine laws themselves. While these laws forbid us from curiously prying into things that are above us, exceed our merits, and surpass our understanding, they simultaneously command us to diligently learn everything that has been permitted and granted to us, and to share those things kindly with others. 

Moved by these reasons, and deterred from the lawful investigation of divine things by neither the hard work required nor by laziness, we have tried to follow those things according to our own small measure...

## CHAPTER IV.

### On the good, light, beauty, love, ecstasy, and zeal; and that evil is neither a being, nor from beings, nor in beings.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*1. He teaches that <term>Goodness</term> <note>original: "bonitas" — here referring to God’s nature as the source of all benefit.</note> is the primary attribute of God, and that all things consist by the divine goodness. 2. From this goodness come the orders and functions of the Angels; likewise souls and their faculties; and similarly all animate and inanimate things. 3. Goodness is above all things, and it calls even those things that do not exist to come into being. 4. This goodness is the cause of the heavens and their motion; the Sun, however, is an image of divine goodness, turning all things toward itself. 5. He teaches why God is called **Light**. 6. That God is an <term>intelligible light</term> <note>original: "lumen intelligibile" — a light perceived by the intellect or soul rather than the physical eyes.</note>, and how great His excellence and power are. 7. He explains how God is called **Beautiful** and **Beauty**, and from where and by what reasoning He is so named; and how He anticipates the beauty of all things as their cause, and how from this beauty of His, all harmonies exist. 8. That the Celestial Spirits are moved by a triple motion. 9. That our own souls are moved by these same motions according to their own capacity. 10. That all things are preserved through the beautiful and the good, and all things desire the beautiful and the good. 11. That the name of **Love** is also used in the Scriptures, and one must account for the meanings rather than just the words. 12. That the Scriptures sometimes prefer the name of <term>Love</term> <note>original: "amor" — often associated with "eros" or intense, passionate desire.</note> over the name of <term>Affection</term> <note>original: "dilectio" — often associated with "agape" or brotherly, charitable love.</note>, even though the common people [regard] the name of love as spirit-*

<margin>An attribute of God.</margin>
...[Goodness] the <term>Theologians</term> <note>Dionysius typically uses this term to refer to the writers of the Holy Scriptures.</note> attribute to God, calling, as I believe, goodness itself the divine essence and the source of <margin>* That is, created or shared divinity.</margin> * divinity; and because God is good by His very essence, as a substantial good, He extends goodness into all things. For just as our sun illuminates all things that are capable of receiving its light, not by thought or will but by the very fact of its existence; so also the Good itself (which stands above the sun as much as an original archetype excels a faint image) pours out the rays of its entire goodness upon all things through its very substance, according to the capacity of each. <margin>All things consist through the goodness of God</margin> By these rays, all <term>intellectual and intelligent substances</term> <note>This refers to the angelic hierarchies and spiritual minds that exist without physical bodies.</note>, their powers, and their activities were established. By their virtue they exist and have eternal and unfailing life, free from all corruption, death, matter, and generation. They are set apart from the unstable and flowing change that moves in different ways toward different things; they are understood as incorporeal and immaterial, and as minds they understand in a <term>super-worldly</term> <note>original: "supermundialiter" — in a manner that transcends the physical universe.</note> manner, being enlightened by the true natures of things. In turn, they pass down their own gifts to those things akin to them. They also have their dwelling from goodness; indeed, their firmness, stability, preservation, and their nourishment of good things depend upon it. While they long for it, they obtain both their existence and their well-being. Furthermore, they are conformed to it as much as is permitted, bearing the likeness of the Good, and—according to the decree of divine law—they make those below them partakers of the gifts flowing from the <term>Supreme Good</term> <note>original: "summo bono" — a common philosophical name for God as the ultimate source of value.</note>.
