<margin>§ 3. The Good is above all things, and calls even those things that are not, so that they might be.</margin>
**§ 3.** But if the Good itself is above all things (as indeed it is), it gives form to that which is formless. In it alone, that which lacks substance is an excellence of substance; that which is inanimate is a most excellent life; and that which lacks mind is supreme wisdom. Whatever exists within the Good represents the super-eminent shaping of formless things. And, if it is right to say so, even that which <term>does not exist</term> <note>Dionysius refers to "non-being" (the state of potentiality or things not yet created) as having a "desire" to find its source and reality in God.</note> is held by a desire for that Good which is above all things; indeed, it strives to be in the truly <term>supersubstantial</term> <note>original: "supersubstantiali" — This term describes God as being "beyond substance," meaning His nature is higher than any form of existence we can define or imagine.</note> Good through the <term>removal of all things</term> <note>original: "ablationem" — Referring to the "via negativa" or "apophatic" way of knowing God by stripping away all worldly concepts to reach the divine mystery.</note>.

<margin>§ 4. The Good is the cause of the heavens and their motions.</margin>
**§ 4.** But, returning to what we had bypassed in the middle, the Good is also the cause of the celestial principles and boundaries. It is the cause of the celestial substance itself—which neither increases nor decreases, and is entirely unchanging—and of the motions of the vast celestial circuit. These motions are silent (if it is proper to speak so); they include the orders of the stars, their beauties, their lights, their fixed positions, and the varied wandering paths of certain stars. <margin>Genesis 1</margin> It is the cause of the circuits of the two lights which Scripture calls "great" <note>Referring to the Sun and the Moon, as described in the creation account of Genesis 1:16.</note>, and their return to the same place from which they set out, by which days and nights are distinguished for us. ### ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER IV.

...of those things which exist in time, they distinguish, count, order, and contain them, as they are completed in a circle. But what should be said of the sun’s ray itself? For light proceeds from the Supreme Good, and it is the image of Goodness; for this reason, the Good is praised by the name of "Light," just as the primary <term>archetype</term> <note>original: "exemplar" — In the thought of Dionysius, an "exemplar" or archetype is the original divine pattern in the mind of God after which all created things are modeled.</note> appears within its own image. 

<margin>He is both the cause of light and of all things.</margin>
For just as the goodness of the Divinity—which is above all things—extends from the highest and most advanced substances down to the very last, and yet remains above them all, so that neither do the superior beings reach its excellence, nor do the inferior ones escape its embrace; but rather, it illuminates all things capable of being light-filled, and creates, gives life, sustains, and perfects them; and it is the measure of those things that exist, their eternity, their number, 

<margin>The sun is the image of divine goodness.</margin>
their order, their embrace, their cause, and their end; in this same way, this great, entirely splendid and ever-shining sun is the expressed image of divine goodness, insofar as a faint echo of that Good resonates within it from afar. It illuminates all things that can <term>participate</term> <note>original: "participare" — A central theological concept where created things do not "own" their existence or light, but "share in" or "take part in" God's attributes according to their own nature.</note> in it, and it possesses a light extended above, which it multiplies through the brilliance of its rays throughout the entire visible world, both the higher and the lower regions. And if anything does not participate in it, the cause is not a weakness or a thinness in the sun's power to illuminate, but rather that the thing itself is not ready for the participation of light, because it is not fit to receive it. 

<margin>The sun illuminates and perfects all things.</margin>
And indeed, there are many such things which the sun’s ray passes over, while still illuminating those things that lie beyond them; there is nothing among the things that can be seen which the sun does not reach with the immense force of its splendor. Furthermore, it contributes to the birth of bodies that fall under the senses, and moves them toward life...

<summary>Dionysius presents the sun and its light as a physical metaphor for God's goodness, explaining that just as the sun illuminates all things capable of receiving light, God's goodness sustains and orders all levels of existence.</summary>

...it nourishes, increases, perfects, purifies, and renews; and it is the measure and the number of the seasons and days, and of all our time. For this is that very light—though it was not yet shaped into its current form <note>The author refers to the light created on the first day of Genesis, before the sun was formed on the fourth day.</note>—which the divine Moses said distinguished that first three-day period of our days.

<margin>The Good is a gathering force and turns all things toward itself.</margin>
And just as Goodness turns all things toward itself and gathers together those primary things that were dispersed—acting as a unifying divinity and the principle of unity—so all things desire it as their beginning, their embrace, and their end. And that is the Good (as Holy Scripture testifies) from which all things have stood firm, having been produced as if by a most perfect cause; it is that in which all things consist, as if guarded and held within a foundation that contains everything. Toward this Good, all things are turned, each to its own particular end. All things desire it: spiritual and rational beings do so with knowledge; those beings with senses do so through their senses; <margin>So also is light.</margin> those that lack senses do so by an innate movement of vital desire; and even those things that lack life and merely exist are inclined toward it by a certain force, seeking to <term>participate</term> <note>original: "participationem" — In this philosophy, "participation" means that a creature doesn't possess its own existence independently, but "shares in" the existence granted by God.</note> in essence alone. 

By the same logic of this most clear likeness, light also collects and turns toward itself all things that are seen, that move, that are illuminated, that are warmed, and that are generally touched by its rays. From this, the <term>sun</term> <note>original Greek: ἥλιος (hēlios)</note> derives its name, because it makes all things <term>gathered together</term> <note>original Greek: ἀολλῆ (aollē) — Dionysius is using a symbolic wordplay common in ancient Greek philosophy, suggesting the word for "sun" is derived from a word meaning "to gather" or "collect."</note>; that is, it keeps all things safe and gathers the dispersed. And all things that have the power of feeling desire it—whether to see, or to be moved, illuminated, and warmed—and finally, to be contained and preserved by the light. 

I do not say this as the thinkers of Antiquity believed—that the sun is God and the author of the universe, who [governs] this world...

<margin>§ 7. God is also called beautiful and beauty.</margin>
This same Good is praised by sacred theologians as the **Beautiful** and as **Beauty**, and as **Love** and as the **Beloved**, and by whatever other divine names are appropriate for the beautiful-making grace and the maker of beauty. However, "the beautiful" and "beauty" are not to be distinguished in the First Cause <note>The "First Cause" refers to God as the origin of all things.</note> which has embraced the whole universe into one. For in all [created] things, we divide these into *participations* and *participants*; thus, we call "beautiful" that which participates in beauty, but we call "beauty" the participation in that Cause which makes all things beautiful.

<margin>From where and by what reasoning he is so named.</margin>
Furthermore, the super-essential <note>A technical term meaning "beyond all being" or "above all categories of existence."</note> Beautiful is called "Beauty" because of that beauty which he communicates to all things according to the capacity of each. He is the cause of all harmony and splendor, breathing into all things the beauty-making distributions of his fontal <note>Meaning "acting as a fountain" or source.</note> ray of light. He calls <note>original: καλεῖ (*kalei*)</note> all things to himself—which is why "beauty" <note>original: κάλλος (*kallos*)</note> is so named <note>Dionysius is using a Greek wordplay here, linking the word for beauty (*kallos*) to the verb "to call" (*kalein*), suggesting that beauty's nature is to attract or call things toward it.</note>—and he gathers all things into the whole, as if into himself. He is called "the Beautiful" because he is beautiful from every side and is "more than beautiful." He is always existing, beautiful in the same way and according to the same manner; he is neither created nor destroyed, neither increasing nor...

...[God's beauty is not] decreasing, nor is it beautiful in one part and ugly in another, nor beautiful at one time and not at another; nor is it beautiful in relation to one thing and unharmonious in relation to another; nor is it beautiful here and different elsewhere, as if it were fair to some but deformed to others. Rather, it is beautiful in itself, through itself, and with itself—always existing as beauty, pre-possessing and anticipating within itself the fountain-head of all beauty in a superior way.

<margin>God anticipates the beauty of all things as their cause.</margin>
For in that simple and supernatural nature of all beautiful things, every beauty and every beautiful thing pre-exists in a unified way according to its cause. From this very Beauty, it falls to all existing things to be beautiful, each according to its own specific nature. Because of the Beautiful, there are all harmonies, and friendships, and communions; and through the Beautiful, all things are joined together. The Beautiful is the principle of all things, acting as the <term>efficient cause</term><note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into existence—the "maker."</note> which moves and holds the universe together by the love of its own beauty. It is also the <term>final cause</term><note>The "final cause" is the ultimate purpose or goal for which a thing exists; here, all things strive toward beauty.</note> and the end of all things, for all things are made for the sake of the Beautiful. Finally, it is the <term>exemplar cause</term><note>The "exemplar" or "formal" cause is the perfect pattern or blueprint upon which all created things are modeled.</note>, because all things are defined according to it. For this reason, the **Beautiful** and the **Good** are the same, since all things seek the Beautiful and the Good for every possible reason; indeed, there is nothing in nature that does not participate in the Beautiful and the Good. I will even dare to say this: it is not merely a matter of "participating" in the beautiful and good; rather, the Beautiful and Good truly exists when it is praised in God as being "above substance" <note>original: "supra substantiam" — a key Neoplatonic concept meaning God exists beyond the limitations of physical or even spiritual "matter" or "being."</note> by the removal of all limited things. In short, this one Good and Beautiful is the singular cause of the many things that are beautiful and good.

<margin>§ 8. Celestial spirits are moved by a threefold motion.</margin>

And they move **obliquely** <note>A "slanting" or "spiral" motion that combines the other two.</note> when, while caring for inferior beings, they remain perpetually in the same state, always revolving around the Good and Beautiful, which is the cause of that very stability.

<margin>§ 9. Similarly for our souls.</margin>
The **circular** motion of the soul is its inward turn from external things into itself. It is the single-minded turning of its spiritual faculties, which grants the soul a fixed movement—like a circle—free from all error. This motion turns the soul away from the many things outside itself and collects it: first into itself, and then, once it has become unified in its powers, it is joined to the truly One. In this way, the soul is finally guided toward the Beautiful and Good...

<margin>
Romans 11:36.
All things seek the beautiful and the good.
</margin>

...union, and simply put, everything that exists comes from the beautiful and the good, exists within the beautiful and the good, and is turned back toward the beautiful and the good. Whatever is and whatever happens, is and happens for the sake of the beautiful and the good. All things gaze upon it, and are moved and preserved by it; and by its grace, and because of it, and within it, is every principle: the exemplary, the final, the efficient, the formal, and the material <note>These refer to the "Five Causes" of classical philosophy: the model (exemplary), the goal (final), the creator (efficient), the essence/shape (formal), and the physical substance (material).</note>. In short, it is every beginning, every preservation, and every end. To say it briefly: all things that exist come from the beautiful and the good; and even all things that do *not* exist are present in the beautiful and the good in a way that is beyond substance <term>suprasubstantialiter: a way of existing in God that is more real than physical existence</term>. It is a source that is more than a source, and a goal that is more than perfect. > *For from him, and through him, and to him are all things* <note>original Latin: "Quoniam ex ipso, et per ipsum, et ad ipsum omnia"</note>, as the Scripture says.

Therefore, the beautiful and the good is desirable and lovable to all, and it is cherished by all. Because of it and for its sake, lower things love higher things by turning toward them; things of the same rank love their equals by sharing with them; greater things love lesser things by providing for them; and individuals love themselves by preserving themselves. All things, by seeking the beautiful and the good, perform and desire whatever they perform and desire.

Indeed, we even dare to say this: that he who is the cause of all things, because of the excellence of his goodness, loves all things, creates all things, perfects all things, contains all things, and turns all things back to himself. This divine love is the "good love of the good, for the sake of the good." For this divine love—which works goodness into the things that exist—existed first in the Good in an overflowing way. It did not allow the Good to remain within itself without fruit <note>The author suggests that God's goodness is so "pregnant" or full that it must overflow into the act of creation rather than remaining isolated.</note>, but instead moved it to act according to the excellence of its power, which brings all things into being.

<note>This passage is central to "Dionysian" thought, merging Christian theology with Neoplatonic philosophy to explain how the universe is held together by a pull toward beauty and goodness.</note>

<margin>Section 11. The name of love is also celebrated in the Scriptures.</margin>

And indeed, no one should think that we celebrate the name of love <note>The author is likely defending the use of the Greek word *eros*, which some contemporary readers found too carnal or pagan compared to *agape*. Dionysius argues they are functionally the same when applied to God.</note> against the authority of Scripture. For it is contrary to reason, I think, and absurd, not to attend to the power <note>original: "vim", meaning the inherent force or essence</note> of the subject itself, but only to the words; nor is this the characteristic of those who desire to understand divine things, but of those who hunt for thin sounds and receive them externally only as far as the ear, yet do not wish to know what such a phrase means, or in what way it might be explained by other equivalent and explanatory words. Instead, they are addicted to symbols and lines <note>original: "elementis ac lineis," referring to the physical characters and strokes of the written alphabet</note> that cannot be understood, and to syllables and unknown words which do not strike their intellect at all, but only make noise around their lips and ears,

<margin>*One should not take account of the words as much as the meanings.*</margin>

as if it were not permitted to signify "four" by "twice two," or "simple lines" by "straight lines," or "motherland" by "fatherland," or anything else by that which is equivalent in many parts of speech. For right reason teaches that we use symbols, syllables, phrases, writings, and words for the sake of the senses, so that when our soul is carried by its intellectual powers toward those things perceived by the intellect, then the senses are used in vain along with sensible objects. The same is true even of the powers of understanding: when the soul, having already been made God-like <term>deiformis: the process of becoming like God or being shaped by the divine</term> through an unknown union, plunges itself into the rays of inaccessible light by sightless leaps <note>original: "exoculatis quasi jactibus." This refers to the mystical "blinding" by the overwhelming light of God, where human reason is surpassed by a higher form of knowing.</note>. But when the mind strives to be awakened to those contemplative intelligences through sensible things, the most excellent of all are the clearest transmissions of the senses, such as the most open discourses and clearest visions; indeed, when those things presented to the senses are not at all clear, then the senses certainly [proffer] <note>The Latin text ends mid-word: "porri-", likely "porrigunt" (they proffer or stretch out).</note> sensible things to the mind—

For since true love is praised not only by us, but by the holy Scriptures themselves in a manner worthy of God, the common crowd of people—not having perceived that simplicity which the divine name of "Love" signifies—naturally slipped toward a love that is passive, corporeal, and fragmented. This is not true love, but an image of it, or rather a fall away from true love. For the multitude cannot grasp in thought that singularity of the divine and one Love. For this reason, the name "Love"—which seems harsher to the common crowd—is used in the divine Wisdom, so that the crowd might be raised up and directed toward the knowledge of true love, and [delivered] from that unseemliness which it [the crowd] conceives to be in it... <note>The text breaks off here mid-sentence, transitioning to the next page's discussion of why "Eros" is a more challenging but necessary term for the divine.</note>

...matter, and having fallen away from that state which Angels hold in their longing for the **Good**, is the cause of all evils both to itself and to others—those things which are said to be perverted and depraved? Or how can the race of demons, produced from that which is entirely **Good**, lack the form of the **Good**? <margin>What evil is, and from where it comes.</margin> Or how was the "good" that was made from the **Good** changed? And what is it that depraved it? And what indeed is "evil" anyway? From what principle does it consist? In what kind of thing does it exist? And why would the **Good** have willed to produce it? Or how, even if He willed it, was He able to do so? For if evil exists from some other cause, what other cause of things can there be besides the **Good**? Furthermore, if Providence <note>Providence (original: *providentia*) refers to God's constant care and guidance over the universe.</note> exists, how can evil be either created at all, or not be entirely removed? Finally, why would any existing thing desire evil instead of the **Good**?

<margin>
§. 19.

Evil is not from the Good.
</margin>

These are the things that someone ignorant of these matters might perhaps say. We, however, will ask him to attend to the truth, and first we shall not fear to say this: **Evil does not come from the Good.** For if it were to come from the **Good**, it would not be evil. It is not the nature of fire to chill, nor is it the nature of the **Good** to produce things that are not good. If all things that exist come from the **Good** (for the nature of the **Good** is to produce and preserve, while the nature of evil is to corrupt and destroy), then nothing that exists comes from evil. Indeed, evil itself would not even exist, since it would even be "evil" to itself <note>Dionysius argues that if evil were a "thing" that destroyed everything, it would eventually destroy itself, meaning it cannot have a stable existence like the Good does.</note>. Unless it were so, evil would not be entirely evil, but would possess some part of the **Good**, by virtue of which it exists at all. And if all things that exist desire the **Beautiful** and the **Good**, and if whatever they do, they do for the sake of that which *appears* to be good, and if every intention of things looks toward the **Good** as both its beginning and its end—for no one does anything while looking toward the nature of evil...

<summary>Dionysius addresses the "Problem of Evil," arguing that since the Divine Good is the source of all existence, evil cannot be a created "substance" or have its own source; rather, evil is a lack or a corruption of the Good.</summary>

Evil, however, is neither among the things that exist, nor among the things that do not exist; rather, it is even further removed from the **Good** than non-existence is, as something alien and "less-than-existent." "From where then does evil come?" someone will ask. "For if evil does not exist, then virtue and vice are the same (at least in the proportion of the whole to the whole, and part to part) or at least that which is opposed to virtue will not be evil."

<margin>Virtue and vice, good and evil, are opposites.</margin>
And yet, moderation and excess <note>original: *temperantia et intemperantia*</note>, and justice and injustice, are indeed opposites. Nor do I say they are opposites only insofar as they proceed from a just or unjust person, or from one who is moderate or excessive; rather, even before the difference between a good man and a wicked man appears outwardly, the vices already differ from the virtues within the soul itself, and the <term>disturbances</term> <note>original: *perturbationes*. In ancient philosophy, these are the "passions" or emotions that disrupt the calm of the rational mind.</note> rebel against reason. Therefore, it must necessarily be granted that some evil exists as a contrary to the **Good**. For the **Good** is not contrary to itself, but because it proceeds from one principle and one cause, it rejoices in communion, connection, and friendship. Nor is a "lesser good" opposed to a "greater good," any more than that which is less hot or less cold is the opposite of that which is more hot or more cold. Therefore, it is in the nature of things...

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil is not a "thing" that exists, but is actually "less than non-existent." He also addresses the objection that if evil doesn't exist, virtue and vice would be the same, explaining that they are true internal opposites within the soul.</summary>

Furthermore, the same thing will certainly not be both good and evil in the same respect, nor are corruption and generation the same power under the same rationale, nor are they the same force, nor the same corruption: for evil itself is neither existent, nor is it good, nor does it have the power of generating, nor does it make things,

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil has no creative power of its own; while the decay of one thing may lead to the birth of another, it is the underlying "Good" that creates, while evil only destroys.</summary>

If, however, they are not always evil, then they are not evil by nature, but rather through a **defect of Angelic goods**.

<margin>Demons have not lost their natural powers.</margin>

...there is entirely in them a certain movement of desire; but they are called wicked insofar as they are weak in their natural activity. Therefore, depravity for them is an evil, a desertion and a frustration of the things suitable to them; it is an imperfection, a lack of power, and a weakness, a driving away, and a slipping away of the faculty that preserves their own perfection. What else, indeed, is evil in demons? An irrational rage, a demented lust, and a headlong imagination. Yet, even if these things are present in demons, they are not present in all of them, nor are these traits evil in and of themselves. For in other animals, such traits are not considered an "affection" <note>In this philosophical context, "affection" refers to a state or condition of being.</note> of this kind; rather, it is the *privation* <note>term: privatio (privation) — a key concept in this philosophy, meaning the absence or "lack" of a quality that should naturally be there, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note> of these traits that would cause the destruction and evil of those animals. In those animals, the trait itself, through its own habit, preserves and establishes the nature of the animal while it possesses them. 

Therefore, the race of demons is not evil insofar as it responds to its nature, but insofar as it fights against it. Nor has the total "good" granted to them been entirely overturned; rather, they themselves have fallen away from the whole good that was handed to them. We do not say that the **Angelic gifts** <note>original: "Angelicas dotes" — the inherent powers and qualities given to them when they were created as angels.</note> which they received were ever completely changed; rather, they are even now intact and clearly visible, though the demons themselves do not see them, because they have blocked the powers of sight by which they could gaze upon their own goods. 

For this reason, insofar as they *exist*, they are from the Good and are good, and they seek the beautiful and the good when they desire to exist, to live, and to understand the things that are. They are called "evil" only because of the deprivation, the turning away, and the falling from the goods that are suitable to their nature. They are evil according to that which they are *not*; and when they desire that which does not exist, they desire evil.

<vocab>Dionysius Areopagite, demons, Angelic gifts, evil, good, privation, movement of desire</vocab>

<summary>Dionysius argues that demons are not evil by their created nature or essence, but are called evil because they have turned away from their original Angelic gifts and natural functions. He maintains that even demons still possess their natural powers and a basic desire for existence, which are inherently good things derived from the Creator.</summary>

<page-num>203</page-num>
# ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER IV.

<margin>§ 24. Whether, and what kind of evil exists in souls.</margin>
Truly, who could say that souls are evil? If it is because they are present to help the wicked in a provident and healthy way, then this is not evil at all, but a good; it comes from the Good and belongs to one who turns evil into good. But if we say that souls are depraved, by what are they depraved? It can only be by a failure of good dispositions and actions, and because they wander and stray from their goal due to their own weakness. Indeed, we say that this air which surrounds us is darkened by the failure and absence of light, even though light itself is always light, and it is the light that illuminates the darkness. Therefore, evil is not a "thing" in demons or in us—as if it were some existing substance—but rather it is a defect and a lack of the perfection of those goods that are proper to our nature.

<margin>§ 25. Neither is there evil in brute animals.</margin>
Furthermore, there is no evil in brute <note>term: brutis (brute) — in this context, it refers to "irrational" animals, distinguishing them from humans who possess reason.</note> animals. For if you take away their rage, their appetite, and the other things which are spoken of—though they are not simply evil by their own nature—you would destroy the animal. A lion that lost its courage and pride would cease to be a lion; likewise, a dog that became gentle to everyone would not be a dog, since it is the dog's nature to be a guardian, to welcome those of the household and drive away strangers. Therefore, the incorruption of a nature is not evil in any way; rather, evil is the corruption, the weakness, and the failure of its natural dispositions, actions, and virtues. And if all things achieve their perfection in time through their own generation, then imperfection is not found in the universal nature.

<margin>§ 26. Neither is there evil in nature.</margin>
But neither is evil found in nature as a whole. For if all natural principles <note>original: "rationes naturales" — these are the "reasons" or "designs" inherent in nature.</note> come from the Universal Nature, then nothing is contrary to it; however, for an individual nature, one thing will be in accordance with its nature, while another thing will not be. For one thing is different for another...

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil is not a positive existence but a "privation" or lack of natural perfection, illustrating this through the behaviors of lions and dogs and the metaphor of light and darkness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the nature of evil. Having previously argued that evil is not a substance within demons or animals, the author now addresses whether evil resides in the physical body or in the fundamental substance of "matter" itself.</meta>

<page-num>204</page-num>
-># ST. DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE<-

...against nature, and what is natural to one is against nature to another. Indeed, a vice of nature is that which is contrary to nature, and it deprives it of its natural qualities. Therefore, nature is not evil, but this is the evil of nature: that which renders it powerless to fulfill those things which are proper to nature.

<margin>**§ 27.**
*Neither is evil in bodies.*</margin>
In truth, evil is not in bodies either. For ugliness and disease are a certain defect of form and a deprivation of order; however, this is not entirely evil, but rather a "lesser beauty." For if there were a complete dissolution of beauty, form, and order, the body itself would perish. Furthermore, that the body is not the cause of malice <note>original: "malitiæ" — in this philosophical context, it refers to a state of badness or moral corruption rather than just spite.</note> in the soul is evident from the fact that malice can cling to someone even without a body, as is clear in the case of demons. Indeed, it is equally evil for spirits and souls as it is for bodies, if they become weak and are cast down from the state of their own goods.

<margin>**§ 28.**
*Neither is evil in matter.*</margin>
Nor is that common saying true, "Evil is in matter," as they say, insofar as it is matter; for matter itself participates in beauty, adornment, and form. But if matter—separated from these things by its own nature—possesses no quality or form <note>original: "speciem" — often translated as species or appearance, but here referring to the formal structure of a thing.</note>, how could matter do anything? Matter does not even have the capacity to be acted upon by itself. <note>original: "ut pati possit" — a technical term in scholastic philosophy referring to 'passivity' or the ability of a substance to receive a new form or change.</note> Moreover, how can matter be evil? For if it does not exist at all or anywhere, it is neither good nor evil. But if it exists in any way at all, and all things that exist are from the Good, then surely matter itself must be from the Good. Thus, either the Good produces evil, or evil itself (insofar as it comes from the Good) would be good—unless perhaps evil could create good, and so good (insofar as it comes from evil) would be evil.

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil is not found in the physical body or in matter itself, because both participate in the "Good" through form and existence; evil is merely a lack of proper order or function.</summary>

Or again, how can they be fundamental principles if they themselves depend upon some other single source? Now indeed, if they say that matter was necessary for the completion of the universe, how can matter be evil? For it is one thing to be evil, and another to be necessary. How could the Good One generate anything from evil? Or how could that which is necessary to the Good be evil? For truly, evil flees the nature of the good. But how does matter generate and nourish nature if it is evil? For evil, insofar as it is evil, generates nothing and nourishes nothing, nor does it accomplish or preserve anything. 

And if they say that matter does not produce malice <note>original: "malitiam" — referring to moral corruption or ontological "badness."</note> in souls, but rather instigates them toward it, how can that be true? For many souls look toward the good. Yet, how could this have happened if matter inclined them entirely toward evil? Therefore, evil in souls does not exist because of matter, but from a certain disordered and erring movement <note>original: "peccante motu" — literally a "sinning" movement, but in this philosophical sense, it means a movement that "misses the mark" of its proper goal.</note>. If they say that souls follow matter entirely, and that this unstable matter is necessary for those who cannot stand firm within themselves, by what logic is evil necessary? Or how can that which is necessary be evil?

<margin>**§ 29.**
*Neither is privation evil in itself.*</margin>
But neither do we say that privation <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</term>, by its own force, opposes the good; for total privation is entirely powerless, while partial privation has power not because it is a privation, but because it is not a total privation. For if the privation of the good is partial, it is not yet evil; and if it were to become complete, the very nature of evil would also vanish. <note>Dionysius argues that evil has no independent existence; it is a parasite on the good. If the good were 100% removed, the thing would cease to exist entirely, and therefore the "evil" would also disappear.</note>

But to speak briefly, the Good exists from a single and whole cause, while evil arises from many partial— <note>The text breaks off mid-word here; the catchword indicates the sentence continues on the next page regarding partial defects.</note>

<margin>Evil; and its source.</margin> ...and by their defects. God knows evil as good <note>original: "Cognovit Deus malum ut bonum" — This suggests that from the divine perspective, which sees the whole of providence, what we perceive as "evil" is understood in relation to the Good it lacks.</note>, and in His presence, the causes of evils are actually beneficial powers. For if evil were eternal, and could create, and had power, and existed, and acted, from where would it receive all these attributes? Would it be from the good? Or would the good come from the evil? Or indeed, do both arise from another cause? 

Everything that exists according to nature is born from a defined cause; but if evil is devoid of cause and definition, it is not according to nature. For there is nothing in the nature of things that is "against nature," <note>The author argues that "nature" implies a goal or design; therefore, evil, being a failure of design, cannot be a "nature" itself.</note> nor is there a "logic of ignorance" within a craft. 

Could the soul then be the cause of evils—just as fire, for example, is the cause of heat—filling everything it approaches with malice? Or is the nature of the soul actually good, while in its actions it behaves sometimes one way and sometimes another? If the soul’s very state were evil by nature, where did it receive that state? Was it from the Good Cause, which is the maker of all things? But if it came from that source, how can it be evil according to its essence <term>essentiam</term>? For all the effects of the Good Cause are good. But if it is evil only through its actions, then this evil is not unchangeable. Otherwise, from where would the soul’s virtues come, unless it were originally made in the "form of good"? It remains, therefore, that evil is a certain weakness and a falling away <note>original: "defectionemque" — a desertion or failing from a standard.</note> from the good.

<margin>
§. 31.
The cause of good things is one; the causes of evil things are many.
</margin> 

The cause of good things is one. If evil is the contrary of the good, then the causes of evils must be many. Yet, these are not "productive" causes—they are not actual powers or faculties of evil—but are rather instances of impotence, and weakness, and a certain discordant mixing of things that do not belong together. 

Evils are not unmoving, nor do they always behave in the same way; instead, they are infinite and indeterminate. In various different things—and those being infinite in number—evils wander in diverse ways. Yet, even of all evils, the beginning and the end is the Good: for the cause of the good...

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil is not a substance or a natural entity, but a "weakness" or "deficiency" of the good. He concludes that while Good has a single source, evil arises from many accidental failures and lacks a true "nature" of its own.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 206, where Dionysius is dismantling the idea that evil has any independent "nature." He is moving toward the famous Neoplatonic and Christian conclusion that evil is not a "thing" but a lack or a "privation" of the Good.</meta>

<page-num>207</page-num>
### ->ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER IV.<-

<margin>All things exist from the good and for the sake of the good.</margin>
...all things are, both those which are good and those which are evil; for we perform even these [evil acts] out of a desire for the good (since no one does what they do with evil as their intended goal). Therefore, evil does not strive toward a substance <term>substantia: the underlying reality or "being" of a thing</term>, but toward a semblance of substance, since the action is carried out for the sake of the good and not for the sake of the evil itself.

<margin>§. 32. Evil exists by accident.</margin>
A status must be attributed to evil only "by accident" <term>per accidens: an incidental occurrence, like a shadow, rather than an intentional creation</term>, and for the sake of something else, rather than from its own starting principle. Thus, while an act is being done, it may indeed seem to be "right" because it is done for the sake of a good; however, in reality, it is not right, because we are judging that to be good which is actually not good.

<margin>What evil is, and what it is capable of.</margin>
It has been shown that what is sought is one thing, and what is actually done is another. Therefore, evil deflects from the path: it is outside of intention, outside of nature, outside of cause, outside of principle, outside of end, beyond limit, outside of will, and outside of substance. Evil, then, is a privation <note>original: "privatio" — Dionysius defines evil not as a "dark matter" but as a hole or a lack, much like blindness is not a "thing" but simply the absence of sight.</note>, and a defect, and a weakness, and a disharmony, and an error, and a failure of aim, of beauty, of life, of intellect, of reason, of perfection, of foundation, and of cause. It is indeterminate, sterile, inactive, powerless, confused, dissimilar, infinite, dark, and lacking in status; and in itself, in no way, nowhere, and as nothing does it exist. 

How then can evil be capable of anything at all, except through a mixture of the good? For that which is entirely devoid of the good is neither anything, nor is it capable of anything. Indeed, if the Good is that which exists, and is desirable, and powerful, and effective, how could that which is contrary to the Good be capable of anything, since it lacks essence, will, power, and action? Not all things are evil to everyone, nor are they evil in the same way or for the same reasons. To a demon <note>original: "Dæmoni" — In this context, referring to spiritual beings who have turned away from God.</note>, evil is to have defected from a "good mind"; to a soul, it is to have defected from reason; to a body, it is to have defected from its natural state.

<summary>Dionysius defines evil as a "privation" or lack of the Good, arguing that it has no independent existence and only "acts" by piggybacking on the power of the Good. He explains that even when we do evil, we do it because we are mistakenly pursuing a perceived good.</summary>

<margin>
§. 33.
How evil can exist while Providence exists.
</margin>
How is it that evil exists at all if Providence exists? Evil, insofar as it is evil, is neither an actual thing <note>original: "res" — in this context, a substance or a positive reality created by God.</note>, nor is it found within the nature of things. Furthermore, nothing escapes the reach of Providence, for there is no evil that is not mixed with some measure of good. If nothing is entirely devoid of good, and if evil is merely the lack <term>defectus: a falling short or a failure to meet a standard</term> of good, then because no thing is completely stripped of all good, divine Providence is present in all things. Not one thing escapes divine Providence; indeed, Providence even makes use of those who have turned out evil, directing them toward their own benefit or the benefit of others, whether for a private or a common good. In this way, it provides specifically for every individual thing.

<margin>
Providence keeps the natures of things unharmed.
</margin>
For this reason, we by no means approve of the empty talk of the many who say that divine Providence ought to drive us toward virtue even against our will. It is not the nature of Providence to violate the nature of the things it governs. Therefore, as Providence is the preserver of each thing’s specific nature, it looks out for those endowed with free movement <note>referring to beings with free will, like humans and angels.</note> as beings that move freely. It provides for the whole and for the individual in a way that is both universal and uniquely suited to each, as far as the nature of those receiving it allows. The benefits of this all-encompassing and multi-faceted Providence are granted to each according to their own capacity.

<margin>
§. 34.
Evil is not a thing, nor a power, but a failure.
</margin>
Therefore, evil is not a substance, nor does evil have a real existence within things. For nowhere does "evil" exist as a thing in its own right; nor does the fact that something becomes evil proceed from a power, but rather from a weakness <term>imbecillitas: in this philosophical sense, it refers to a lack of strength or a failure to maintain one's proper state.</term>. Even regarding the demons, that which they *are* comes from the Good and is itself good; the "evil" that happened to them through their fall from their own rightful goods is a change in their state and condition. It is a weakness in the perfection that was appropriate and fitting for them as Angels. They even continue to desire the good, insofar as they desire to exist, and to live, and...

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil is not a created substance but a "lack of good" and a "weakness" of nature. He explains that divine Providence does not force virtue upon us because it respects the free will and natural properties of all creatures.</summary>

What the sin of ignorance is.

## CHAPTER V.

### On Being, in which the Models are also discussed.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*1. He teaches that God, as He is in Himself, can neither be known nor explained; and he shows how the name of "the Good" extends further than the name of "Being." <note>Dionysius argues that "The Good" is the most fundamental name for God because it reaches even to things that do not yet exist but have the potential to be, whereas "Being" refers to things that already have existence.</note> 2. He states that his purpose is to preach God according to His providences or emanations. <term>emanationes: the "outflowings" or ways God makes Himself present and active in the created world.</term> 3. That those things which participate more in God are closer to Him. 4. That God is all things in all things in an eminent way. 5. That eternity, time, and all things are from God: and that the rank of Being is the first or most ancient gift of God. 6. That the rank of Being and all things are from God and exist in God as a unity. 7. That in God, as the cause of all, even contrary things are united. 8. That from God, celestial spirits, souls, and all things obtain their rank of being and whatever they possess; and that God is in all things in an exempt way <note>original: "exempte" — meaning God is present in things but remains distinct and transcendent from them</note>, which he confirms by the example of the sun; and simultaneously he explains what the Models are. 9. He teaches that those things which are most fundamental in reality are not properly relations, nor the Models themselves, but the things modeled, and that God embraces all things by His simple perfection. 10. How God is the beginning and the end of all things.*

<margin>§. 1. God as He is in Himself cannot be explained.</margin>
**N**ow we must pass on to the theological name of "Being," <term>ens: a philosophical term for anything that exists</term> which truly exists. However, we shall comment on this only as much as the requirements of our purpose demand: for it is not our purpose to explain the Substance <note>original: "substantia" — referring here to the "Ousia" or essence of God.</note> which is beyond substance, insofar as it is beyond substance.

(for this is ineffable and unknown, and cannot be fully expressed, and it surpasses the very union of the mind) but rather, [our purpose is] to celebrate the substance-giving emanation of the deifying substance—which is the principle of all substance—toward all things that exist.

<margin>The name of the Good extends further than the name of Being.</margin>
Indeed, the name of "the Good" regarding God declares all the emanations <term>emanationes: the "outpourings" of God's grace and creative power into the world</term> of the Author of all things; and this naming of God from "the Good" is extended both to those things that exist and to those things that do not exist, and it is above those things that exist and those that do not. But the name of "Being" <note>original: "entis"</note> extends to all things that exist, and stands out above the essences themselves. Truly, the name of "Life" is extended to all living things, and is above living things. The naming of God from "Wisdom" is extended to all things that understand, that reason, and that feel, and it is above all those things.

<margin>§. 2. Dionysius’s purpose is to praise God according to His providences or emanations.</margin>
It is therefore our purpose to praise these names of God, which reveal the providences of God: for our discussion does not promise to explain and reveal the beyond-essential <term>superessentialis: a term Dionysius uses to show that God is not just "a being," but exists on a plane entirely above and beyond our concept of "existence"</term> goodness and essence, life and wisdom of the super-essential Divinity itself. That Divinity has placed its seat in hidden places, as the Scriptures <note>original: "Eloquia" — literally "the Oracles," usually referring to the Holy Bible</note> hand down, far above all goodness, divinity, essence, wisdom, and life. Rather, our discourse celebrates the providence made known to us—that provider of good things, that most excellent goodness, and the cause of all good things. It praises God as Being, and Life, and Wisdom; as the provider and cause of substance and life, who grants wisdom to those who participate in substance, life, mind, reason, and the senses. This discussion of ours does not say that "the Good" is one thing, and "Being" another, and "Life" or "Wisdom" yet another, nor that there are many <note>The text likely continues to explain that these names all refer to the same unified God, despite our different words for Him.</note>

<summary>Dionysius explains that while God's inner essence is unknowable, we can praise Him through His "emanations" or names. He argues that the name "the Good" is the most comprehensive, as it applies even to things that do not yet exist, whereas names like "Being" or "Wisdom" apply to specific levels of creation.</summary>

causes, and other gods who create other things, some higher and some lower, but rather all the good emanations <term>emanationes: the "outpourings" of God's grace and creative power into the world</term> of the one God, and the names of God praised by us; and that there is indeed one name which declares the entire providence of the one God, while others reveal providences that are more or less general.

<margin>§ 3. Those things that participate more in God are closer to Him.</margin>
**§ 3.** Someone might say: "Since 'Being' <note>original: "ens"</note> is more extensive than 'Life,' and 'Life' more than 'Wisdom,' why do living things surpass mere beings, and sentient things surpass living things, and rational things surpass sentient ones, and the spirits themselves <note>original: "ipsi spiritus," likely referring to the angelic orders</note> surpass rational ones—all surrounding God and approaching Him more closely? After all, it would seem appropriate that those who participated in the greater gifts of God should also stand out and surpass the others."

This would certainly be correctly said if one supposed that spiritual beings lacked both existence and life. But since divine Spirits surpass all other beings in their existence, and live more excellently than other living things, and understand and know beyond sense and reason, and desire and participate in the Beautiful and the Good beyond all beings—for this reason they are closer to the Good. By participating more brightly in it, they have also received more and greater gifts from it. Just as rational beings surpass sentient ones because they possess a more abundant reason, and sentient ones surpass others by their sense, and others by their life. And this is, in my opinion, true: those things that participate more in the one God, who abounds in infinite gifts, also exist closer to Him and are more divine than those things that are surpassed in these matters.

**§ 4.** Since we have also discussed these things, come now, let us praise the Good as truly existing, and as the maker of the substances <note>original: "substantias," here meaning the essential reality or "whatness" of a thing</note> of all things. "He Who Is" <note>A reference to Exodus 3:14, where God reveals His name to Moses as "I Am Who I Am"</note> is the source of all essence...

<summary>Dionysius explains that although "Being" is the most universal category, beings with intellect and life are "closer" to God because they participate more fully in His diverse gifts. He begins to praise God under the name "He Who Is" as the source of all substance.</summary>

<margin>God is all things in all things in an eminent way <note>eminently: in a way that transcends and includes all characteristics of the thing described</note></margin>
...of every possible supernatural essence, He exists as the substantial cause and the producer of being, existence, personhood, substance, and nature. He is the principle and measure of the ages <note>original: "saeculorum," often referring to vast cycles of time or eternal durations</note>, the entity of times, and the <term>aeon: a duration of time that is everlasting or outside of linear time</term> of all beings. He is time for those things that are made, "being" for those things that exist in any way, and "generation" <note>the process of coming into being</note> for those things that are born. From "Him Who Is" <note>This refers to the divine name revealed in Exodus 3:14</note> come eternity, substance, existence, time, generation, and that which is brought forth. He is the "things that are" within all things that exist—both those things that exist in any way and those that exist through themselves. For God is not a being in just any specific way, but simply and infinitely He embraces and anticipates all being within Himself at once; for which reason He is also called the **King of Ages**, as the one in whom and through whom the "being" of everything both exists and is sustained. In Him, there was no "was," nor will there be a "will be," nor was anything "made," nor is it being "made," nor "will it be made"—indeed, it "is" not <note>Dionysius argues that God's existence transcends all temporal categories of past, present, and future</note>; rather, He Himself is the very being for all things. Not only are the things that exist from Him, but the very existence of things comes from the Pre-eternal Being, for He Himself is the Eternity of Eternities, existing before every age.

<margin>§ 5. That eternity, time, and all things come from God.</margin>
**§ 5.** Therefore, taking up the matter from a higher perspective, let us say that for all things and all ages, existence itself comes from Him Who Pre-existed. And indeed, every age and time is from Him; the principle and cause of every age, time, and any thing whatsoever is He who pre-exists. All things participate in Him, and He withdraws from no being; He is before all things, and all things consist in Him. Simply put, if anything exists in any way, it is within the Pre-existent One that it is, is understood, and is preserved. Before all His other "participations" <note>the ways in which created things share in divine qualities</note>, "Being itself" is presupposed. Being-in-itself is more ancient <note>meaning more fundamental or logically prior in the hierarchy of creation</note> than Life-in-itself, or Wisdom-in-itself, or Likeness-in-it...

<summary>Dionysius explains that God is the "Pre-existent" source of all being, time, and eternity, transcending past and future. He argues that "Being" is the most fundamental divine gift, acting as the necessary foundation for life and wisdom.</summary>

# SAINT DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE

<margin>Being itself is the most ancient gift of God.</margin>
...[divine beauty], and whatever other qualities are shared by those things that exist, they share in "being" before any other participation. Truly, even those very qualities which are shared by existing things—and by which those things exist—themselves share in "Being in itself." There is nothing whose essence and <term>aeon: a state of being that is eternal or exists outside of linear time</term> is not Being itself. Therefore, since God is (as is only right) the primary source more so than all other things, He is praised as **Being** <note>original: "ens"</note> because of this, His most ancient gift. For since He possesses "being" in a prior and more excellent way, He first created "being" itself—I mean Being in its own right—and through that Being, He caused everything that exists in any way to have its existence.

Indeed, all the principles of things that exist share in "being"; they exist, and they are principles; they exist first, and then they are principles. And if you wish to say that "Life itself" is the principle of living things (insofar as they live), and "Likeness itself" is the principle of similar things (insofar as they are similar), and "Union itself" for joined things, and "Order itself" for ordered things—and likewise for all other things that share in this or that, or both, or many qualities—you will find that these "principles in themselves" <note>The author is referring to the abstract concepts or "Forms" that give things their characteristics</note> first share in being. Thus, they first *exist* as what they are, and then they are the principles of this or that; they exist by sharing in "being," and they are shared by others. But if these principles (which are counted as the sources of other things) exist only by sharing in Being itself, how much more so do the things that share in those very principles?

<margin>§. 6. Being itself and</margin>
Therefore, since that "Goodness-beyond-all" <note>A title for God, who is seen as the source existing above even the concept of goodness</note> produces "Being-in-itself" as its first gift, God is rightly praised by this most ancient...

<summary>Dionysius argues that "Being" (existence) is the fundamental gift of God, preceding and enabling all other qualities like life, wisdom, or order. He establishes that even the abstract principles of things must first "be" before they can exert influence on the world.</summary>

# ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER V.

<margin>All things exist from God and are united in God.</margin>
...[He] is praised by the more ancient and first of all participations <note>A "participation" is a philosophical term meaning a way that created things share in God's qualities, like goodness or existence</note>; and from Him and in Him is Being itself, the <term>principles: the fundamental origins or starting points</term> of things, and all things whatever they are, and in whatever way they exist; and this He contains in an incomprehensible, joined, and singular way. For in unity, every number pre-exists in a uniform way, and unity holds every number within itself singularly; every number is joined into one and exists in unity, and the further it proceeds from unity, the more it is divided and multiplied. And in the center of a circle, all the lines of that circle exist together in a single joining; and the central point holds all the straight lines uniformly joined to one another and to the one principle from which they emerged, and in that center they are entirely joined. Those lines slightly distant from the center are slightly divided from each other, but those further away are more so; and, to put it simply, the closer they are to the center, the more they are joined with it and with each other; and the more they are distant from the center, the more they are distant from each other.

<margin>§. 7. In God, as the cause of all things, even all contrary things are united.</margin>
Indeed, in the entire nature of the universe, the <term>rational principles: the underlying blueprints or laws of nature</term> of each individual nature are collected together in a single, non-confused joining. Likewise, in the soul, the powers that provide for all parts of the body are uniformly joined. It is not, therefore, absurd for us—ascending from these small and minute images and examples to the Cause of all things—to contemplate with <term>supermundanis: eyes that look beyond the physical world</term> all things within the Cause of all, even those things that are opposite to one another, in a uniform and joined way. For He is the beginning of all things, from whom comes Being itself, as well as everything that exists in any way: every principle, every end, every life, every immortality, every wisdom, every...

<summary>Dionysius uses the analogies of numbers and circles to explain how God contains the diversity of the universe within a single, unified source. He argues that just as all lines meet at the center of a circle, all seemingly contrary parts of creation are united in God, the "Cause of all."</summary>

<margin>What the Exemplars are.</margin>

Every life and every vital movement comes from that Life which is above all life and is the source of all life. From this Life, souls possess their quality of not perishing, and all animals and plants possess that life which they enjoy in the <term>lowest degree of life</term> <note>The "last" or "ultimate" grade refers to the physical life of plants and simple organisms in the Great Chain of Being</note>. **§. 2.**
This [Life] imparts a suitable life to every living thing.
</margin>

And it grants, first of all, to "Life itself" the power to be Life, and to every life and each individual life, it grants the power to be what it is according to its own nature. To the heavenly lives, it grants an immaterial, <term>God-like: having the form or character of God</term> <note>original: "deiformem"</note>, and unchangeable immortality, along with a perpetual movement that is free from all error or deviation. It extends itself even to the life of demons through its abundance of goodness; for even they do not possess their being or their life from any other cause than this. Furthermore, it gives to human beings—even though we are <term>composite beings: made of both physical body and spiritual soul</term>—a life that very nearly approaches the Angelic life. Even when we turn away from it, it converts and recalls us to itself through the overflowing of its kindness.

# CHAPTER VII.
## On wisdom, mind, reason, truth, faith.
### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*1. It teaches that the wisdom of God is the creator of all wisdom, and exists above all wisdom as unsearchable and incomprehensible; nor is it to be measured according to our understanding. 2. From this wisdom of God, it says that the Angels have their nature as intellectual beings <term>intellectiles</term> <note>referring to beings that perceive truth through direct intuition rather than step-by-step logic</note>, and men have their nature as rational beings, and other things are sensible. It asks, furthermore, how God knows all things without any action; and how He anticipates all things in His knowledge, and knows them in Himself through His own self-knowledge; and how Angels also perceive sensible things intellectually <gloss>¹ through the intellect</gloss>. 3. It shows that God, as He is in Himself, is unknown to us, and that He is known partly through concepts <term>notionem</term> <note>logical or mental representations</note>, and partly without concepts, and that this latter knowledge is more divine and truer than the former. 4. How God is the Word <term>Verbum</term> <note>original: "Verbum," translating the Greek "Logos," implying both "Word" and "Reason"</note>, which is the simple truth and the foundation of faith.*

According to this [union], therefore, divine things are to be understood, not in our own way, but insofar as we renounce our whole selves from our whole selves, and pass entirely into God: since it is far better that we belong to God than to ourselves; for thus divine things can be given to us, if we have been joined with God in this way. ...however much a person is truly mindless—neither knowing what they desire nor wishing to attain it—this should more accurately be called a falling away from wisdom. But since the divine wisdom has been called the principle, the cause, the procreatrix <note>The feminine form of "creator," used here because "Wisdom" (Sapientia) is a feminine noun in Latin.</note>, the perfection, the protector, and the ultimate boundary of wisdom itself—and indeed of every mind, reason, and sense—how then is God Himself preached as a Wisdom that is wise beyond wisdom, and as Mind, Word, and Knowledge?

<margin>How God knows all things without an act of effort.</margin>
For how could He understand any of the objects of the intellect <term>intellectilium</term> if He does not possess a spiritual act of mind? Or how could He perceive sensible things <note>Things perceived by the five senses.</note> if He is situated far above all sensation? And yet the Oracles <note>original: "Eloquia." Dionysius uses this term to refer to the Holy Scriptures.</note> hand down the truth that God knows all things, and that nothing escapes the divine cognition. Truly, as I have often said, divine attributes must be understood in a way that is fitting for God.

<margin>That those things which are expressed as negations are attributed to God by way of excess.</margin>
For "mindlessness" and "insensibility" are attributed to God by way of excess <note>original: "per excessum." In this theological context, this means God does not "lack" a mind, but rather possesses something so much greater than a mind that our word "mind" is too small to describe Him.</note>, not by way of defect. In the same way, we attribute a "lack of reason" to Him who is above reason, and "imperfection" to Him who is beyond-perfect and pre-perfect. We also assign "darkness"—which eludes both touch and sight—to the "Inaccessible Light," because that light so far surpasses the light we can see with our eyes. Therefore, the divine mind encompasses all things with a certain eminent knowledge. By this knowledge, acting as the cause of all things, God anticipates the knowledge of everything within Himself. He knew the Angels before they were made, thereby creating them; He knows all other things from within and from their very origin <term>exordio</term>, so to speak, bringing them forth into the nature of reality. I believe the Scripture signifies this when it says, *He who knows all things before they come to be.*

<margin>Daniel 13:42. How God [knows] all things.</margin>
For the divine mind does not learn about things from the things themselves; rather, it knows them from within itself and in itself, possessing the knowledge, the concept, and the essence of all things according to its role as the Cause...

For if God imparts existence to all things through a single Cause, then by that same unique Cause He will know all things as existing from Him and pre-existing in Him; He does not receive His understanding of things from the things themselves, but rather He bestows upon each individual thing the knowledge of itself and of others. Thus, God does not possess one specific knowledge of Himself and another common knowledge encompassing all things. For the Cause of all things, in knowing itself, can in no way be ignorant of those things which proceed from it and of which it is the Cause. On this foundation, he shall have the constancy of an immovable and unchangeable identity. For it is hidden from them, as is natural, that he has departed from error through the truth of the true faith. In this way, our first teachers of divine wisdom die daily for the truth, testifying, as is fitting, in both word and deed, that this singular recognition of Christian truth is the most simple and most divine of all—or rather, that this alone is the true and unique simple knowledge of God.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## Concerning power, justice, salvation, and redemption; wherein inequality is also discussed.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

1. *He asks how God, who is above all virtue <term>virtus; in this context, the word means "power" or "miraculous strength" rather than just moral goodness.</term> and power, is also called virtue or power.* 2. *He states that God is named virtue or power because He is almighty and the author of all virtue and power.* 3. *He shows how divine omnipotence pervades all things.* 4. *That He imparts to the Angels all the force and power by which they prevail.* 5. *Similarly, how He strengthens and preserves humans, animals, and all other things in their own state.* 6. *He demonstrates that it is a mark of the highest power that God cannot deny Himself.* 7. *He explains why God is also called justice and describes its function.* 8. *Why God allows the Saints to be afflicted in this world.* 9. *From what source God is also named salvation and redemption.*

<margin>**§. 2.** *That God is called power, as its author and as the Almighty.*</margin>
We say, therefore, that God is Power because He possesses beforehand within Himself all power—and possesses it in a way that transcends power itself. He is the author of all power, bringing forth all things by an unshakeable and uncircumscribed power. He is the source of the very existence of power, whether universal or particular. He is "Infinitely-Powerful," <note>original: "infiniti-potens," a technical term Dionysius uses to describe power that is not just great, but fundamentally without limit.</note> not only by producing all power, but by existing above all power and above Power-itself <term>original: "per se potentiam" — Power as an abstract essence or Platonic form</term>. Furthermore, from His heights He can produce countless other infinite powers; these infinite powers, even if produced in infinite numbers, could never dull the exceedingly infinite effect of His power-making activity. 

His power is ineffable, unknowable, and unthinkable, transcending all things. Through its sheer abundance of strength, it makes even weakness powerful. It contains and penetrates even the outermost limits of existence, just as we see in things that strike our senses with great force: brilliant lights dazzle even dull eyes, and they say that massive noises can penetrate even the ears of those who are otherwise hard of hearing. For that which does not hear at all is no longer "hearing," nor is that which sees nothing at all "sight."

<margin>**§. 3.** *The omnipotence of God pervades all things.*</margin>
Therefore, this infinitely-powerful power of God passes into and proceeds through all things that exist. Nothing that exists is so completely stripped of strength that it does not possess some power; rather, everything has power, whether it be intellectual, rational, sensory, vital, or the power proper to its own substance. Even "being" itself, if... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page, establishing that even the basic fact of existence is a form of power derived from God.</note>

# CHAPTER IX.

## On Great, Small, Same, Other, Like, Unlike, Rest, Motion, and Equality.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*1. He states that God is called great, small, the same, other, etc., in the Scriptures. 2. He explains in what sense God is called Great. 3. In what sense Small. 4. In what sense Same. 5. In what sense Other, and how length, breadth, and depth are to be understood in God. 6. In what sense God is called Like, even though there is no proper likeness between causes and their effects. 7. In what sense He is called Unlike. 8. In what sense He is said to stand or sit. 9. In what sense He is said to move, and how a threefold motion applies to God. 10. In what sense He is called Equal.*

<margin>
§. 1. God is called Great, Small, Same, Other, etc., in the Scriptures.
</margin>
**S**ince, indeed, the terms "great" and "small" are also attributed to the Author of all things, as well as "same" and "other," "like" and "unlike," "rest" and "motion," let us also look upon these images of the Divine Names insofar as they are open to us. In the Scriptures, God is praised as Great, both in His actual magnitude and in the "thin breeze" <note>original: "aura tenui." He is also the Same, as in that passage of the 
<margin>
Psalm 101:28 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 102:27: "But you are the same, and your years will have no end."</note>
</margin>
Scriptures: *But thou art the same.* He is also called "Other" and "Diverse" when He is depicted by that same Scripture in many figures and forms. He is called "Like" as the Creator of similar things and of likeness itself; and "Unlike," as He is beyond all...

<margin>§. 2. In what sense God is called great.</margin>
Indeed, God is called **Great** according to the greatness proper to Himself, which communicates itself to all great things, and is poured out and expanded over every external greatness, encompassing every place, exceeding every number, leaping across every infinity, and according to His own "super-fullness" <note>original: "supraquam plenitudinem"</note> and magnificence, and His fountain-like distributions. This greatness is both infinite and devoid of quantity or number; and this is the excellence according to the absolute and "super-extended" effusion of a magnificence that cannot be grasped by the mind.

<margin>§. 3. In what sense God is called small.</margin>

Yet that "smallness" is also the elementary cause of all things; for you will never find any instance of smallness that does not participate in Him. Thus, "small" must be understood in God as moving, operating, and pervading all things and through all things without obstacle,

<margin>§. 4. In what sense God is called the Same.</margin>
The **Same** is He who is super-substantially <note>meaning existing in a way that exceeds all created being or "substance"</note> eternal, unchangeable, remaining always according to the same things in Himself, and existing in the same way, equally present to all. He is firmly and purely established by Himself and in Himself within the most beautiful boundaries of His super-essential <note>original: "supraessentialis"</note> identity. He is immutable, without fall, permanent, invariable, unmixed, immaterial, most simple, without need, not increasing, and not diminished. He is unbegotten <note>original: "ingenitum"; here meaning He was not created and has no beginning</note>—not in the sense of being "not yet made," or "imperfect," or "not made by this or that," nor as if He does not exist at all; but as being entirely unbegotten, absolutely unbegotten, always existing, and perfect in Himself. He is the "Same" according to Himself, uniformly defined by Himself and within the same form. He imparts this same identity to all those capable of receiving it; as the cause and abundance of identity, He coordinates different things with one another, and likewise holds within Himself even those things that are contrary to each other, according to the one and unique eminent cause of all identity.

<margin>§. 5. In what sense God is called Other.</margin>
He is called **Other**, however, because God is present to all things through His providence, and for the sake of the preservation of all things, He becomes "all things in all" <note>A reference to the biblical concept that God's power sustains every part of creation.</note>, while remaining within Himself and His own identity without departing <note>original: "inemananter"; a technical term meaning that God acts upon the world without ever leaving His own transcendent nature.</note>. Adhering to Himself according to one unceasing operation, He gives Himself through a certain unfailing power to be imprinted upon those who have turned toward the divine form. ### ON DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER IX.
-> <page-num>239</page-num> <-

...[al]terity <note>original: "alteritate"; likely continuing the discussion of God as "Other" from the previous page</note>, we must think that something different is signified than what is suggested by visible things. For just as if someone, while thinking about the soul, were to represent it in the manner of a bodily shape, and were to attach bodily parts to a thing that has no parts, we would understand the parts attributed to it in a different way, namely in a way that fits its **indivisibility** <term>individuitas: the quality of being a single, undivided spirit rather than a physical body made of pieces</term>. 

Thus, we would call the head **intelligence**, the neck **opinion** (as it is the middle ground between reason and irrationality), the chest **anger** <note>original: "iram"; in ancient psychology, this refers to the "spirited" or "irascible" faculty of the soul that deals with courage and willpower</note>, the belly **desire**, and finally the legs and feet **nature**, using the names of these parts as symbols for various faculties. 

In a much more powerful way, then, when speaking of Him who excels all things, that diversity of forms and figures must be described through certain sacred, God-befitting, and mystical explanations in an **anagogical** manner <note>original: "anagogice"; an interpretation that "leads upward" from the physical world to spiritual truths</note>.

<margin>What length, breadth, and depth are in God.</margin>

And if you wish to attribute the three-part figures of a body to God Himself—who cannot be touched or shaped—then **divine breadth** should be called the widest progression toward all things; **length** should be the power that expands over all things; and **depth** should be that secret inaccessible to all, and the ignorance of it <note>This refers to "divine unknowing," where God's depth is so great that it remains hidden even when He reveals Himself</note>. 

However, lest we deceive ourselves while we persist in explaining various figures and forms, by confusing the incorporeal names of divine things with the names of sensible signs, we have discussed these matters in our **Symbolic Theology** <note>Dionysius refers here to another of his works, now lost or possibly a conceptual reference, which dealt specifically with physical symbols used for God in the Bible</note>. 

But for now, let us consider **divine diversity**, so that we do not suspect it to be some kind of change in Him who is immutably the same, but rather a singular **multiplication** and simple **emanations** <term>emanationes: the "flowing out" of God's power and goodness into the created world</term> toward all things.
