<margin>In what sense God is called similar.</margin>
§. 6. If anyone calls God "Similar" in the sense that He is "the same," and that He is uniformly and **indivisibly** similar to Himself throughout His whole being, this divine name of "Similar" is not to be rejected. However, <term>theologians</term> <note>original: "Theologi"; in the context of Dionysius, this usually refers to the inspired authors of the Bible rather than later academic scholars</note> assert that God, who is above all things, is in His own essence similar to no one. Rather, they say He grants a divine likeness to those who turn toward Him, insofar as they imitate Him—who is beyond all definition and reason—to the best of their abilities. Indeed, this is the power of divine likeness: it draws all created things back toward their Author. Therefore, these created things should be called "similar" to God, as they are formed according to His image and likeness; but God should not be called "similar" to them. Just as a man is not said to be "similar" to his own portrait, so too with God and His creation. While things that are equal to one another can be said to be reciprocally similar <note>Meaning if A is like B, then B is like A; this applies to peers, but not to the relationship between a Creator and a creation</note>, and that likeness can be applied to both in a mutual way according to a shared form; 

<margin>There is no reciprocal likeness between a cause and its effects.</margin>
in the relationship of a Cause to its effects, we can by no means allow such a reciprocal relationship. For God does not merely grant similarity to this or that thing; He is the very cause of why all things that share in likeness are similar at all. He is the author of likeness itself. Everything in the world that is "similar" exists as such because of a certain **trace** <note>original: "vestigio"; a philosophical term suggesting that creation bears the "footprints" or marks of the Creator’s design</note> of divine likeness, and it is this likeness that completes their union with Him.

<margin>In what sense God is called dissimilar.</margin>
§. 7. But why is this said? For <term>Scripture</term> <note>original: "Scriptura"; the Holy Bible</note> itself also says that God is **dissimilar**, that He is beyond comparison to anyone else, that He is distinct from all things, and—what is even more wonderful—that "nothing is like Him." Yet, this is in no way a contradiction of His likeness. For the very same things are both similar and dissimilar to God: they are similar according to their possible **participation** <note>original: "participari"; the foundational idea that all things exist by "taking part" in God’s qualities, such as Life, Beauty, or Goodness</note> in Him, which they cannot fully...

<summary>This page explains that while creation is "like" God as a reflection of its Creator, God is "unlike" creation because He is the unique, non-reciprocal source of all existence. This paradox allows God to be described as both Similar and Dissimilar simultaneously.</summary>

§. 8.
**In what sense God is said to "stand" or "sit."**

What then shall we say of the divine "standing" or "seat"? What else, I ask, but that God remains within Himself, firmly fixed in the same immobile state, and is established with stability beyond any foundation? He acts according to the same principles, toward the same ends, and in the same manner; He is entirely unchangeable by His own nature, incapable of being moved, and is totally immobile in a way that transcends His very substance. For He Himself is the author of every state of "standing" and "sitting," existing as He does above all sitting and standing; in Him all things consist, while they are preserved unshaken in the state of their own goodness.

<margin>
§. 9.
**In what sense God is said to "move."**
</margin>
Furthermore, when the <term>theologians</term> <note>referring to the inspired authors of Holy Scripture</note> teach us again that He who is immobile "proceeds" and "moves" toward all things, must this not also be understood in a manner fitting for God? For we must piously believe that He moves—not according to physical transport, or change, or alteration, or turning, or movement from place to place—whether that movement be straight, circular, or a combination of both—nor by movement that is **intellectual** <note>original: "intellectilem"; referring to the movement of a mind or spirit</note>, or animal, or natural. Rather, He is said to move in the sense that God brings all things into the nature of reality and sustains them; He provides for all things in every way and is present to all, embracing all things in an incomprehensible way through all the paths and operations of His providence.

§. 10.
**In what sense God is said to be "equal."**
</margin>
If, however, anyone should find in the Holy Scriptures that God is named "the Same" or "the Just," and takes this to mean the divine name "Equal," we must explain that God is "Equal" not only because He is without parts and cannot deviate from the right path, but because He moves through all things and across all things equally. He is the very author of equality, by which He works similarly upon all things through their own interactions with one another. He grants a participation in Himself to those who share in Him equally, according to what each is capable of receiving, and distributes to all an equal portion according to each one's worthiness. He has also anticipated and united within Himself all equality—whether it be **intelligible** <note>accessible to the mind</note>, **intelligent** <note>possessing a mind</note>, **reasoning**, **sentient** <note>perceiving through senses</note>, **substantial**, **natural**, or **voluntary**—in a way that transcends them all and remains the source of every equality.

<margin>God the Almighty.</margin>
And He is indeed called **Almighty** <note>Latin: *omnitenens*, literally "the one who holds all things."</note> because He is the seat of all things, containing and embracing all, and establishing, grounding, and binding everything together. He renders the universe indissoluble within Himself and produces all things from Himself as if from an **all-holding** root. He turns all things back toward Himself as if to an all-containing foundation, holding them together as the all-encompassing seat of all things. He fortifies all things that are contained within a single, pre-eminent connection, not allowing them to fall away from Him, lest they perish as if a perfect house had been moved from its place. Furthermore, God is called Almighty because He holds all things under His dominion and presides over the things He governs without being mingled with them; and because He is desirable and lovable to all, imposing a voluntary yoke upon everyone, along with the sweet pangs of divine and all-encompassing love and His own indissoluble goodness.

<margin>§. 2. Why God is said to be the "Ancient of Days."</margin>
God is also praised for His **antiquity of days** <note>A reference to the vision in the Book of Daniel 7:9.</note> because He is the eternity and the time of all things, existing before days, before eternity <term>eternity: *aevum*, often used in medieval theology to describe the "age" or timeless state of angels and spiritual beings</term>, and before time. Indeed, He Himself should be called "Time," "Days," and "Seasonableness" <note>original: *tempestivitas*, meaning the right or opportune time</note> in a manner befitting God, as one who is immutable and immovable in every movement, yet always moving while remaining in Himself—the very author of eternity, time, and days. For this reason, in the sacred accounts of **mystical visions**, He is depicted as both "Ancient" and "New." The former signifies that He is the Ancient One who has existed from the beginning, while the latter signifies that He does not grow old; or rather, both terms declare that He proceeds from the beginning to the end through all things. Alternatively, as our **divine teacher** <note>Dionysius refers here to Hierotheus, his supposed mentor.</note> says, both terms indicate the divine antiquity: the "Old Man" represents that which is first in the order of time, while the "Young Man" (or the "New") represents that which is most excellent in number; for—

For those things which are commonly called "eternal," "incorruptible," "immortal," and "immutable," and which remain in the same state, are not completely and absolutely "unbegotten" <note>original: *ingenita*, meaning without a beginning or uncreated</note> and truly everlasting. An example is when the Scriptures say, *Lift up, O eternal gates* <note>original: *Elevamini portæ æternales*</note>, and other similar passages. Oftentimes the Scriptures even signify the most ancient things by the name of "eternity," as when they call the entire duration of our time "eternity," insofar as being ancient and immutable and measuring the whole state of things is the proper characteristic of eternity.

But they call "time" <note>original: *tempus*</note> that which measures coming-to-be <note>original: *generatio*</note>, corruption, and change, and that which exists in one way at one time and another way at another. And thus the Scripture teaches that we—who are here defined and circumscribed by time—shall attain eternity, when we have reached the eternity that does not perish, but always remains the same. Furthermore, in the Scriptures, a "temporal age" and "eternal time" are sometimes celebrated; although we know that, more properly speaking, things which truly *are* <note>meaning spiritual or permanent realities</note> are expressed through "the age," while things that *become* <note>meaning physical things that change and die</note> are expressed through "time." 

Therefore, one must not simply assume that those things called "eternal" are co-eternal with God, who exists before eternity; but rather, following the most venerable Scriptures without corruption, we ought to understand "eternal things" and "things in time" according to the ways they are used therein. Indeed, those things are counted as intermediate between the things that *are* and the things that *become*, which share partly in the age and par- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely continuing as "partly in time."</note>

Indeed, through participation in divine peace, the primary reconciling powers <note>likely referring to the highest ranks of the angelic hierarchy who mediate God's will</note> are joined both within themselves and with each other, and are united with the one primary peace of the entire world. <margin>What the unknown silence of God may be.</margin>
Regarding this divine peace and silence, which the holy Justus <note>Saint Justus; a teacher often cited by Dionysius as an authority, though his historical identity is debated by scholars</note> calls "voicelessness" <term>voicelessness: *insonantia*, a state where God is beyond the "sound" of human speech or rational concepts</term> and "immobility" in relation to every known emanation <term>emanation: the process by which God’s presence "flows out" into the created world</term>; what this actually is, how God rests and remains silent, how He exists in and within Himself, and how He is entirely with Himself in a state of "beyond-unity"—these are mysteries. In this state, He does not need to enter into Himself, nor does He abandon His unity when He multiplies Himself; rather, He goes out to all things while remaining entirely within Himself. Because of the excellence of this union which surpasses everything, it is neither lawful nor possible for any created being to describe or even conceive of it. 

However, while we cannot otherwise speak of this or grasp it through the intellect, we can still be drawn upward toward this divine peace, placed as it is beyond all things. Let us therefore consider those participations <note>the ways in which created things "share in" or reflect the qualities of God</note> in peace that can be understood and named—doing so as far as humans (and especially we, who are far inferior to many holy men) are able to achieve.

# ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER XI.

<margin>
§ 2.
*How God coordinates all things peacefully.*
</margin>
First, it must be stated that God Himself is the author of both "peace-in-itself" <note>peace as an abstract divine quality</note> and of all peace, whether universal or specific. It is He who mingles all things with one another in a way that allows them to join without being confused or losing their identity. In this joining, they cling together without being split or distanced, yet each individual thing remains pure within its own specific form. They are not disturbed by the blending of opposites, because nothing can interrupt that precise union and purity. Let us, therefore, contemplate the single and simple nature of this peaceful union, which binds all things to itself, to their own essences, and to each other. It preserves the universe through a certain embrace where all things are tempered together while remaining unmixed. 

Through this peace, the **divine minds** <note>original: *divinæ mentes*; Dionysius uses this term to refer to the angelic orders</note> are joined together; they are united both with their own thoughts and with the things they understand. From there, they ascend further to an unknown contact with those realities that transcend the mind entirely. Through this peace, **souls** connect their many different reasonings and are brought back to a certain spiritual purity. They proceed in their own proper way and order, moving through immaterial and undivided understanding toward a union that is higher than the intellect itself. Because of this peace, there exists a single, indissoluble connection of all things, established according to God's own harmony. Everything is fitted together in perfect concord and agreement; the universe is gathered together without confusion and held together without falling apart.

<margin>
*How divine peace reaches all things.*
</margin>
Indeed, the integrity of perfect peace reaches out to all existing things through its simplest and pure presence of unifying power. It joins all things together, connecting the furthest extremes to one another by means of the things in the middle, all according to a single, natural friendship <note>original: *amicitia*; in this context, it refers to the "cosmic sympathy" or the natural attraction and bond that holds the different levels of creation in their proper places</note>.

*How peace is maintained among so many and such contrary things.*

However, if the person speaking this way asserts that "diversity" and "distinction" are simply the specific property of each thing—since no thing, while it remains in its own state, wishes to lose its identity—we will not oppose him at all. Instead, we will state that this very desire to remain oneself is actually a desire for peace. For all things love to have peace with themselves and to be joined within their own being, and they desire that they and all they possess persist unmoved and unharmed. Indeed, that perfect peace is the preserver of the unmixed property <note>The unique, unblended characteristics of a species or individual</note> of each thing. Through its own peace-granting providences <note>original: *providentias*; acts of divine care and governance</note>, it guards all things—both in relation to themselves and in relation to others—without rebellion or confusion. It stabilizes all things with a steady power that never falters, anchoring them in their own internal peace and stability.

</margin>

<margin>§. 6. *How God is called "life itself," and the author of "life itself," etc.*</margin>

But because you have asked me elsewhere in a letter what I mean by <note>original: "per se esse, per se vitam, per se sapientiam"</note> **existence itself**, **life itself**, and **wisdom itself**; and because you say you have wondered why I sometimes call God "life itself," but at other times call Him the "provider of life itself," I have judged it necessary, O holy man of God, to free you from this doubt as far as I am able. 

And first, to repeat what has been said a thousand times, it is not contradictory to say that God is **power itself** and **life itself**, and also to say that God is the **creator of life itself**, or of peace, or of power. For God is called the latter based on created things—especially those primary things—as He is the cause of all things that exist. However, He is called the former because He exists <term>suprasubstantially</term> <note>This term refers to God's nature being "above" or "beyond" the essence of created things. It implies that God doesn't just "have" life, He is the very definition of it in a way that transcends our understanding.</note> above all things that are, even those that were created first. 

You ask, then, what exactly we mean by "existence itself," or "life itself," or any of those things that we describe as existing absolutely and primarily, which were first created by God. We respond that this is not a convoluted point, but a straightforward one that has a simple explanation. For we do not say that "existence itself" is some kind of divine or angelic substance <note>The author is refuting the idea that there are "intermediate" gods or beings between the Creator and the world, like the "Forms" in Platonic philosophy.</note> which acts as the cause for all other things to exist. For only He who is "beyond substance" is the principle, the essence, and the cause for all things to exist—including "existence itself." 

Nor do we propose that there is some other divinity that gives birth to life, other than that "life beyond divinity" which is the cause of all things that live, and even the cause of "life itself." To put it briefly, we do not suggest there are other primary causes or creators of things...

<summary>Dionysius clarifies a linguistic paradox: God is described as both "Life Itself" (his transcendent nature) and the "Creator of Life" (his action toward the world). He argues that these terms are not separate entities or minor gods, but different ways of understanding the same singular Source.</summary>

# ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER XI

<margin>
What "goodness itself" and "divinity itself" mean.
</margin>

...subsisting entities, which some people have rashly blurted out are the gods and creators of things. Neither those people nor their fathers or ancestors ever truly or properly knew these supposed gods, for they did not actually exist. On the contrary, when we speak of **existence itself**, **life itself**, and **divinity itself**, we are referring in a primary, divine, and causal sense to the one Principle and Cause of all things, who is <term>beyond-principle</term> <note>The author uses "beyond" prefixes to show that God is not just the first in a line, but of a completely different order of being.</note> and beyond any substance. 

However, we also use these terms to describe how God is shared in through His gifts. We speak of the <term>providences</term> <note>The acts of divine care and the outward reach of God into the created world.</note> that flow from God—who in His own essence cannot be shared or "participated" in—as being the very acts of "producing substance," "giving life," and "granting divinity." Those created things which share in these gifts according to their own capacity are, and are called, "substantial," "living," and "divine." The same logic applies to all other attributes. 

Therefore, that Good One is called the author of those first principles <note>Dionysius refers here to the "archetypes" or the highest forms of existence that God creates first.</note>; next, He is the author of those things which participate in those principles generally and universally; and finally, of those things which participate in them only in part. 

But why should we speak further of these things? For some of our divine teachers also give the name "goodness itself" and "divinity itself" to that which establishes goodness and divinity—calling it the "beyond-good" and "beyond-divine" source. They say this is a "good-making" and "god-making" gift that proceeds from God. They speak of **beauty itself**, a "beauty-making" outpouring, as well as universal beauty and particular beauty, and things that are beautiful as a whole or beautiful in part. 

All these terms, and any others used in this way, describe the providences and goodnesses shared by things in the natural world. These qualities flow and stream in a generous outpouring from God, who Himself remains beyond any such sharing, so that He who is the cause of all things might be perfectly beyond all things.

# CHAPTER XII

### On the Holy of Holies, King of Kings, Lord of Lords, God of Gods.

->CHAPTER SYNOPSIS<-

*1. Sets forth the outline of this chapter. 2. Explains what Holiness, Kingdom, Lordship, and Divinity mean. 3. In what sense these names are attributed to God. 4. In what sense God is also said to be the "Holy of Holies."*

<margin>**§ 1.** Outline of the chapter.</margin> Since those things which needed to be said on these matters have reached, I believe, a fitting conclusion, we must now praise the One who possesses infinite names as the **Holy of Holies**, as the **King of Kings**, as **reigning forever and beyond**, and as **Lord of Lords**, and **God of Gods**. First, therefore, we must explain what we understand "holiness itself" to be, what "kingdom" is, what "lordship" is, and what "divinity" is, and what the Scriptures intend to signify by the <note>original: "geminationem". This refers to the Hebrew and biblical habit of repeating a word to show its supreme degree, such as "Holy of Holies."</note> doubling of all these terms.

<margin>**§ 2.** What Holiness, Kingdom, Lordship, and Divinity are.</margin> **Holiness**, then (to speak according to our custom), is a purity free from every stain, entirely perfect and completely unblemished. **Kingdom** is the distribution of every boundary, world, law, and order. **Lordship** is not only a superiority over those of lesser rank, but also the complete possession of everything beautiful and good, as well as a true and unshakable stability; for this reason, "lordship" in Greek is derived from the name <term>kyrios</term> <note>original: "κῦριος". This Greek word means "Lord." Dionysius is connecting the word for "Lordship" (kyriotēs) to the root word for "authority," "power," or "validity" (kyros), suggesting that God's lordship is the source of all true stability and power.</note>...

Therefore, all these titles must be applied in an absolute sense to that <term>transcendental cause</term> <note>Dionysius uses "transcendental" to describe God as the source that exists far beyond the limits of the physical world and human logic.</note>. For from Him, in a singular and abundant way, has flowed and spread every pure perfection of all unmixed purity. From Him comes every arrangement and distinction of things—which wipes out discord, inequality, and disproportion—shaping and holding those who have been found worthy to participate in Him into a well-ordered oneness and righteousness. Indeed, He is the perfect possession of everything beautiful, and the entirety of divine providence, which watches over and preserves everything it cares for, kindly offering itself to shape a <gloss>divine nature</gloss> in those who turn toward Him.

<margin>§ 4. In what sense God is called "Holy of Holies," etc.</margin>
Because the Author of the universe is most full of all things, He is named the **Holy of Holies** according to one single excellence that stands above all else. This follows the same pattern as His other titles, based on His overflowing cause and exceptional pre-eminence. It is as if one were to say: just as holy, divine, lordly, or royal things are superior to things that are not, and just as the <term>participations</term> <note>original: "participationes". In this philosophy, "participations" are the divine qualities themselves (like Holiness or Beauty) as they flow out from God; they are considered "closer" to God and more real than the physical objects that receive them.</note> themselves are superior to those who participate in them, so much more is He sublime who is above all things.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### On the Perfect, and the One.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

1. *He teaches in what sense God is called "perfect."*
2. *In what sense He is called "one"; and at the same time shows that unity is found in all things.*
3. *That if unity is removed, all things perish, and that all things exist from the one God; and how God is to be praised as "one," and the Holy Trinity is the most eminent unity.*
4. *He provides the conclusion of the work.*

---

§ 1. <margin>In what sense God is called perfect.</margin> **A**nd so, let these things be said regarding this matter. But if it pleases you, let us move our discussion to the most important point: for Theology attributes everything, and indeed all things at once, to the Author of all things, praising Him both as "perfect" and as "one."

He is "perfect," therefore, not only because He is perfect in Himself, and uniformly defined by Himself through Himself, and most perfect as a whole according to His whole self; but also as being <term>supra-perfect</term> <note>original: "supraquam perfectus." This suggests a perfection that does not just meet a standard, but overflows and transcends the very concept of being "complete."</note>, according to His transcendence over all things. He defines every infinity, yet He is expanded beyond every limit, and is neither grasped nor contained by anything, but [reaches] to all things...

# ON THE DIVINE NAMES — CHAPTER XIII.

...reaching out equally and above all things with unfailing gifts and never-ending activities. He is likewise called **Perfect**, as one who receives no increase and is always perfect, nor can He be diminished. He possesses all things beforehand in Himself and overflows with one and the same unceasing, more-than-full, and undiminishable bounty, through which He makes all perfect things complete and fills each thing with its own appropriate perfection.

<margin>§ 2. In what sense He is called "One"—that is, without composition.</margin>
He is called **One** because He is all things uniquely according to the excellence of a single unity, and because He is the cause of all things without losing His own unity. Indeed, nothing is devoid of that "One." Just as every number participates in unity—and we speak of "one" pair, "one" decade <note>original: "denarius." Referring to a group of ten as a single unit.</note>, "one" half, "one" third, and "one" tenth—similarly, all things and every small part participate in the One. By the very fact that they are "one" thing, they are everything that they are.

<margin>Unity is found in all things.</margin>
But that "One," which is the cause of all things, is not one thing among many, but is that which exists before every "one" and every multitude, defining every "one" and every multitude. For a multitude is never without unity: those things that are many in their parts are one thing as a whole; those that are many in their <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentibus." In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities (like color or size) that a thing has, which do not change its fundamental nature.</note> are one thing in their subject; those that are many in number or powers are one thing in species; those that are many in species are one thing in genus; and those that are many in their <term>processions</term> <note>original: "processionibus." This refers to the "flowing out" of created things from the Divine Source.</note> are one thing in their principle. There is nothing in the nature of things that does not, in some way, participate in the One within that which is unique through all things, and which uniquely anticipated all things—even the entire universe and opposites. And indeed, without the One, there will not be...

# ON MYSTICAL THEOLOGY

## CHAPTER I.

### What the divine darkness is.

### CHAPTER SUMMARY.

*1. Having invoked the Most Holy Trinity, the author teaches that one must rise to mystical contemplation by abandoning ourselves and all things. 2. He shows how one must proceed in divine matters through affirmations and negations. 3. What the brief and the lengthy Theology are. Also, what the "darkness" is, and how one must enter it.*

---

<margin>§. 1. Invocation of the Most Holy Trinity.</margin>
**T**rinity beyond being, and beyond divinity, and beyond goodness <note>The author uses "beyond" (super/supra) to emphasize that God exceeds all human categories of "good" or "divine."</note>, Guardian of the Divine Wisdom of Christians: direct us to the mystical Oracles' summit—a peak that is beyond proof, beyond light, and the highest of all. There, the simple, absolute, and unchangeable mysteries of Theology are revealed within the darkness <note>original: *caligine*—this refers to the "Cloud of Unknowing," a state where the mind is dark because it is overwhelmed by God's light.</note> of a silence that teaches secrets; a darkness which, in its deepest gloom, shines more clearly than the brightest light. In a state where nothing can be touched or seen, this silence overfills the blinded minds of the soul with splendors of exceeding beauty.

<margin>Toward the mystical contemplation of ourselves</margin>
These, indeed, are my prayers. But you, dear Timothy, in your pursuit of mystical contemplations, through persistent practice, must leave behind the senses and the operations of the intellect. Leave behind all things that can be perceived by the senses and all things that can be understood by the mind, and <note>The text breaks off here as the author prepares to explain how to transcend the self to reach the Divine.</note>

<margin>How all things are to be affirmed and denied in God.</margin>
**§. 2.** See to it, however, that none of the uninitiated hear these things. By this I mean those who cling to natural things and imagine that nothing exists supernaturally beyond what they can perceive; indeed, they think they can know by their own human understanding Him who "made darkness His hiding place" <note>This is a reference to Psalm 18:11 (or 17:12 in the Vulgate). It suggests that God's "hiding place" is the very light that humans cannot see through.</note>. But if the teachings of these divine mysteries are beyond the grasp of such people, what can be said of those who are even more unrefined? These are the ones who describe the Supreme Cause of all things by using the lowest elements of nature. They claim He is no better than the godless, many-formed images they fashion for themselves. In reality, while it is necessary to establish all the affirmations <note>term: affirmation <gloss>also known as "cataphatic" theology; describing what God is (e.g., God is Good, God is Light)</gloss></note> of created beings in Him—since He is the cause of all—it is even more proper to deny <note>term: negation <gloss>also known as "apophatic" theology; describing what God is NOT to emphasize His transcendence (e.g., God is not a body, God is not finite)</gloss></note> all these things of Him, because He exists far beyond everything. We should not think that these negations contradict the affirmations; rather, we must realize that He who is much prior and superior to all loss or lack is Himself far above every removal and every position <note>The author argues that God is "above" both saying what He is and saying what He is not.</note>.

<header>ON MYSTICAL THEOLOGY — CHAPTER I.</header>

<margin>*Those who enter the divine darkness.*</margin>
...there is neither speech nor understanding, because He transcends all created things in a way that is beyond essence <term>beyond essence: *superessentialiter* — a key term in this theology suggesting God is not just "a being" but is the source of being itself, existing beyond the very category of "existence" as we understand it</term>. He is revealed truly and without coverings only to those who pass through all things that are impure and even those that are pure, and who transcend every ascent of all holy peaks, and leave behind all divine lights, sounds, and heavenly words, and are absorbed into the darkness where He truly is, who—as Scripture says—is beyond all things.

<margin>Exodus 19.</margin>
For it is not without reason that the divine Moses is first commanded to be purified himself, and then to be separated from those who have not been purified. After every purification, he hears the many-toned trumpets and sees many lights casting forth pure and many-sided rays. Afterward, he is separated from the crowd and, with the chosen priests, reaches the highest peak of the divine ascents.

<margin>Exodus 33.</margin>
But even then, he does not yet dwell with God Himself, nor does he see Him (for He is invisible), but only the place where He stood. I believe this signifies that the most divine and highest things that are seen and understood are certain underlying principles <note>original: *rationes* — here meaning the manifestations or conceptual "tracks" God leaves behind</note> that present to the mind those things that are subject to Him who surpasses all. Through these, His presence—which overcomes every thought of the mind—is made known, resting as if on the highest intellectual footsteps of His most holy places. Then, having been freed and released from both the things seen and the ones who see, he enters into the truly mystical darkness of unknowability <note>original: *incognoscibilitatis* — a state where God is known by not knowing Him through the intellect</note>. In this state, he excludes all intellectual grasp and remains in that which is completely intangible and invisible, belonging entirely to Him who is beyond all. He belongs to no one else, not even to himself, but is united with Him who is completely unknown...

## CHAPTER II.

### How it is necessary to be united, and to give praise to the Author of all, who is above all things.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*He desires to be introduced into the divine darkness, and to know God without concepts, which happens especially through the removal <note>original: ablationem — the act of "taking away" or negating</note> of all things that are not God, imitating sculptors who carve out a statue by the removal of material: and at the same time he shows that one proceeds through removals in a manner opposite to how one proceeds through assertions.*

<margin>
How removals <term>removals: *ablationes* — the process of "saying what God is not" (negative theology)</term> and assertions <term>assertions: *positiones* — the process of "saying what God is like" (affirmative theology)</term> are to be celebrated in God.
</margin>

After the entire ascent, it will become utterly silent and be joined completely to the Ineffable God.

<meta>This page concludes Chapter III and begins Chapter IV of "Mystical Theology." In the previous section, Dionysius explained that when we speak affirmatively about God, we start with the highest concepts (like "Goodness") and descend to the lowest. Here, he explains that when we speak negatively (the "way of negation"), we do the opposite: we start by negating the most physical, distant things and work our way up to negating even the highest intellectual concepts to reach the "Divine Darkness."</meta>

<page-num>267</page-num>
<header>ON MYSTICAL THEOLOGY — CHAPTER III.</header>

...do we begin the removal <note>original: *ablationem* — a technical term in "negative theology" referring to the process of stripping away concepts to better understand the incomprehensible nature of God.</note> from the outermost things? It is because, surely, when we were establishing that which is above all affirmation, we had to set the foundation of our affirming from that which is most closely related to Him. But when we negate that which is above all negation, we must begin by removing those things that are most distant from Him. Is God not more truly Life and Goodness than He is air or a stone? And is He not more truly "not-hungover" and "not-angry" than He is "not-spoken" or "not-understood"? <note>Dionysius argues it is easier and more "accurate" to say God isn't a rock than to say He isn't Wisdom, though ultimately both affirmations and negations fall short.</note>

# CHAPTER IV.

## That He who is the Author of every sensible thing according to His excellence is none of the sensible things themselves.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*He provides examples of negative theology and demonstrates how nothing perceptible to the senses is applicable to God.*

<margin>That God is nothing sensible.</margin>
**W**e say therefore, that the Cause of all things, which is above all things, is not without essence <term>essence: the fundamental nature or "beingness" of a thing</term>, nor without life, nor without reason, nor without mind; yet He is not a body, nor does He possess shape, nor form, nor quality, nor quantity, nor bulk. He is not in a place, nor is He seen, nor does He possess a touch perceptible to the senses. He does not perceive by the senses, nor does He fall under the category of things sensed. He does not admit of disorder, nor of the disturbance stirred up by material passions <note>original: *passiones* — in ancient philosophy, "passions" refer to being acted upon by external forces or emotions like rage and lust.</note>, nor is He weak or subject to the accidents of the senses. He does not exist in need of light, nor does He experience change, or corruption <note>original: *corruptio* — meaning decay or the state of falling apart</note>, or division, or any other thing that sensible objects are, or possess, or experience.

<summary>Dionysius explains that "negative theology" works by first stripping away physical, material traits from our concept of God before moving to intellectual ones. He begins a systematic list of physical attributes—such as weight, location, and sensory perception—that cannot be attributed to the Divine Cause.</summary>

## CHAPTER V.

->That He who is the Author of every intellectual thing according to His excellence is none of the intellectual things.<-

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

*He teaches that God is none of those things which we know; but rather, He is above all those things, whatever they may be and in whatever way they can be conceived by us or perceived by the intellect.*

He is not number, nor order, nor magnitude, nor smallness, nor equality, nor similarity, nor dissimilarity. He neither stands, nor moves, nor rests. He does not have power, nor is He power, nor light. He does not live, nor is He life. He is not substance <term>substance: "substantia," the underlying reality or "beingness" of a thing</term>, nor is He an age, nor time. ## LETTER I.
### To Gaius the Monk.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.

> *It teaches that the ignorance of God, which he commends in the book on "Mystical Theology" as being above all cognition, is to be understood not as a lack of knowledge, but as a superior state. At the same time, it shows that all the information we have about God through knowledge is received from created things.*

<margin>God cannot be comprehended by the intellect.</margin>
**D**arkness is removed by light, especially by abundant light; ignorance is removed by knowledge, especially by extensive knowledge. Taking these things in a superlative <note>In this context, "superlative" refers to the "Way of Eminence," where God is described as being "beyond" or "more than" a quality, rather than simply possessing it.</note> and not a privative <note>A "privative" sense would mean a simple lack or absence of knowledge, like being uneducated. Dionysius argues this "ignorance" is actually a higher form of contact with God.</note> sense, state more than truthfully that this "ignorance" concerning God is hidden from those who possess true light and the knowledge of things. Indeed, His "darkness"—which towers above all light—is concealed and hides all knowledge. And if anyone, having seen God, understands what he saw, he has not by any means seen God Himself, but rather something from those things of His which exist and are known. He Himself, however, remains consistently above the mind and substance <term>substance: from the Latin "substantia," referring here to the essential nature or being of a thing</term>; He exists above substance and is known above the mind through this very negation of knowledge and essence. And that ignorance—which is most perfect in a positive sense—is the true knowledge of Him who is above all things that fall within the scope of knowledge.

<summary>This letter introduces the concept of "Divine Darkness," explaining that true knowledge of God is reached by moving beyond human intellect and recognizing God's transcendence over all created things.</summary>

# LETTER II.
## To the same Gaius, a Monk.
### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.

*He explains in what sense God is said to be the "source-above-the-source" of divinity and goodness—specifically, the divinity and goodness that are shared with and created within us.*

<margin>God is the source of divinity and goodness.</margin>
**H**ow is He who is above all things also above the source <term>source: the Latin "principium" (and Greek "arche") refers to a starting point, origin, or governing principle</term> of divinity and above the source of goodness? This is true if you understand "divinity" and "goodness" to mean the very substance of the God-making and good-making gift, and that incomparable imitation of Him who is "beyond-God" <note>original: "supraquam Dei." Dionysius uses "beyond" (super/hyper) to show that God is not just the best version of a category, but entirely outside and above the category itself.</note> and "beyond-Good," through which we are divinized <term>divinized: the process of becoming like God or being "made divine" through His grace, often called "theosis" in Eastern Christian thought</term> and made good. For since this gift is the source of divinization and the making-good of those who are being divinized and made good, then He who is the "source-above-every-source" exists as superior even to what we call "divinity" and "goodness." Insofar as He is the source of divinity and the source of goodness, He is incomparable and incomprehensible; He stands far above all imitations and understandings, just as He excels those who imitate Him and participate in Him.

<header>LETTER III.</header>

Regarding Christ’s humanity, I believe the divine word intended to hint that He, who is <term>beyond-substance: Latin "suprasubstantialis," describing God as existing above the very category of "being" or "essence"</term> in His hidden state, came forth into our sight by becoming substantial <note>original: "substantiatum," meaning to take on a physical or real existence in the world</note> in a human way. Yet He remains hidden even after this manifestation; or, to speak more divinely, He is hidden *within* the manifestation itself. For this mystery of Jesus remains secret, and cannot be expressed by any speech or intellect; indeed, even while it is being spoken of, it remains a mystery; and while it is being understood, it remains unknown.

# LETTER IV.

## To the same Gaius, a Monk.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.

->*That Christ was both a true man and, at the same time, by a supernatural logic, the God-man who assumed human nature.*<-

<margin>Christ is a true man.</margin>
**H**ow, you ask, is Jesus—who is superior to all things—substantially joined with other men? In this context, He is not called "man" merely as the Author of humanity, but as one who is truly a man according to the entire substance of a human being. However, we do not define Jesus in a purely human way, for He is not only a man (since He would by no means be <term>beyond-substance</term> if He were only a man). Rather, He is truly a man who, out of a singular love for humanity, took on a substance <note>In this context, "substance" refers to the actual physical and spiritual reality of being human.</note> from the substance of men. He did this according to the nature of men, and yet in a way that is above men, for He existed above all substance even as He took substance upon Himself.

<margin>Christ is the God-man.</margin>
Nevertheless, He is filled beyond measure with <term>beyond-substance: the quality of being above all created categories of existence</term>, as one who is always above substance.

...through a certain abundance of <term>beyond-substance: Latin "suprasubstantialitas," describing a state of being that is more "real" or "higher" than the physical existence we understand</term>; even while coming truly to take on a substance, He was made substantial in a way that is above substance. He knows this very thing: that He exists in all things, both those perceived by the <term>senses: things we can see or touch</term> and those understood by the <term>intellect: things we can grasp with the mind</term>. As the <margin>Psalm 139:6 <note>The original cites Psalm 138, following the Vulgate numbering.</note></margin> Prophet declares: *Your knowledge has become wonderful to me; it is strengthened, and I cannot reach it.* In the same way, Saint Paul is said to have known God when he recognized that He exists above all knowledge and understanding. For this reason, Paul also asserts that <margin>Romans 11:33.</margin> His ways are unsearchable, His judgments are inscrutable, His gifts are unspeakable, and His <margin>Philippians 4:7.</margin> peace surpasses all understanding. Indeed, Paul had found Him who is above all things and had recognized Him who is the author of all things as being superior to all things, even beyond the reach of the mind.

## LETTER VI.

### To Sosipater, the Priest.

### SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.

->*He advises Sosipater that he should busy himself not so much with arguing against false opinions as with establishing the truth.*<-

**D**o not think this a victory, venerable Sosipater, that you attack a religion or an opinion which does not seem good. For it does not follow that because you correctly refute a wrong idea, Sosipater's own position is automatically proven right. It is possible that, amidst many false and apparent things, the one thing which is hidden and true may escape both you and others.

Since, by His command, the Sun and Moon—with a power and position that is marvelous—along with this whole universe, were reduced to a state of total immobility; and for the space of an entire day, all things stood still within the same signs <note>original: "signis"; referring to the signs of the Zodiac or astronomical positions</note> of the heavens.

Furthermore, another day was made almost three times longer in duration; for a full twenty hours, the universe—in an entirely equal space of time—went backward and returned by most wonderful retro-rotations in a contrary motion. 

Or, it may be said that the sun itself in its course, having contracted that five-fold motion <note>A reference to the complex planetary movements understood in ancient astronomy.</note> into ten hours, then by a retrograde step—entering a certain new path for another ten hours—retraced its way. This event certainly and rightly terrified the Babylonians and subdued them to <term>Hezekiah: the King of Judah who saw the shadow on the sundial move backward as a sign from God (Isaiah 38:8)</term> as if to one nearly equal to God or superior to ordinary men, without a single fight.

...they recall. Indeed, let him be permitted—whether through ignorance or a lack of scientific skill—to disparage faith in these accounts. For at that time, we were both present together at Heliopolis <note>A major city in ancient Egypt, its name means "City of the Sun." It was a center for astronomical study.</note> and standing there, we saw the moon coincide with the sun in a marvelous way. Yet, it was not the time for a natural conjunction <note>original: "conjunctionis"; in astronomy, this is when the moon is between the earth and the sun, usually occurring during a New Moon. The Crucifixion happened at Passover, during a Full Moon, when a natural eclipse is impossible.</note>. Then, we saw the moon supernaturally restored to a position diametrically opposite the sun starting around the ninth hour <note>Roughly 3:00 PM, the traditional hour of Jesus' death.</note> until evening. 

Furthermore, recall another detail to his memory: for he knows how we saw that meeting of the moon begin from the East and reach all the way to the edge of the sun, and then finally leap back. And again, we saw that the meeting and the withdrawal did not happen from the same side, but from opposite points of the diameter. These are the things which then happened entirely above the laws of nature; they could be performed only by Christ, the Creator of all things, who does great and stupendous things without number.

<margin>
Section 3.
He convicts Apollophanes by his own confession.
</margin>
Tell him these things, if it is right to do so. And you, Apollophanes, refute them if you can—and do so against me, who was present there with you, and who watched and observed all these things with wonder. Let this be enough for what we have said through this letter. You are able to supply whatever else is missing and lead this man perfectly to God. He is indeed wise in many matters, and perhaps he will not disdain to learn, with a meek and humble spirit, the truth of our Religion, which is a wisdom beyond all others.

# EPISTLE VIII.

## To Demophilus the Monk, concerning his proper duty and clemency.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER.

1. He shows that the foremost friends of God—Moses, David, Job, Abel, and Joseph—were famous for the praise of their gentleness; and that in Christ Himself, above all other virtues, clemency and gentleness shone most brightly. From this contrast, he reproaches Demophilus for his own cruelty, because he had treated a penitent who had been absolved by a Priest with such brutality, and had also wildly and rashly attacked the Priest for having absolved the penitent. He deters him with examples of those who had been punished for similar rashness.
2. He proposes an objection that Demophilus might likely make, and strikes it down.
3. He shows that it is by no means appropriate for inferiors, such as Demophilus was <note>As a monk, Demophilus occupied a lower rank in the ecclesiastical hierarchy than a priest or bishop.</note>, to rebuke their superiors.
4. He teaches that order and subordination must be maintained everywhere, and places before his eyes the example of Christ, the good and most gentle shepherd.
5. He says that Christ’s gentleness should be imitated rather than the zeal of Elijah <note>Referring to the prophet Elijah's calling down of fire, which the New Testament suggests is not the primary model for Christian conduct.</note>, and at the same time shows what the reward is for the gentle and for the cruel.
6. He confirms the entire matter with a wondrous vision of Saint Carpus, which he describes.

<margin>§. 1. Moses is commended for his gentleness.</margin>

**T**he histories of the Hebrews <note>Referring to the Old Testament scriptures.</note> hand down, noble Demophilus, that even that holy man Moses was judged worthy of the sight of God because of his great **gentleness**. And if they ever write that he was deprived of the divine vision, they do not show him being excluded by God until he had first turned away from gentleness. For they assert that God was angry with him when he acted somewhat arrogantly and resisted the divine counsels...

</margin>

...while I might say he seemed to trample upon and cast down from his position of authority? But you, O man, are so reckless in those matters which belong to the merciful and kind God, and which touch upon His own <term>Pontifical</term> <note>original: "Pontificium"; referring to the office of the High Priest or Bishop, who holds the supreme authority in the local church hierarchy.</note> institution. Indeed, these things would have to be said even if someone, while attempting things greater than his merits, seemed to bring forward something equitable; for even this is not lawful for anyone. 

For what absurd thing did <term>Uzziah</term> <note>original: "Ozias"; King of Judah who was struck with leprosy for trying to take over the priest's duty of burning incense (2 Chronicles 26).</note> do when he offered incense to God? What did Saul do while he sacrificed? What did the fierce demons do when they most truly proclaimed Jesus to be the Son of God? 

Truly, in <term>Theology</term> <note>original: "Theologia"; here meaning the sacred knowledge and the ordered arrangement of the Church’s divine service.</note>, everyone who looks upon matters not his own is to be cast out; instead, each person shall attend to the ministries of his own order. Only the <term>Pontiff</term> shall enter the <term>Holy of Holies</term> <note>original: "Sancta sanctorum"; the most sacred inner sanctuary.</note> once a year, and even then, only with all the <term>Pontifical</term> purity that the law prescribes. The Priests, for their part, cover the holy things, but the <term>Levites</term> <note>The lower order of ministers.</note> may not even touch the holy things, lest they die. 

The Lord was enraged with anger because of the rashness of Uzziah; and <term>Miriam</term> <note>original: "Maria"; referring to the sister of Moses, whose name is the same as Mary in Latin/Greek. She was struck with leprosy for challenging Moses's unique authority (Numbers 12).</note> became a leper because she tried to dictate the law to the Lawgiver. The demons leaped upon the sons of <term>Sceva</term> <note>Seven brothers who tried to perform an exorcism using the name of Jesus without being believers or authorized ministers (Acts 19).</note>. And He says: *I did not send them, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.* And: *The impious man who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who kills a dog.* 

To put it simply, the perfect justice of God does not tolerate those who violate the laws. To those who say, "In your name we have performed many miracles," He responds: *I do not know you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.* It is therefore a great sin—as the sacred <term>Oracles</term> <note>original: "Eloquia"; a common term in Dionysius for the Holy Scriptures.</note> testify—to perform even those things which are just if they are not done according to one’s dignity. Everyone must take heed to himself, that he does not think himself higher or deeper than he is, but instead focuses only on those things which have been assigned to him according to his merits.

<summary>Dionysius warns Demophilus that acting outside of one's assigned spiritual rank is a grave sin, citing biblical figures like Uzziah and Miriam who were punished for usurping the roles of their superiors.</summary>

Dionysius refutes this by arguing that hierarchy is not about personal merit alone, but about an ordered capacity to receive and transmit divine light.</meta>

<margin>
**§ 2.**
Romans 2:23.
*He presents Demophilus's objection and refutes it.*
</margin>
What then, you ask? Is it not necessary for Priests who are found to have acted either impiously or wrongly to be corrected? And shall it be permitted only to those boasting in the law to dishonor God by <term>breaking the law</term> <note>original: "praevaricationem legis"; literally a "straddling" of the law or a transgression by someone who should know better.</note>? And how are they the "interpreters" of God? For in what way can they announce divine virtues to the people when they are ignorant of the power of those very virtues? <margin>Acts 19:2.</margin> Or how will they illuminate others when they themselves are darkened? By what reasoning will they impart the Divine Spirit, they who have believed in the Holy Spirit neither in their inward affection nor in truth? 

To these things I myself will answer you: for Demophilus is not an enemy, nor will I allow you to be deceived by <term>Satan</term> <note>original: "satana"; meaning the Adversary who seeks to disrupt the divine order.</note>. For every order of those dwelling around God is more <term>God-like</term> <note>original: "deiformior"; a central Dionysian concept meaning to take on the form or likeness of God through participation in the hierarchy.</note> than the order which stands further away; likewise, those things which approach closer to the true light are at once brighter and more clear. I would not have you measure this "closeness" by physical distance, however, but by the capacity for receiving God. 

<margin>*Who is worthily a Priest.*</margin> 

If, therefore, the order of Priests possesses the power of <term>enlightening</term> <note>original: "illustrandi"; the second stage of the Dionysian path (Purification, Illumination, Perfection).</note>, then anyone who lacks this power of enlightening is utterly removed from the priestly order and its faculty; and much more so is he who has not even been enlightened himself. 

Indeed, such a person seems to me exceedingly reckless if he claims priestly duties for himself. He is restrained neither by fear nor shame from pursuing divine things beyond his <term>rank</term> <note>original: "dignitatem"; referring to one's assigned place in the sacred hierarchy.</note>, and he thinks those things are hidden from God of which he himself is conscious. He imagines he can deceive God, whom he calls "Father" with a false name; he even dares to pronounce his wicked blasphemies—for I would not call them prayers—over the <margin>Matthew 7.</margin> divine mysteries <term>after the manner of Christ</term> <note>original: "Christiformiter"; acting in the person or form of Christ during the liturgy.</note>. That man is not a Priest—he is not—but an enemy, a deceiver, a mocker of himself, and a wolf in sheep’s clothing armed against the Lord’s flock.

<summary>Dionysius argues that a priest who lacks spiritual light is not a true priest, but emphasizes that this does not give a subordinate the right to usurp that role. He defines "closeness" to God as a spiritual capacity rather than a physical location.</summary>

-> # LETTER VIII. <-

<margin>
§ 3. He shows how it is not appropriate for inferiors to rebuke superiors.
</margin>
But it is not lawful for Demophilus to correct these things. For if the divine word commands that **"what is just be pursued justly"** <note>original: "justa juste prosequi"; a reference to Deuteronomy 16:20.</note> (and to pursue justly is to give to each what is his own according to merit), then justice must be pursued by all, but not beyond one's own dignity or rank. For it is just that duties be assigned and defined for the <term>Angels</term> <note>original: "Angelis"; celestial messengers who occupy specific ranks in Dionysius's famous heavenly hierarchy.</note> according to their merits; yet this is not defined by us, O Demophilus, but through them to us from God, and to them from the higher Angels. And speaking simply, in all things, the first give to the second through the most right and equitable <term>providence</term> <note>original: "providentia"; God's governing care and foresight over the universe.</note> of all, so that just things are given to each according to their merits. Thus, it follows that those who have been ordained by God as the <term>Presides</term> <note>original: "Præsides"; leaders or those who preside, referring here to the higher clergy like bishops and priests.</note> of others should also distribute to their inferiors and subjects according to their merits. Therefore, let Demophilus set a limit to his speech, his fury, and his desire, as is fitting; let him not violate the order, but let higher reason dominate lower things.

<margin>
*An illustration by way of example.*
</margin>
For if, when we see in the marketplace a servant cursing his master, a youth an elder, or even a son his father, and also rushing forward to strike him, we feel that piety is being violated unless we run to help the superior, no matter how much they might have perhaps previously done wrong; why then are we not ashamed when we see reason being violated by anger and desire, and being cast down from the <term>dominion</term> <note>original: "principatu"; the leadership or sovereignty that reason should hold over the passions.</note> divinely entrusted to it? Why do we neglect this and stir up within ourselves an impious and unjust recklessness, sedition, and confusion?

<margin>
1 Timothy 3:5.
Titus 1.
</margin>
Rightly indeed does our divine <term>lawgiver</term> <note>original: "legifer"; referring to the Apostle Paul, whose instructions on the qualifications for clergy are cited in the margin.</note> forbid a man to be placed in charge of the **Church of God** who has not previously governed his own household well. For he who knows how to rule himself will also rule another; and he who rules another will also rule a house; and he who rules a house, also a city...

<summary>Dionysius argues that social and ecclesiastical order reflects a divine hierarchy where superiors must not be corrected by inferiors. He emphasizes that a person must first master their own passions and household before they are fit to lead or judge others in the Church.</summary>

Furthermore, regarding that cruelty toward the man (as you call him) who is impious and lost, I do not know with what tears I shall mourn the ruin of my most beloved one. You think that we appointed you as his servant; but unless you are indeed a worshiper of that Supreme Good, you must surely be a stranger to us and to all worship of our religion. You must seek another God and other priests, so that you may be carried away by madness rather than initiated among them, and become an implacable minister of the cruelty you love. As if we ourselves were perfectly holy and had no need of divine mercy!

Heaven was astonished at this, and I shuddered, and I can hardly believe myself. Let this be certain to you: if I had not read your own letter (which I wish I had never seen)...

<margin>*Gentleness should be imitated rather than the zeal of Elijah.*</margin>
<margin>2 Timothy 2:24.</margin>

Indeed, our most divine **Teacher** also instructs those who oppose God's doctrine with gentleness: for it is proper for the ignorant to be taught, not to be afflicted with punishments; just as we do not torment the blind, but rather lead them by the hand. You, however, stood in the way of a man who was beginning to breathe again in the light by striking him with a blow; and when he approached with the greatest modesty, you rashly repelled him—<margin>Luke 15:6.</margin> that man whom (and this is a thing worthy of horror) **Christ** calls back as he wanders and flees in the mountains, and having finally found him, lifts him onto His shoulders.

Please, let us not take such bad counsel for ourselves, nor drive the sword into our own hearts: since those who strive to violate others with injuries, or on the other hand to cherish them with benefits—even if they cannot do what they wished—nevertheless acquire for themselves either malice (according to their own purpose) or goodness, and so will be filled either with divine virtues or with fierce **passions** <note>original: "passionibus"; in this context, it refers to uncontrolled, destructive emotions or vices that dominate the soul.</note>. And those [the good] as followers and companions of the holy **Angels**, both in this life and the next, with all peace and freedom from all evils, will inherit that most blessed rest in the eternal age, and—what is the greatest of all goods—they will always be with God. But these [the wicked], who fall away from both divine and their own peace, will be with those cruel **demons** both here and after death. Therefore, we must take the greatest care to cling to the good God, and always be with the **Lord**, and not be separated with the wicked by the most just judgment of God, and undergo the due punishments from our own actions—which I fear most of all.

One ought to have prayed kindly to God for both of them: that by His saving help He might turn the one from error, and overcome the other with His goodness. One should not have stopped admonishing them throughout their whole lives until, at last, they might be brought to divine knowledge today or some other day; then, finally, the things that seemed ambiguous and obscure would become clear to them, and they would be compelled by the lawful truth to repent for the things they had rashly committed against reason.

Around midnight—the time he was accustomed to wake for divine hymns—he awoke and rose, having had a sleep that was far from quiet and frequently interrupted, and not without disturbance. <margin>Symbolic Theology presents absurd images to the unrefined.</margin>
**§. 1.** Holy Timothy, my excellent Titus, I do not know if he has failed to hear of the <term>Theological Symbols</term> <note>Dionysius's term for the physical metaphors used in the Bible to describe God.</note> passed down by me; for in the *Symbolic Theology* <note>A now-lost or perhaps theoretical work by Dionysius that explained biblical metaphors.</note> we distinctly explained to him all those things in the Divine Oracles <note>original: "Oraculi"; referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note> that seem miraculous and strange to most people. For those Fathers who hand down secret wisdom leave a heavy impression of absurdity on the minds of the unrefined, when they propose that divine, mystical truth—inaccessible to the profane—under certain bold and secret riddles. This is why, in the divine mysteries, we sometimes hardly believe the words themselves, as long as we only see them through the related physical symbols. But for those who possess love, these things must be looked upon as naked and pure in themselves: for by contemplating them in this way, we will venerate the source of life, seeing it poured out into itself and standing within itself—a single, simple power, moving of itself, acting of itself, never abandoning itself, but remaining the <term>notion of all notions</term> <note>The supreme Idea or Principle from which all other thoughts and things originate.</note>, and always contemplating itself through itself.

<margin>What various Symbols signify.</margin>
Therefore, we have judged, both for ourselves and for others, as far as possible, that we must explain the various forms of that sacred symbolic representation of God. For how full of unbelievable and fictitious monsters are its external appearances! For example, when it depicts the <term>supersubstantial</term> <note>original: "suprasubstantiali"; that which exists beyond the level of created "substance" or "being."</note> generation of God by describing a womb of God physically giving birth, or a human heart belching forth a "word" <note>A reference to Psalm 45:1, traditionally interpreted as the Father begetting the Son.</note> poured into the air, or a breath breathing from a mouth, or describing the God-bearing <note>original: "Deigenos"</note> bosoms...

<margin>Theology is twofold: namely mystical and philosophical.</margin>
...veiling it from the inexperienced; if anyone could look upon the beauty hidden within these things, they would find all to be mystical and divine, filled with abundant theological light. Nor should we think that the signs of visible forms were created only for their own sake, but rather that they are coverings for secret knowledge, hidden from the common crowd of men, so that the most holy things are not easily understood by the <term>profane</term> <note>In this context, "profane" refers to the uninitiated or those who treat sacred things with common irreverence, rather than simply "evil" people.</note>; but are revealed only to those who truly study holiness, who have freed themselves from all childish thinking regarding sacred <term>symbols</term> <note>Dionysius views symbols as "veils" that both hide and reveal truth simultaneously.</note>, and who, with a sharp mind and a faculty of intellect fit for contemplation, can attain the simple truth placed above the nature of the symbols. 

Furthermore, it must be noted that there is a twofold tradition of theologians: one secret and mystical, the other open and more manifest. The former is symbolic and belongs to the mysteries, while the latter is philosophical and <term>demonstrative</term> <note>Using logical proofs or arguments that can be explained clearly to others.</note>; and the secret is connected with the open. This [the philosophical] creates faith and binds the truth of what is said, while that [the mystical] acts within God and strengthens the soul in those teachings that are not publicly taught. 

And indeed, even in the most holy mysteries, the sacred teachers of both our discipline <note>Referring to the Christian Church.</note> and the <term>Mosaic discipline</term> <note>The Jewish tradition and the laws of Moses.</note> did not abstain from symbols suited to God; rather, we see the Angels, full of all holiness, mystically putting forth divine matters through <term>enigmas</term> <note>original: "ænigmata"; spiritual riddles or obscure hints that require meditation to solve.</note>, and Jesus speaking of divine things in parables, and handing down the deifying Sacraments through the symbolic arrangement of the table <note>A reference to the Eucharist or Last Supper.</note>. For it was fitting that not only should the Holy of Holies be kept undefiled from the common crowd, but that human life itself, which is at once undivided and divided, should receive light...

<summary>Dionysius explains that theology has two modes—one logical and one mystical—and that spiritual truths are intentionally hidden behind "veils" or symbols to protect them from the uninitiated while challenging the faithful to look deeper.</summary>

<margin>§ 2. *Symbols are to be explained in various ways.*</margin>

And they do this sometimes through apparent laws, and sometimes from hidden oracles, as fits the sacred subjects and the minds and souls of those involved: for every word set before them there contains not some meager history, but a life-giving perfection. Therefore, we too must set aside common opinion about these things and penetrate the sacred signs themselves with a sacred reason, as is fitting. We must not dishonor them, since they are natural and distinct likenesses of divine things, and clear images of secret and supernatural spectacles. ...[Divine Wisdom] offers, namely one solid and durable, the other liquid and flowing in a cup, which designate His beneficial providences. The cup, therefore, since it is round and open, is a **Symbol** <note>original: "Symbolum." A physical object used to represent a spiritual truth.</note> of universal **providence** <note>The way God cares for and governs the creation.</note>, which lacks beginning and end, and contains and penetrates all things. But because while it proceeds toward all things, it also remains within itself, formed by an immovable **identity** <note>original: "identitate." This refers to God's unchanging nature; even when He acts in the world, His essence does not change.</note> from which it never falls away, the cup likewise remains constantly unmoved. Moreover, **Wisdom** is said to build a house for herself, in which she sets out solid foods, and drinks, and a cup, so that it might be clear to all those who rightly bring divine offerings that He, whose providence it is, is the perfect cause for all things to both exist and to exist well. It shows that He reaches out to the universe and exists in all things and contains all things, and yet again that He, since He is excellently in Himself, is in no thing in any part, but is hidden from all things. He exists in Himself in the same eternal way, and persists and remains, and is always the same, and conducts Himself in the same manner. He never leaves Himself, nor leaves His seat and immovable dwelling place, or, as it were, His **hearth** <note>original: "larem." A Roman term for the household god or the protective spirit of the home; here it represents the central, stable 'home' of the Divine essence.</note>. Rather, in that dwelling He performs all the perfect gifts of His providence, proceeding to all things while remaining in Himself; always standing still and yet moving; and neither standing still nor moving; but as one might say, He possesses the actions of His providence within His perseverance, and His perseverance within His providence, both naturally and in a way that is above nature.

...proclaimed to provide. I believe, therefore, that this **solid food** signifies an intellectual and enduring perfection and **identity** <note>original: "identitatis." **Liquid food** <note>original: "Liquidum vero cibum."</note>, on the other hand, signifies that overflowing doctrine which, while it spreads through all things, simultaneously leads those it nourishes through various and manifold signs toward the simple and constant knowledge of God, by a goodness adapted to each person's capacity. 

For this reason, those divine and spiritual **Scriptures** <note>original: "Eloquia." This is because they have the power to give life and fertility, as in water; to lead toward growth, as in milk; to refresh, as in wine; and simultaneously to purify and preserve, as in honey. Divine Wisdom surely grants these to her followers, providing them with an abundance of overflowing and never-failing delights, even as she herself remains more than full. This is truly what it means to **feast** <note>original: "epulari." In mystical theology, the "banquet" or "feast" represents the soul's joyful consumption and contemplation of divine mysteries.</note>, and for this reason, Wisdom is celebrated as one who gives life, nourishes the young, and both renews and perfects them.

This is because of the utter fullness and the perfect, unspeakable immensity of the divine feasting—or, to speak more accurately, of God's "good habit" or state of being—which surpasses all human understanding. For just as the drunkenness we experience is taken in a negative sense as an immoderate overfilling, because of which...

<header>ST. DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE</header>

<margin>Section 6.
What is the sleep and waking of God.</margin>
I know well that you will certainly demand an explanation of that famous **sleep** and **waking** of God. We say that **divine sleep** <note>original: "somnum." Dionysius explains that when the Bible describes God as "sleeping," it refers to His hidden, transcendent nature that remains "unreachable" by the world He created.</note> is that which is hidden and incommunicable in God—the part of Him set apart from the things governed by His providence. On the other hand, His **waking** <note>original: "evigilationem." This refers to God's active "paying attention" or His intervention in human history.</note> is the attention of His providence toward those who stand in need of discipline or salvation. Once this is said, you will immediately move on to other theological symbols. Therefore, believing it unnecessary to repeat the same points about the same things (which might seem as if we are saying something else entirely), and being conscious that we have complied with your wishes as was right, we bring this letter to a close here; I believe we have fulfilled more than we owed to your correspondence. Furthermore, we are sending you our entire *Symbolic <term>Theology</term>*, <note>original: "Theologia." This refers to a specific (now lost) work by Dionysius that explained how physical objects in the Bible represent spiritual truths.</note> in which you will find the seven pillars <note>A reference to Proverbs 9:1: "Wisdom has built her house; she has set up its seven pillars."</note> explained alongside the house of wisdom, as well as its "solid food" divided into sacrifices and loaves. Moreover, you will find treated there more extensively what the "mixing of wine" signifies, as well as the "hangover" <note>original: "crapula." In this mystical context, it refers to the overwhelming "after-effect" of being filled with God's presence, rather than its usual negative meaning.</note> arising from **divine drunkenness**, and those very matters we just mentioned. For that work is, in my opinion, the best guide for discovering symbolic meanings in theology, and it is consistent with the sacred traditions and truths of the Holy Scriptures.

<header>LETTER X.</header>

->*Regarding liberation from exile, and the return to Asia, where by his own example he might benefit many.*<-

<margin>St. John the beloved disciple.</margin>
**I** salute your holy soul, O beloved one, for this is permitted to me more familiarly with you than with others. Greetings, O truly beloved, and exceedingly beloved to Him who is truly to be loved, desired, and cherished <note>original: "diligendus." Dionysius uses several Latin verbs for love—amandus, expetendus, diligendus—to emphasize the depth of devotion to Christ.</note>. What wonder is it if Christ speaks the truth, and the wicked expel His disciples from the cities? In doing so, they only bring upon themselves what they deserve, for the criminal inevitably separate and withdraw themselves from holy men.

<margin>The evil hate the upright.</margin>
Truly, the things which are seen are manifest images of the things which are not seen <note>This reflects a core idea in Dionysius's philosophy: the physical world acts as a mirror or "icon" of the spiritual reality that is normally hidden from human eyes.</note>. For in the ages to come, God will not be the cause of the just separations from Himself; rather, those who have utterly sequestered themselves from God will be the authors of their own distance. On the contrary, we already behold others here who are joined with God; because they love the truth, they distance themselves from every affection for material things. Being freed from all evils, and moved by a purely divine love, they pursue the peace and holiness of all good things. They taste in advance the first fruits of the future life in this present world, living among men in an Angelic manner <note>original: "Angelico more." To live in an "Angelic manner" meant to live a life of prayer and contemplation, being in the world but focused entirely on the divine, much like the angels.</note>, with all tranquility of mind, God’s blessing, goodness, and His other gifts.

Indeed, I am not so insane as to think that you suffer anything in your exile; rather, I believe you feel the sufferings of the body only to the extent that you perceive them through the physical senses. As for those who treat you with injuries and wrongly think they can blot out the sun of the Gospel, I rightly and deservedly rebuke them. I wish that they would abstain from those actions they commit against their own souls and be converted to the good; by drawing you to themselves, they might become sharers of the light. We, however...

<summary>In this letter, Dionysius consoles Saint John the Evangelist during his exile on Patmos, arguing that the wicked only harm themselves by persecuting the righteous. He describes the saintly life as a "taste" of the future heavenly life lived even while on earth.</summary>
<keywords>Saint John the Evangelist, exile, Patmos, persecution, spiritual vision, Angelic life, Gospel, divine love</keywords>

<page-num>304</page-num>
<header>ST. DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE</header>

world; nothing of this diverse <note>original: "diverso." In Dionysian philosophy, the "diverse" or "manifold" refers to the fragmented material world, which stands in contrast to the singular, unified light of divine truth.</note> world shall deprive us of the most brilliant ray of John. For the present, indeed, we shall enjoy the memory and the renewal of your most true Theology <note>In the early Church, "Theology" was a term often specifically applied to the Gospel of John because of its deep focus on the divine nature of the Word (the Logos).</note>; but a little while after (I might dare to say, though somewhat boldly), we shall be joined to you yourself.

Certainly, I am worthy of belief, since I both learn and report back those things foreknown to you by God: that you will surely be freed from the prison <term>ergastulum<gloss>A Roman term for a workhouse or private prison, highlighting the grueling nature of the Apostle's labor and confinement on Patmos.</gloss></term> of Patmos and will return to Asia, where you will provide examples of imitating the goodness of God, and leave those examples to those who come after.

->THE END.<-

<summary>In this concluding fragment of Letter X, Dionysius prophesies that Saint John will soon be released from his exile on Patmos and return to Asia to continue his work as a living example of divine imitation.</summary>
